question: A 24-year-old man comes to the emergency department because of an 8-hour history of abdominal pain, nausea, and vomiting. He takes no medications. He has a family history of pancreatitis and hyperlipidemia. His temperature is 37°C (98.6°F), pulse is 170/min, and blood pressure is 125/85 mm Hg. Abdominal examination shows mild distention and diffuse tenderness with no rebound tenderness; bowel sounds are decreased. Serum studies show a glucose concentration of 50 mg/dL, triglyceride concentration of 3500 mg/dL, and lipase concentration of 400 U/L (N=14-280); the serum appears milky. The most likely cause of this patient's condition is a deficiency of which of the following?
explanation: This patient has acute pancreatitis triggered by severe hypertriglyceridemia (>1000 mg/dL). In familial chylomicronemia syndrome (type I hyperlipoproteinemia), deficiency of lipoprotein lipase or its cofactor apoC-II prevents clearance of chylomicrons, leading to markedly elevated triglycerides, eruptive xanthomas, lipemia retinalis, and recurrent pancreatitis. Apo B-100 deficiency affects LDL transport; ApoE deficiency causes type III dysbetalipoproteinemia; hormone-sensitive lipase mobilizes triglycerides from adipose tissue and is unrelated to chylomicron clearance.
educational_objective: Severe hypertriglyceridemia can cause acute pancreatitis; lipoprotein lipase deficiency prevents chylomicron clearance, leading to triglyceride accumulation.

question: A 20-year-old man is brought to the physician by his mother because of bizarre behavior for 6 months. Although he had always been a good student, he failed all his classes at college last term. He no longer showers or shaves, and his appearance has become disheveled and unkempt. He appears distracted at the beginning of the interview and then begins talking nonstop to unseen people in the corner of the examining room. His mother looks upset and says, "It seems as if he's hearing voices all the time now. He's really scaring our family." Which of the following initial responses by the physician is most appropriate? better care of himself?" causing his behavior?" with now?" girlfriend when all of this started?"

options.A: "He needs to take a shower. Have you tried sitting down with him and talking to him about taking
options.B: "How frightening for you to see your son like this. Do you have any idea about what might be
options.C: "Was he under any unusual stress at home or at school or did he have any problems with a

explanation: This patient has psychosis (likely schizophrenia) and his mother is distressed. The most appropriate initial response uses empathy and open-ended questions to gather more information. Labeling the diagnosis prematurely, giving advice, or making assumptions is inappropriate at this stage.
educational_objective: In psychiatric interviews, initial responses should convey empathy and invite elaboration to build rapport and gather information.

question: A previously healthy 16-year-old girl is brought to the physician by her 18-year-old sister because of a 2- day history of a thick, yellow vaginal discharge and burning with urination. She does not want her parents to know that she is sexually active. Her temperature is 37°C (98.6°F), pulse is 70/min, and blood pressure is 110/70 mm Hg. Examination shows a mucopurulent discharge at the cervical os and friability of the cervix. The uterus is small, firm, and nontender. There are no adnexal masses or external vaginal lesions. A Gram stain of the discharge shows gram-negative diplococci in pairs and greater than 30 leukocytes/hpf. Urinalysis is within normal limits. Testing for Neisseria gonorrhoeae and Chlamydia trachomatis is ordered. Which of the following is the most appropriate course of action?

options.A: Obtain written consent from a parent before prescribing antibiotics
options.B: Obtain written consent from her sister before prescribing antibiotics
options.C: Prescribe antibiotics without notifying her parents

explanation: This adolescent has cervicitis due to Neisseria gonorrhoeae. In most US states, minors can consent to diagnosis and treatment of STIs without parental involvement. Delaying treatment risks complications.
educational_objective: In the US, minors can consent to STI care without parental notification; prompt treatment prevents complications.

question: A 65-year-old woman dies 6 months after the onset of severe headaches. Her brain as seen at autopsy is shown in the photograph. Which of the following is the most likely cell of origin of this neoplasm?
explanation: The most common primary malignant brain tumor in adults is glioblastoma multiforme, derived from astrocytes. Endothelial cells give rise to hemangioblastomas; melanocytes to melanomas; squamous epithelium to carcinomas.
educational_objective: Glioblastomas are aggressive astrocytomas presenting with headaches, seizures, and focal deficits.

question: A study is conducted to identify healthy women at risk for cardiovascular disease. Because atherosclerosis is an inflammatory process, the concentration of plasma C-reactive protein (CRP), a marker of inflammation, is measured. The plasma CRP concentration is increased in women who subsequently develop coronary artery disease. Which of the following is the most likely site of C-reactive protein biosynthesis?
explanation: CRP is an acute-phase reactant synthesized by the liver in response to IL-6 during inflammation. Bone marrow produces blood cells; the heart does not synthesize CRP; thymus is for T-cell maturation.
educational_objective: CRP is a liver-synthesized acute-phase reactant that rises in systemic inflammation.

question: A 56-year-old man is brought to the emergency department because he has had severe chest pain radiating to the back for the past 30 minutes. X-rays of the chest do not show widening of the aorta. Aortic angiography shows an extra lumen in the media of the proximal aorta. Which of the following is the most likely cause of this finding?
explanation: Aortic dissection (intimal tear creating a false lumen in the media) is most strongly associated with long-standing hypertension in older adults; this classically involves the proximal (ascending) aorta. Incorrect: Diabetes mellitus is a vascular risk factor but not a primary cause of dissection; Fibromuscular dysplasia affects medium-sized arteries (e.g., renal), not the aorta; Syphilis causes vasa vasorum endarteritis leading to thoracic aortic aneurysm with root dilation, not an acute dissection per se.
educational_objective: Hypertension is the major risk factor for proximal aortic dissection in older adults.

question: A 51-year-old man develops diaphoresis, tachycardia, and a blood pressure of 155/100 mm Hg 24 hours after undergoing an abdominal operation. Two hours later, he has a generalized tonic-clonic seizure. Which of the following is most likely responsible for these adverse effects in this patient?
explanation: Alcohol withdrawal typically begins within 6–24 hours after cessation with autonomic hyperactivity (anxiety, tremor, diaphoresis, tachycardia, hypertension) and can progress to seizures in 6–48 hours. Incorrect: Acute renal failure and sepsis would not predictably cause early seizures; Anaphylaxis presents with hypotension, bronchospasm, and urticaria, not delayed seizures.
educational_objective: Early alcohol withdrawal (6–48 h) causes autonomic hyperactivity and can lead to generalized seizures.

question: A 60-year-old man has a round, semitransparent nodule on his nose. Examination of tissue obtained on biopsy shows small basophilic cells forming tumor islands surrounded by clear spaces and extending across the basement membrane. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation: Pearly, translucent papule on sun-exposed skin with basaloid cells forming palisading nests/islands; extension across the basement membrane confirms invasion. Incorrect: Actinic keratosis is premalignant scaly plaque; Compound nevus shows nests of benign nevus cells; Melanoma shows atypical melanocytes with pagetoid spread; Seborrheic keratosis shows well-demarcated "stuck-on" lesions with pseudocysts.
educational_objective: Pearly nodules on sun-exposed skin with basaloid nests and peripheral palisading are characteristic of basal cell carcinoma.

question: A 6-month-old girl is brought to the emergency department by her parents because of vomiting for 6 hours. She has been feeding poorly for 1 day because of an upper respiratory tract infection. Her temperature is 37°C (98.6°F), pulse is 100/min, respirations are 13/min, and blood pressure is 88/58 mm Hg. Physical examination shows lethargy and a clear nasal discharge. Laboratory studies show: Serum: Ammonia increased Citrulline decreased Glutamine increased Urine: Orotic acid increased This patient most likely has a deficiency of which of the following enzyme activities?
explanation: OTC deficiency (X-linked) causes hyperammonemia with low citrulline and elevated orotic acid from carbamoyl phosphate shunting into pyrimidine synthesis. Incorrect: Arginase deficiency affects urea nitrogen excretion with ↑ arginine; Argininosuccinate synthetase deficiency (citrullinemia) features ↑ citrulline; Argininosuccinase deficiency (ASA lyase) leads to ↑ argininosuccinate.
educational_objective: Hyperammonemia with ↓ citrulline and ↑ urinary orotic acid is diagnostic of ornithine transcarbamylase deficiency.

question: A physician is assigned to a search and rescue team attempting to locate and recover the victim of a light plane crash with only the pilot onboard. The plane crashed in a remote mountainous region of Alaska and has been missing for more than 2 weeks. A search helicopter detected what was believed to be a signal from the area of the downed plane and has picked up the pilot. The pilot has only minor injuries but has complications of exposure and has lost a considerable amount of weight. While the pilot was able to locate a good water supply, he had no food during his period of isolation. The pilot most likely has which of the following conditions at this time?
explanation: Prolonged fasting leads to muscle proteolysis and net protein catabolism with urinary nitrogen loss—i.e., negative nitrogen balance. Incorrect: Positive nitrogen balance occurs with growth, pregnancy, or anabolic states; "Increased/decreased nitrogen retention" are nonspecific and do not capture the net catabolic state described.
educational_objective: Prolonged starvation produces negative nitrogen balance due to net protein catabolism.

question: A 62-year-old woman comes to the physician because of a 3-year history of a mild cough that has produced purulent sputum for the past 7 weeks. She has smoked 2 packs of cigarettes daily for the past 42 years. She drinks 3 to 6 beers daily. Findings on physical examination show swelling of the metatarsals, metacarpals, and proximal phalanges. X-rays of the affected bones show new bone formation. There is also arthritis of adjacent joints and clubbing of the digits. Which of the following is the most likely underlying disease?
explanation: Hypertrophic osteoarthropathy (clubbing, periostosis/new bone formation, arthralgias) is a paraneoplastic phenomenon most classically associated with lung cancer. Incorrect: Cyanotic congenital heart disease can cause clubbing but typically without periostosis in older adults; Interstitial fibrosis and RA can cause clubbing but less characteristic of the full HO syndrome; Ankylosing spondylitis and systemic sclerosis are not typical causes of HO.
educational_objective: Hypertrophic osteoarthropathy with clubbing and periostosis is most strongly linked to bronchogenic carcinoma.

question: A 28-year-old woman at 37 weeks' gestation comes to the physician because of a 4-day history of fever and back pain. She says that during this time she also has been crying frequently. Her temperature is 38°C (100.4°F). Physical examination shows costovertebral angle tenderness. The photomicrograph shown represents her disease. Which of the following mechanisms is the most likely cause?
explanation: Third-trimester pregnancy predisposes to acute pyelonephritis due to urinary stasis from extrinsic ureteral compression and progesterone-mediated smooth muscle relaxation; biopsy would show neutrophilic infiltration with intratubular neutrophil casts. Incorrect: Chorioamnionitis/endometritis involve uterine/placental infection; Glomerulonephritis causes hematuria/proteinuria without CVA tenderness; PID is ascending infection of the upper genital tract, not kidneys.
educational_objective: Pregnancy causes urinary stasis and vesicoureteral reflux leading to pyelonephritis—an obstructive uropathy mechanism.

question: A 45-year-old man is undergoing a surgical procedure. Which of the following maneuvers by the anesthesiologist would result in an increase in intracranial pressure?
explanation: Cerebral blood flow (and ICP) increase with hypercapnia. Decreasing RR raises PaCO₂ → cerebral vasodilation → ↑ ICP. Incorrect: Increasing RR lowers PaCO₂ and reduces ICP; Changes in FiO₂ minimally affect ICP unless profound hypoxemia occurs; Lower airway pressures reduce intrathoracic and venous pressures, tending to lower ICP.
educational_objective: Hypoventilation (↑ PaCO₂) causes cerebral vasodilation and elevates intracranial pressure.

question: A 45-year-old man comes to the office for counseling prior to a bariatric operation for weight loss. He was recently diagnosed as prediabetic. He is 170 cm (5 ft 7 in) tall and weighs 116 kg (256 lb); BMI is 40 kg/m². Physical examination shows no other abnormalities. In addition to recommending that the patient follow a balanced diet postoperatively, it is most appropriate for the patient to avoid ingesting excessive amounts of which of the following?
explanation: This presentation is classic for hypersensitivity pneumonitis ("bird fancier's lung") caused by inhaled avian proteins, producing a lymphocytic interstitial pneumonitis with noncaseating granulomas and reticulonodular changes. Incorrect: Dust exposure at a library can irritate airways but does not typically cause granulomatous hypersensitivity pneumonitis; Diet and wool exposure are not implicated here.
educational_objective: Chronic antigen exposure to bird proteins can cause hypersensitivity pneumonitis with interstitial lymphocytic infiltrates and granulomas.

question: A 47-year-old woman comes to the physician because of a 6-month history of increasingly severe cough and shortness of breath. She has had no fever, chills, or muscle aches. She does not smoke. She works as a librarian and is often exposed to dusty books. She lives alone with four parakeets. She became a vegetarian 2 years ago. She is an avid knitter and can spin her own wool. Crackles are heard in the lower lung fields. Laboratory studies show an erythrocyte sedimentation rate of 40 mm/h. A chest x-ray shows areas of reticulogranular changes. Examination of a biopsy specimen of the lung shows interstitial infiltrates of lymphocytes and granulomas. Which of the following is the most likely cause of this patient's condition?
explanation: Bird fancier's lung (hypersensitivity pneumonitis) is triggered by inhaled avian proteins, leading to interstitial lymphocytic infiltrates and noncaseating granulomas with reticulonodular/reticulogranular changes and crackles. Incorrect: Library dust exposure usually causes irritant symptoms without granulomatous interstitial disease; diet (soy) and wool exposure are not typical causes of granulomatous hypersensitivity pneumonitis.
educational_objective: Chronic exposure to bird antigens can cause hypersensitivity pneumonitis with interstitial lymphocytic inflammation and granulomas.

question: A 23-year-old woman sustains significant blood loss in a motor vehicle collision. She is given 3 units of blood and has an uneventful recovery. Four weeks later, she becomes jaundiced. She is afebrile. Laboratory evaluation shows anemia and reticulocytosis; there is no evidence of infection. Which of the following additional studies is likely to be most useful in establishing the diagnosis?
explanation: Delayed hemolytic transfusion reaction (extravascular hemolysis) arises weeks after transfusion due to an anamnestic alloantibody response; a direct antiglobulin (Coombs) test is typically positive. Incorrect: Electrophoresis evaluates hemoglobinopathies; bilirubin fractionation and iron studies don't establish immune hemolysis; EPO level is not diagnostic.
educational_objective: Delayed hemolytic transfusion reactions present weeks later with anemia/jaundice and a positive direct Coombs test.

question: A 14-year-old girl is brought to the physician because of a 1-month history of migraine-like headaches, vomiting, and multiple left-sided focal seizures. She has had hearing loss since the age of 11 years. Her mother and maternal grandmother have high-tone deafness. Physical examination shows loss of vision in one half of the visual field of the right eye and weakness of the right upper and lower extremities. Serum and cerebrospinal fluid concentrations of lactic acid are increased. This patient most likely has a mutation of which of the following?
explanation: MELAS (mitochondrial encephalomyopathy with lactic acidosis and stroke-like episodes) with maternal inheritance and sensorineural hearing loss is classically due to mutations in mitochondrial tRNA (often tRNA^Leu). Incorrect: ER glycosylation, lysosomal enzymes (e.g., Pompe), and peroxisomal enzymes (e.g., catalase) are not causes of MELAS.
educational_objective: MELAS is maternally inherited and commonly involves mutations in mitochondrial tRNA genes (e.g., tRNA^Leu).

question: A 32-year-old woman has had fecal incontinence since giving birth to her first child 1 year ago. Which of the following is the most likely cause of the fecal incontinence in this patient?

options.B: Increased pressure of the anal sphincter

explanation: Obstetric anal sphincter injury (external anal sphincter and/or pudendal nerve) during vaginal delivery is a common cause of postpartum fecal incontinence. Incorrect: Achalasia and spasticity would increase outlet resistance; increased sphincter pressure would not cause incontinence.
educational_objective: Postpartum fecal incontinence commonly results from obstetric damage to the anal sphincter and/or pudendal nerve.

question: A 17-year-old girl comes to the emergency department because of a swollen tender ankle. An x-ray of the ankle is strongly suggestive of osteosarcoma. She and her parents are told only that "further evaluation is needed." Which of the following next steps is most appropriate?

options.A: Request the presence of the hospital chaplain, then discuss the findings
options.B: Speak with the parents alone about the findings
options.C: Speak with the patient and her parents about the findings

explanation: For a minor with serious findings, disclose information to the patient and parents together when possible, engaging the adolescent in developmentally appropriate discussion and shared decision-making. Incorrect: Excluding the patient undermines autonomy; chaplain involvement is optional and not a prerequisite; immediate subspecialist involvement is not required to disclose test results.
educational_objective: In minors, discuss significant findings with both the patient and parents, involving the adolescent in decisions.

question: An otherwise healthy 16-year-old girl comes to the physician because of a 2-month history of episodes of wheezing and shortness of breath while participating in track meets with her high school team. Her respirations are 12/min. Physical examination shows no abnormalities. A diagnosis of exercise-induced asthma is made. Exposure to which of the following is most likely to precipitate a similar episode in this patient in the future?
explanation: Exercise-induced bronchoconstriction is commonly precipitated by hyperventilation of cold, dry air, which increases airway water loss and cooling, provoking bronchospasm. Incorrect: Warm or moist air is less likely to trigger bronchospasm.
educational_objective: Cold, dry air commonly triggers exercise-induced asthma by promoting airway cooling and water loss.

question: A study is conducted to assess the effect of a new screening test on the mortality rate of prostate cancer. Prior to implementation of screening, the overall 5-year survival rate was 70%. After initiating the screening in the randomly selected study population, the 5-year survival rate increases to 85%. During this time, there were no changes in the treatment of prostate cancer. The apparent decrease in mortality could be due to which of the following types of bias?
explanation: Screening detects disease earlier, artificially inflating measured survival time from diagnosis without truly prolonging life—classic lead-time bias. Incorrect: Compliance bias concerns differences between adherent vs nonadherent participants; recall bias pertains to self-reported exposures.
educational_objective: Earlier detection can falsely increase apparent survival time (lead-time bias) without reducing mortality.

question: A new antiplatelet agent is developed for the prevention of recurrence of stroke. In a large randomized clinical trial with equal numbers of men and women, the rates of stroke are lower in patients receiving the new agent than in patients receiving the standard treatment. Results are shown: Recurrent Stroke Rates per 1000 Person-Years Standard Treatment: Women 12, Men 24, Overall 18 New Antiplatelet Drug: Women 4, Men 8, Overall 6 Based on the results, which of the following is the absolute risk reduction in women?
explanation: Absolute risk reduction is the absolute difference in event rates: 12 − 4 = 8 units. (Given the table uses "per 1000 person-years," this corresponds to 8 per 1000 PY, i.e., 0.8%; among the provided percentage options, 8% matches the absolute difference numerically.) Incorrect: Other options reflect relative reductions (e.g., ~67% is RRR), not the absolute difference.
educational_objective: ARR equals the absolute difference in event rates between control and treatment groups.

question: A previously healthy 32-year-old woman is brought to the emergency department because of a 2-hour history of severe epigastric pain, nausea, and vomiting blood. Her temperature is 36°C (96.8°F), pulse is 125/min, respirations are 18/min, and blood pressure is 85/45 mm Hg. Physical examination shows cool skin and a tender abdomen. A decrease in which of the following hemodynamic parameters is the most likely cause of this patient's hypotension?
explanation: Hypotension results when cardiac output falls (CO = HR × SV); in acute hemorrhage, reduced effective stroke volume leads to hypotension. Among listed determinants of arterial pressure, a drop in contractility directly lowers stroke volume and CO, causing hypotension. Incorrect: HR is increased (tachycardic compensation), LV compliance is not the primary issue, and systemic vascular resistance typically increases via sympathetic vasoconstriction.
educational_objective: Decreases in cardiac output (e.g., via reduced contractility) lower arterial pressure; in hemorrhagic states, CO reduction is the proximate cause of hypotension.

question: A 31-year-old man has a large, yellow, soft mass deeply infiltrating the gluteus maximus muscle. Microscopic examination of the excised mass shows irregular vacuolated cells and clear cells with frequent mitoses. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation: A deeply infiltrating soft-tissue malignant tumor with frequent mitoses in skeletal muscle is most consistent with rhabdomyosarcoma (malignant skeletal muscle tumor). Incorrect: Lipoma and fibroma are benign (no frequent mitoses, noninfiltrative); fibrosarcoma is a spindle-cell tumor without vacuolated/clear cells typical of lipogenic differentiation; rhabdomyoma is benign.
educational_objective: Malignant soft-tissue tumors arising in skeletal muscle with infiltrative growth and high mitotic activity are rhabdomyosarcomas.

question: A 10-year-old boy with mild mental retardation is brought to the physician by his parents because of a 2- week history of frequent staring spells. Examination of the skin shows pale oval-shaped areas on the trunk. A CT scan of the head without contrast shows multiple calcified subependymal and cortical lesions. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation: Hypopigmented "ash-leaf" macules with cortical and subependymal tubers (calcified) and seizures/intellectual disability are characteristic of tuberous sclerosis complex. Incorrect: Cysticercosis shows cystic brain lesions; hyperparathyroidism does not cause these findings; metachromatic leukodystrophy causes demyelination without these cutaneous or calcified tuber features.
educational_objective: Ash-leaf spots with calcified cortical/subependymal tubers and seizures indicate tuberous sclerosis.

question: A 57-year-old man has a hemoglobin concentration of 18.5 g/dL. A peripheral blood smear is shown. These findings are most consistent with which of the following disorders?
explanation: Elevated hemoglobin suggests secondary polycythemia from chronic hypoxemia (e.g., COPD). Incorrect: Myelofibrosis (agnogenic myeloid metaplasia) and myelodysplasia typically cause cytopenias and abnormal cells rather than isolated erythrocytosis; hemochromatosis causes iron overload, not polycythemia.

question: A 19-year-old man who is a college student is brought to the emergency department because of the sudden onset of right-sided chest pain and difficulty breathing after an accident in which he was thrown from his bicycle. He has difficulty walking and cannot climb stairs because of pain and shortness of breath. He is slightly cyanotic, afebrile, and tachypneic. Which of the following is most suggestive that fractured ribs caused the respiratory problem?
explanation: Rib fractures predispose to pneumothorax or hydropneumothorax. A succussion splash (splashing sound over the chest with movement) suggests air–fluid levels in the pleural space, consistent with traumatic rib fracture complications. Incorrect: Bronchophony indicates consolidation; stridor (inspiratory/expiratory) points to upper airway obstruction.
educational_objective: A chest succussion splash indicates hydropneumothorax, a complication of rib fractures causing respiratory distress.

question: A 66-year-old man is brought to the emergency department 30 minutes after sustaining injuries in a motor vehicle collision. He is pronounced dead on arrival. A photograph of the left kidney and a photomicrograph of a section of the distal left ureter taken at autopsy are shown. Examination of the right kidney and ureter shows no abnormalities. Which of the following was the most likely predisposing factor in the development of the ureteral lesion in this patient?
explanation: Urothelial (transitional cell) carcinomas of the renal pelvis, ureter, and bladder are strongly associated with smoking (major risk), which exposes urothelium to carcinogens in urine. Incorrect: Aromatic amines (aniline dyes) are risk factors but less common; Schistosoma haematobium predisposes to squamous cell carcinoma of the bladder; vinyl chloride causes hepatic angiosarcoma; alcoholism is not a risk for urothelial cancer.
educational_objective: Smoking is the leading risk factor for urothelial carcinoma anywhere along the collecting system, including the ureter.

question: A 70-year-old woman is transferred to a rehabilitative service 2 days after operative repair of a fracture of the right femur. She weighs 65 kg (143 lb). Findings on physical and mental status examinations are unremarkable. Which of the following is the most important predictor of success in the rehabilitation of this patient?
explanation: Pre-injury functional/fitness status is the strongest predictor of rehab outcomes after hip/femur fracture. Incorrect: Age, hemoglobin, or vitamin D levels are less predictive of functional recovery than baseline activity level.
educational_objective: Baseline functional status best predicts rehabilitation success following major orthopedic injury.

question: A sedentary 50-year-old man with hypertension comes to the physician because of a 6-week history of depression, anxiety, difficulty sleeping, fatigue, decreased appetite, and poor memory and concentration. He had an anterior wall myocardial infarction 3 months ago. He has one glass of wine each evening. He is 165 cm (5 ft 5 in) tall and weighs 61 kg (148 lb); BMI is 22 kg/m². His pulse is 104/min, respirations are 16/min, and blood pressure is 117/89 mm Hg. His ECG is unchanged from his last appointment. Laboratory studies show a hemoglobin concentration of 13.8 g/dL and serum LDL-cholesterol concentration of 127 mg/dL; serum LDL-cholesterol concentration was 117 mg/dL at his last visit. Which of the following is most likely to decrease this patient's risk for mortality over the next 2 years?

options.A: Diet high in omega-3 fatty acids

explanation: Omega-3 fatty acids (e.g., from fish oil) have evidence for reducing post-MI sudden cardiac death/arrhythmic events and overall cardiac mortality. Incorrect: Abstaining from a single small daily drink has no mortality benefit; weight loss without obesity doesn't reduce near-term post-MI mortality; anxiolytics improve symptoms but not survival.
educational_objective: Increasing omega-3 fatty acid intake after MI can reduce cardiac mortality, particularly arrhythmic death.

question: A 43-year-old woman, gravida 7, para 1, at 10 weeks' gestation comes to the physician for an initial prenatal visit. Physical examination shows a uterus consistent in size with a 10-week gestation. This patient is at increased risk for a child with Down syndrome if she has which of the following sets of ultrasound and serum findings? chorionic gonadotropin chorionic gonadotropin chorionic gonadotropin human chorionic gonadotropin chorionic gonadotropin chorionic gonadotropin

options.A: Increased nuchal translucency, decreased pregnancy-associated plasma protein, increased human
options.B: Increased nuchal translucency, increased pregnancy-associated plasma protein, decreased human
options.C: Decreased nuchal translucency, increased pregnancy-associated plasma protein, increased human
options.D: Normal nuchal translucency, normal pregnancy-associated plasma protein, normal human

explanation: First-trimester screening in trisomy 21 shows ↑ nuchal translucency, ↓ PAPP-A, and ↑ β-hCG. Incorrect patterns (e.g., normal nuchal translucency, ↑ PAPP-A, or ↓ hCG) are not consistent with Down syndrome risk.
educational_objective: In the first trimester, Down syndrome screening shows increased nuchal translucency, low PAPP-A, and elevated β-hCG.

question: An investigator compares the DNA sequences of a group of newborns with achondroplasia with the sequences of a group of healthy newborns. DNA sequence analysis shows a G→C mutation in the fibroblast growth factor 3 receptor (FGFR3) gene on chromosome 4. The sequences for the two groups are shown: Achondroplasia: 5'-TACCGGGT-3' Healthy: 5'-TACGGGGT-3' As a result of this mutation, an MspI restriction enzyme site is created that allows for a convenient diagnostic test. Which of the following sequences most likely represents the substrate specificity of MspI?
explanation: The mutation introduces the palindromic sequence CCGG in the mutant strand (…TACCGGGT…), which corresponds to a recognition site for the isoschizomers HpaII/MspI (CCGG). The complementary strand reads GGCC; among the options, 5′ GGCC best represents this recognition site. Incorrect: Other sequences do not match the CCGG/MspI site.
educational_objective: Creation of a CCGG site (complement GGCC) enables digestion by MspI/HpaII, facilitating RFLP-based genotyping.

question: An 18-year-old woman comes to the physician because she has never had a menstrual period. Physical examination shows a 1-cm invagination where the vagina would normally be present. No uterus is palpable on rectal examination. Laboratory studies of serum show: Follicle-stimulating hormone: 6.3 mIU/mL Luteinizing hormone: 6.7 mIU/mL Estradiol: 700 pg/mL (N=30-400) Testosterone: 3 nmol/L (N=<3.5) Which of the following structures is most likely normal in this patient?
explanation: Primary amenorrhea with absent uterus and upper vagina but normal female-range testosterone and elevated estradiol suggests Müllerian agenesis (MRKH) with normal ovarian function. Incorrect: Uterus/cervix are absent; testes/ductus deferens do not form in 46,XX; hormone profile is not androgen-insensitivity.
educational_objective: Müllerian agenesis presents with absent uterus/upper vagina but normal ovaries and female secondary sex characteristics.

question: A patient with a 1-week history of diarrhea has reduced tissue turgor. Arterial pH is 7.3; serum bicarbonate concentration is 15 mEq/L. This patient is also likely to have which of the following?
explanation: Diarrhea causes a non–anion gap (hyperchloremic) metabolic acidosis from bicarbonate loss. Respiratory compensation is hyperventilation (↓PaCO₂). Incorrect: Volume depletion increases, not decreases, ADH and aldosterone; the anion gap is typically normal, not increased.
educational_objective: Diarrheal bicarbonate loss causes non–anion gap metabolic acidosis with compensatory ↓PaCO₂ via hyperventilation.

question: A 36-year-old African American man with recently diagnosed hypertension comes to the physician for a follow-up examination. At his last visit 1 month ago, the patient agreed to initiate a regimen including increased physical activity, a low-sodium diet, and pharmacotherapy. He has had no weight loss since then. He is 175 cm (5 ft 9 in) tall and weighs 82 kg (180 lb); BMI is 27 kg/m². His blood pressure is 150/95 mm Hg. Physical examination shows no other abnormalities. Which of the following best describes the role of ethnicity when the appropriate medication is selected for this patient? importance group is greater than the different responses among ethnicities ethnicities

options.A: It should not play a role because use of ethnicity could lead to stereotyping
options.B: It should not play a role because the variability of response to medications within a single ethnic
options.C: It should play a role because the efficacy of certain classes of medications varies among different
options.D: It should not play a role because the variability of response to medications within a single ethnic group is greater than the differences among ethnicities

explanation: Although average responses can differ by ancestry (eg, thiazides/CCBs often lower BP more in Black patients as monotherapy), individual variation within groups exceeds between-group differences; treatment should be individualized to avoid stereotyping. Incorrect: Relying on ethnicity risks bias; cost/adherence/adverse effects should guide choices.
educational_objective: Prioritize individual factors (efficacy, AEs, adherence, cost) over ethnicity, since within-group variability exceeds between-group differences.

question: A 70-year-old man has a 3-month history of weakness and a 10-kg (22-lb) weight loss. He has smoked 2 packs of cigarettes daily for 50 years. An x-ray of the chest shows a 4-cm lesion in the right upper lobe. Serum calcium concentration is 13.5 mg/dL. There are no bone metastases. A malignant lesion arising in a segmental bronchus is seen during lobectomy. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation: Squamous cell carcinoma is typically central (segmental bronchi), strongly linked to smoking, and commonly produces PTHrP → hypercalcemia without bone mets. Incorrect: Adenocarcinoma is more peripheral; carcinoid often endobronchial but rarely causes hypercalcemia; leiomyosarcoma is rare in lung.
educational_objective: Central lung mass with PTHrP-mediated hypercalcemia in a smoker points to squamous cell carcinoma.

question: An 18-year-old boy has just been diagnosed with schizophrenia. His identical twin brother is unaffected, but he and his parents are concerned about his likelihood of developing the disorder. Which of the following best represents the brother's risk for developing schizophrenia?
explanation: Monozygotic (identical) twins have a concordance for schizophrenia of roughly 40–50%, so the best estimate among the options is 50%. Incorrect: 10% approximates first-degree relatives in general; 25% underestimates monozygotic concordance; 100% would imply complete penetrance, which is not the case.
educational_objective: Monozygotic twins have high but not complete concordance for schizophrenia (~50%).

question: A 25-year-old man comes to the physician 8 hours after the onset of severe pain of his low back that radiates down his left leg. He started a weight-lifting regimen earlier in the day during which he tried to lift a bar loaded with 91 kg (200 lb) from the ground to over his head. The pain began almost immediately after this attempt. Which of the following is the most likely cause of this patient's pain?

options.C: A torn muscle in the low back

explanation: Sudden heavy lifting commonly causes posterolateral disc herniation with radicular pain radiating down the leg (sciatica). Incorrect: Vertebral fracture usually follows high-energy trauma and focal tenderness; deltoid tendon rupture is a shoulder injury; a simple muscle strain causes localized back pain without leg radiation.
educational_objective: Acute radicular pain after heavy lifting is most consistent with a lumbar intervertebral disc herniation.

question: A 65-year-old man is brought to the emergency department because of substernal chest pain, nausea, and sweating for 1 hour. He has a 10-year history of type 2 diabetes mellitus and hypertension. His pulse is 120/min, respirations are 24/min, and blood pressure is 98/50 mm Hg. Physical examination shows a jugular venous distention of 12 cm. Crackles are heard halfway up the lung fields posteriorly. Which of the following ECG findings is most likely in this patient?
explanation: Acute transmural myocardial infarction typically shows ST-segment elevation in the affected leads. Incorrect: PR-segment depression/elevation suggest pericarditis/atrial infarction; QRS widening is seen with conduction blocks/hyperkalemia; QT shortening occurs with hypercalcemia.
educational_objective: ST-elevation on ECG is characteristic of acute transmural myocardial infarction.

question: A 56-year-old woman has frequently burned herself while cooking over the past several months. Examination shows loss of pain and temperature sensation in both upper extremities and in a portion of her trunk from the clavicles to just below the nipples. Touch, vibratory sensation, and proprioception are normal. There is some wasting of the small muscles of her hands. Which of the following findings is most likely on MRI of the head and spine?

options.A: Edema in the postcentral gyri on both sides secondary to multiple strokes
options.B: Sclerotic plaques bilaterally in the anterolateral white matter of the spinal cord
options.C: Tumors compressing the lateral funiculi of the spinal cord at C-4

explanation: The "cape-like" bilateral loss of pain/temperature with hand muscle wasting indicates a cervical central cord process (e.g., syringomyelia or intramedullary tumor) producing compression at the cervical level. Among the options, a cervical compressive lesion best matches the distribution and associated LMN hand findings. Incorrect: Supratentorial lesions won't produce this dissociated sensory loss; MS plaques are typically multifocal and don't selectively cause this symmetric, segmental pattern.
educational_objective: Central cervical cord lesions (syrinx/intramedullary mass) cause bilateral pain–temperature loss in a cape distribution with hand wasting.

question: Which of the following changes in the cardiovascular system occurs with normal aging?
explanation: Normal aging is associated with increased arterial stiffness (decreased compliance) and compensatory concentric LV hypertrophy (↑ myocardial mass). Incorrect: Basal heart rate generally decreases (fewer SA node cells); mitral stenosis is pathologic (rheumatic); atherosclerosis is common but not an inevitable "normal" change.
educational_objective: Aging leads to arterial stiffening and increased LV wall thickness/mass.

question: A 26-year-old woman of Eastern European Jewish descent comes to the office 2 days after she noticed a lump in her left breast. Her maternal grandmother was diagnosed with ovarian cancer at the age of 34 years and died at the age of 60 years; her maternal aunt and mother were diagnosed with breast cancer at the ages of 36 and 40 years, respectively. The aunt died as a result of the disease at the age of 50 years. The patient is concerned that she may have inherited a genetic mutation that would predispose her to breast and/or ovarian cancer. Genetic testing of this patient and her mother are most likely to show a germline mutation in a component of which of the following pathways?
explanation: BRCA1/2 encode proteins involved in homologous recombination repair of double-strand DNA breaks; germline mutations confer high breast/ovarian cancer risk, particularly in Ashkenazi populations. Incorrect: Mismatch repair (Lynch), base excision (BER), and polymerase proofreading defects cause other cancer syndromes.
educational_objective: BRCA1/2 mutations impair homologous recombination repair of double-strand DNA breaks.

question: A 50-year-old woman with a restrictive pulmonary disorder with no obstructive component is most likely to have which of the following sets of pulmonary volumes?

options.A: Decreased functional residual capacity, normal residual volume, decreased vital capacity
options.B: Decreased functional residual capacity, normal residual volume, normal vital capacity
options.C: Normal functional residual capacity, normal residual volume, normal vital capacity

explanation: Restrictive disease reduces TLC and its components (FRC, RV) and decreases vital capacity due to limited lung expansion. Incorrect: Normal RV/FRC or normal VC would suggest preserved lung volumes, which is inconsistent with restriction.
educational_objective: Restrictive lung disease lowers FRC, RV, and VC.

question: A 12-year-old girl is brought to the physician for a follow-up examination. Three months ago, she sustained a complex fracture of the left tibia, which required cast immobilization. The cast is removed. Examination of the left calf shows that it is smaller than the right calf. Which of the following processes in this patient's myocytes is the most likely cause of these findings?
explanation: Disuse atrophy involves ubiquitin–proteasome pathway activation targeting myofibrillar proteins for degradation. Incorrect: Shifts in energy metabolism (glycolysis, FA oxidation, glycogenolysis) don't explain loss of muscle mass.
educational_objective: Disuse atrophy reflects ubiquitin–proteasome–mediated proteolysis of muscle proteins.

question: A 56-year-old man is brought to the emergency department 30 minutes after the onset of severe chest pain while mowing his lawn. His pulse is 170/min, respirations are 20/min, and blood pressure is 105/70 mm Hg. Physical examination shows cool, clammy, diaphoretic skin. Two hours after admission, pulmonary catheterization shows a pulmonary artery pressure of 40/25 mm Hg; the left atrial pressure is 25 mm Hg. Compared with a healthy person, which of the following sets of pulmonary pressure changes is most likely in this patient?

options.A: Increased capillary hydrostatic, increased interstitial hydrostatic, decreased interstitial oncotic
options.B: Increased capillary hydrostatic, decreased interstitial hydrostatic, increased interstitial oncotic
options.C: Decreased capillary hydrostatic, decreased interstitial hydrostatic, decreased interstitial oncotic

explanation: Cardiogenic pulmonary edema raises pulmonary capillary hydrostatic pressure, which drives fluid into the interstitium (↑ interstitial hydrostatic) and dilutes interstitial proteins (↓ interstitial oncotic). Incorrect: Decreased capillary hydrostatic would not cause edema; increased interstitial oncotic is more typical of protein-rich inflammatory exudates.
educational_objective: Cardiogenic pulmonary edema increases capillary and interstitial hydrostatic pressures and lowers interstitial oncotic pressure.

question: A 97-year-old woman who was recently admitted to a nursing home because of progressive dementia has large purpuric lesions over the dorsa of both forearms and hands. Her family states that she has had similar lesions on and off for years and that, to the best of their knowledge, these lesions occur in the absence of trauma. The woman appears well. Which of the following is the most likely cause of these lesions?
explanation: Senile (actinic) purpura is due to age- and sun-related dermal collagen and elastic fiber atrophy, which reduces perivascular support and causes easy ecchymoses on the extensor forearms/hands without true coagulopathy. Incorrect: Abuse would present with patterned injuries or concerning history; autoimmune vasculitis would be painful/palpable purpura and systemic signs; platelet dysfunction causes mucosal bleeding and petechiae, not isolated, recurrent forearm ecchymoses in a well-appearing patient.
educational_objective: In older adults, recurrent ecchymoses on sun-exposed forearms are usually from dermal atrophy (senile purpura), not a bleeding disorder.

question: A newborn is born with a lethal chromosome defect. He is unable to suck sufficiently to maintain life. He has episodes of crying that occur every 2 hours and are relieved by tube feeding. Which of the following best describes the most appropriate clinical approach?

options.A: Feed by whatever means necessary to maintain comfort
options.B: Give foods according to normal caloric requirement for age

explanation: In a neonate with a lethal condition and inability to feed, the ethically appropriate approach is palliative care: prioritize comfort (e.g., tube feeds for comfort), not aggressive nutrition targets or insisting on oral feeds. Incorrect: "Feed by mouth only" disregards the infant's limitations; meeting full age-based caloric goals may cause burdens without meaningful benefit.
educational_objective: In terminal neonatal conditions, focus on comfort-centered feeding (palliative care) rather than aggressive nutrition or insisting on oral intake.

question: The frequency of an autosomal recessive disease in a population is 1/1600. A deletion has been identified that accounts for 80% of the mutations at this locus. Twenty percent of the mutations result from point mutations. The frequency of deletion carriers in the population is closest to which of the following?
explanation: q²=1/1600 ⇒ q=1/40=0.025; carrier frequency ≈2pq≈2(0.975)(0.025)=0.049≈1/20. Because 80% of mutant alleles are the deletion, deletion-carrier frequency ≈0.8×0.049≈0.039≈1/25. Incorrect: 1/50 underestimates; 1/5 overestimates; 4/5 is nonsensical for carrier frequency.
educational_objective: If a specific mutation accounts for 80% of alleles in an AR disease, multiply the overall carrier rate (≈2pq) by 0.8 to estimate mutation-specific carrier frequency.

question: A 46-year-old man has dyspnea, orthopnea, and a midsystolic murmur that is best heard over the cardiac apex. An ECG shows a left atrial abnormality. Echocardiography shows an enlarged left atrium and a normally sized left ventricle. Which of the following is the most likely cause of these findings?
explanation: MR produces a systolic murmur best at the apex and leads to left atrial enlargement due to volume overload; LV size can be normal early, before chronic remodeling. Incorrect: Aortic stenosis/regurgitation typically enlarge the LV; VSD causes a holosystolic LLSB murmur and biventricular volume changes.
educational_objective: A systolic apex murmur with isolated LA enlargement is most consistent with mitral regurgitation.

question: A 45-year-old man comes to the emergency department because of a tooth abscess. He has not seen a physician or a dentist in over 10 years. He lives alone, is unemployed, and receives income from an inheritance. When asked what he does with his time, he says that he reads "books on physics." He has no friends, maintains minimal contact with relatives, and says that he is "really quite comfortable." Examination shows no symptoms of a thought disorder. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation: The vignette describes a socially isolated individual who has minimal relationships yet is comfortable with this arrangement and shows no psychosis. In the absence of a "schizoid personality disorder" option (the best fit for contented social detachment), the closest Cluster A diagnosis provided is paranoid personality disorder, which commonly features social isolation. Incorrect: Avoidant PD involves desire for relationships but fear/rejection (not "comfortable"); antisocial, borderline, narcissistic, and OCPD require features not present here (rule-breaking/impulsivity, instability, grandiosity/need for admiration, or perfectionism/control).
educational_objective: Social isolation with lack of interest in relationships suggests a Cluster A personality; when schizoid is not available, paranoid PD is the closest among the listed options, though classic schizoid best fits contented detachment.

question: A 59-year-old man develops fatigue and decreased appetite 3 months after receiving a mechanical aortic valve replacement. His pulse is 88/min, respirations are 12/min, and blood pressure is 140/54 mm Hg. He appears tired. Physical examination shows mild scleral icterus. Jugular venous pressure is 6 cm H2O, and carotid upstrokes are normal. Lung fields are clear. Cardiac examination shows crisp prosthetic valve sounds and a grade 2/6, decrescendo diastolic murmur at the left sternal border. Abdominal examination shows no tenderness, normal liver size, and normal bowel sounds. Laboratory studies of serum show a total bilirubin concentration of 4 mg/dL and a direct bilirubin concentration of 1 mg/dL. Which of the following is the most likely cause of the jaundice in this patient?
explanation: Mechanical valves can cause shear stress–induced intravascular hemolysis, producing unconjugated (indirect) hyperbilirubinemia (total 4, direct 1). Normal liver exam and clear lungs argue against hepatic congestion or cholestasis.
educational_objective: Prosthetic valves may cause hemolysis with predominantly unconjugated hyperbilirubinemia.

question: A 23-year-old woman, who was diagnosed with Sjögren syndrome 6 years ago, comes to the physician because she has had burning pain in her toes for the past month. She rates the pain as a 3 on a 10-point scale. She uses capsaicin cream as needed for the pain, which has produced partial relief. Medical history is otherwise unremarkable. Vital signs are within normal limits. Neurologic examination shows decreased perception of temperature over the feet bilaterally. Sensation to vibration, proprioception, reflexes, muscle strength, muscle tone, and bulk are normal. Which of the following neurotransmitters is most likely mediating this patient's pain?
explanation: Burning pain and temperature sensation loss imply small-fiber neuropathy affecting C fibers. Capsaicin depletes substance P from nociceptive nerve endings; substance P is a key neuropeptide mediator of pain transmission. Incorrect: GABA is inhibitory; dopamine not primary for nociception; enkephalins modulate pain but are not the main peripheral transmitter here.
educational_objective: Small-fiber neuropathy pain is mediated by C fibers that release substance P; capsaicin reduces this transmitter.

question: A 3-year-old boy is brought to the physician because of a 1-month history of pale skin. His parents are of European descent. He has no personal or family history of major medical illness. Physical examination shows pallor. Laboratory studies show: Hemoglobin: 8 g/dL (N=11-15) Hematocrit: 24% (N=25-45) Mean corpuscular hemoglobin concentration: 34% Hb/cell (N=31-36) Mean corpuscular volume: 90 μm³ (N=77-98) A photomicrograph of a peripheral blood smear is shown. Genetic testing is most likely to show which of the following findings in this patient?

options.A: Heterozygous mutation in the α-globin gene
options.B: Heterozygous mutation in the β-globin gene
options.C: Homozygous mutation in the α-globin gene
options.D: Homozygous mutation in the β-globin gene

explanation: In a young child of European descent with normocytic anemia and (likely on smear) spherocytes, hereditary spherocytosis due to ankyrin (or spectrin, band 3, protein 4.2) defects is most likely; it is typically autosomal dominant (heterozygous). Incorrect: Thalassemias alter MCV (microcytosis) or are lethal in α-major; homozygous β defects (β-thal major) present earlier with microcytosis.
educational_objective: Hereditary spherocytosis (often AD ankyrin defect) causes normocytic anemia with spherocytes in patients of Northern European ancestry.

question: A 23-year-old woman who is 6 months pregnant develops deep venous thrombosis. Intravenous administration of heparin is started. Seven days later, platelet count is 44,000/mm³. Which of the following is most likely responsible for the decreased platelet count in this patient?
explanation: Heparin-induced thrombocytopenia (HIT) results from IgG antibodies against heparin–platelet factor 4 complexes, causing platelet activation, consumption, and thrombosis. Incorrect: Hemodilution doesn't cause severe thrombocytopenia; antimegakaryocyte/stem cell antibodies fit other etiologies (e.g., ITP/aplastic anemia).
educational_objective: HIT is caused by antibodies to heparin–PF4 complexes that activate and clear platelets.

question: A 67-year-old woman comes to the physician for a health maintenance examination. Her brother and mother have a history of colon cancer. The physician recommends colonoscopy, but the patient says that she would prefer only for her stool to be tested for blood. The physician explains that testing the stool for occult blood is not appropriate in this case. The physician is most likely concerned about which of the following regarding this test?
explanation: Fecal occult blood testing misses many advanced adenomas and right-sided cancers; in high-risk patients, colonoscopy is preferred due to higher sensitivity. Incorrect: While false positives can occur, the key limitation in high-risk screening is sensitivity (risk of missed disease).
educational_objective: In higher-risk patients, FOBT lacks sufficient sensitivity; colonoscopy is the appropriate screening modality.

question: A 22-year-old woman who recently emigrated from rural Mexico is brought to the emergency department 20 minutes after a generalized tonic-clonic seizure. She has a 6-week history of headaches, nausea, vomiting, and decreased visual acuity. Funduscopic examination shows bilateral papilledema. An MRI of the brain shows enlargement of the right ventricle and findings consistent with cysticercosis. Which of the following is the most likely mechanism of the hydrocephalus in this patient?

options.A: Obstruction of the right aperture of the fourth ventricle (foramen of Luschka)
options.B: Obstruction of the right interventricular foramen (foramen of Monro)
options.D: Obstruction of the right interventricular foramen (foramen of Monro)

explanation: Neurocysticercosis can obstruct CSF pathways. Unilateral (right-sided) ventricular enlargement localizes the blockage proximal to that ventricle, most specifically the right foramen of Monro, producing noncommunicating hydrocephalus. Other options are less consistent with isolated right ventricle dilation: aqueduct or Luschka obstruction would cause bilateral/nonselective ventricular enlargement; subarachnoid hemorrhage causes communicating hydrocephalus.
educational_objective: Unilateral ventricular enlargement indicates obstruction at the corresponding foramen of Monro, producing noncommunicating hydrocephalus.

question: During a clinical study, an investigator tests a new drug for the treatment of breast cancer. A population of 10,000 patients with breast cancer is recruited and randomized into a treatment group and control group. Analysis of the data shows a p-value of 0.1 and no significant difference in the treatment outcomes between the experimental group and the control group. When repeating this study, which of the following is most likely to decrease the likelihood of making a beta error?

options.A: Conduct the study for a shorter duration

explanation: Beta error (Type II) is failing to detect a true effect (low power). Increasing sample size increases statistical power and decreases the probability of a Type II error. Adding a second treatment arm, shortening duration, or lowering alpha do not improve power in the same way (decreasing alpha actually reduces power).
educational_objective: Increase sample size to raise power and reduce Type II (beta) error.

question: A 13-year-old girl has an episode of severe cellular rejection necessitating maximal immunosuppression 6 months after a cadaveric renal transplantation. Two weeks later, she develops lymphadenopathy and hepatosplenomegaly. Examination of lymph node tissue obtained on biopsy shows a monomorphous population of B lymphocytes. Which of the following findings is most likely on further evaluation of these cells?
explanation: Post-transplant lymphoproliferative disorder is typically driven by EBV infection of B cells under intense immunosuppression, causing monomorphic B-cell proliferations. Adenovirus, CMV, HIV, and parvovirus are not the classic drivers of PTLD.
educational_objective: EBV-driven B-cell proliferation causes PTLD in heavily immunosuppressed transplant recipients.

question: A 62-year-old man comes to the physician because of pain in the left hip for 3 weeks. An x-ray of the hip shows a 4.5-cm, destructive, osteoblastic lesion with an associated fracture in the proximal femur and two separate similar smaller lesions in the bony pelvis. A needle core biopsy of the femur shows metastatic carcinoma. Which of the following is the most likely primary site of the cancer?
explanation: Prostate cancer commonly produces osteoblastic (sclerotic) bone metastases. Kidney and lung primaries more often cause lytic lesions; colon metastases are less characteristically osteoblastic.
educational_objective: Osteoblastic bone metastases are characteristic of prostate cancer.

question: A 2-year-old child undergoes resection of the right kidney because of chronic infections secondary to reflux. The left kidney is grossly normal. Which of the following structural adaptations will eventually occur in the left kidney?
explanation: The remaining kidney undergoes compensatory hypertrophy and hyperfiltration, leading to increased glomerular size. Atrophy, metaplasia, or hyperplasia of parietal epithelium are not expected compensatory changes.
educational_objective: After unilateral nephrectomy, the contralateral kidney undergoes compensatory hypertrophy with enlarged glomeruli.

question: A 3-month-old boy is brought to the physician because of facial abnormalities and weakness since birth. Physical examination shows coarse facial features and hypotonia. Urinary excretion of mucopolysaccharides is within the reference range. The concentrations of lysosomal enzymes are increased in serum and decreased in cultured skin fibroblasts. Which of the following molecular markers is most likely decreased in this patient's lysosomal enzymes?
explanation: I-cell disease (mucolipidosis II) results from deficient N-acetylglucosamine-1-phosphotransferase, preventing addition of the mannose-6-phosphate tag; lysosomal enzymes lack proper tagging and are secreted extracellularly (↑ serum, ↓ in fibroblasts). Among listed markers, the affected tagging reaction involves N-acetylglucosamine transfer.
educational_objective: Failure to add mannose-6-phosphate (via N-acetylglucosamine-1-phosphotransferase) causes I-cell disease with extracellular secretion of lysosomal enzymes.

question: An 83-year-old man is brought to the emergency department after being found at home bedridden and confused. He takes no medications. Temperature is 35.6°C (96°F), pulse is 100/min, and blood pressure is 63/50 mm Hg. Blood pressure is unchanged after intravenous infusion of 1 liter of isotonic saline. A pulmonary artery catheter is inserted and the following findings are obtained: Cardiac output high, Pulmonary capillary wedge pressure low, Systemic vascular resistance low. Which of the following is the most likely cause of the hypotension?
explanation: Early sepsis is distributive shock: high cardiac output, low SVR, and low filling pressures (PCWP), with poor response to fluids alone. GI bleeding causes hypovolemia (low CO), MI causes cardiogenic shock (low CO, high PCWP), and hypothyroidism does not fit the hemodynamics.
educational_objective: Early septic shock presents with high CO, low SVR, and low PCWP with refractory hypotension.

question: A 62-year-old man comes to the physician because of a 1-week history of muscle cramps accompanied by painful spasms in his arms and legs. He tells the physician that, for the past 4 months, he has had trouble opening jars and using silverware. Examination shows muscle weakness and exaggerated deep tendon reflexes. An appropriate treatment of the muscle cramps and spasms in this patient includes systemic administration of a drug with which of the following mechanisms of action?

options.B: Blockade of acetylcholine release from nerve terminals

explanation: Spasticity with hyperreflexia responds to antispastic agents such as baclofen, a GABA_B receptor agonist that reduces excitatory neurotransmission at the spinal level. Glycine antagonists worsen spasticity; botulinum toxin blocks ACh release but is usually local; benzodiazepine inverse agonists cause anxiety/seizures.
educational_objective: Treat spasticity with baclofen, a GABA_B agonist that reduces spinal motor neuron excitability.

question: A 54-year-old woman with terminal metastatic pancreatic cancer comes to the physician for a follow-up examination. She asks the physician to prescribe her a sufficient quantity of medication to allow her to commit suicide if the pain becomes unbearable. The physician refuses to do so, but he informs the patient that he will do everything he can to manage her pain. The physician's decision in this situation is most consistent with which of the following ethical principles?
explanation: Refusing to provide means for suicide honors the principle of nonmaleficence ("do no harm") while still committing to pain control (beneficence). Autonomy is respected by shared decision-making, but it doesn't obligate a physician to assist suicide.
educational_objective: Nonmaleficence is avoiding harm; declining to assist suicide while treating pain exemplifies this.

question: Two days after admission to the hospital because of drug-induced thrombocytopenia, a 37-year-old woman develops a severe headache and becomes comatose. On admission, examination showed a few petechiae over the lower extremities, and her platelet count was 3000/mm³. A CT scan of the head shows an intracranial hemorrhage. A platelet transfusion is recommended, but the patient is a Jehovah's Witness and had stated on admission that she did not want to receive transfusion of any blood products. Her husband is not a Jehovah's Witness and wants her to have the transfusion. Which of the following is the most appropriate management regarding transfusion?

options.A: Obtain consent from the hospital ethics committee
options.B: Obtain consent from the patient's husband
options.C: Proceed with the transfusion without consent

explanation: A competent patient's explicit prior refusal of blood products must be honored (autonomy), regardless of family wishes. Ethics committee or spouse consent cannot override the patient's clear directive.
educational_objective: Respect patient autonomy: do not transfuse when a competent patient has refused blood products.

question: A 41-year-old woman with systemic lupus erythematosus is scheduled to undergo surgical placement of a peritoneal dialysis catheter. The surgeon asks the resident physician to get the consent form signed the evening before the procedure. The resident has never seen this procedure performed and has read little about it. He will not be assisting with the procedure. Which of the following actions by the resident physician is most appropriate? morning

options.A: Ask the attending physician to obtain informed consent
options.B: Ask the patient to sign the form and tell her that the surgeon will answer questions the next
options.C: Try to answer any of the patient's questions concerning the procedure

explanation: Informed consent should be obtained by the clinician performing the procedure, who can explain risks/benefits/alternatives and answer questions. Delegating to someone uninvolved or unknowledgeable is inappropriate.
educational_objective: The operating clinician should obtain informed consent.

question: A 23-year-old man comes to the physician because of a 1-month history of weakness and muscle pain after vigorous exercise. His mother, sister, and grandmother have a similar condition; however, his father's sister and her children are unaffected. A muscle biopsy specimen shows ragged red fibers. This condition most likely results from a mutation in a gene located in which of the following structures?
explanation: Maternal inheritance with ragged red fibers indicates a mitochondrial myopathy (mtDNA mutation). ER, Golgi, and ribosomal DNA mutations do not explain maternal transmission with myopathic findings.
educational_objective: Mitochondrial myopathies show maternal inheritance and ragged red fibers from mtDNA mutations.

question: A 45-year-old woman develops proteinuria and hematuria. She has taken 3 g of ibuprofen for headaches almost daily for the past 2 years. Which of the following findings is most likely in tissue obtained on renal biopsy?
explanation: Chronic NSAID use causes analgesic nephropathy with chronic interstitial nephritis and possible papillary necrosis; crescents, FSGS, or IgA deposition are not typical NSAID patterns.
educational_objective: Long-term NSAID use can cause chronic tubulointerstitial nephritis.

question: A 35-year-old man comes to the physician because of a 2-month history of inflamed thickened skin covered with silvery scales on the scalp, trunk, elbows, and knees. This condition has been poorly responsive to coal tar preparations, calcipotriene, and triamcinolone cream. Which of the following drugs is the most appropriate next step in treatment?
explanation: For moderate–severe or refractory psoriasis, systemic therapy (e.g., methotrexate) is indicated. Azathioprine and cyclophosphamide are not standard first-line psoriasis agents; topical tretinoin is for acne/photoaging, not plaque psoriasis.
educational_objective: Refractory psoriasis often requires systemic agents such as methotrexate.

question: A patient has sustained a cerebral infarction. The brain stem is shown. Which of the following neurologic deficits was most likely present in this patient after his cerebral infarction?

options.B: Loss of joint position sense in the left extremities

explanation: A brainstem lesion involving the right cerebellar pathways (e.g., right lateral medulla/pons cerebellar peduncle involvement) produces ipsilateral limb ataxia/dysmetria. Contralateral motor or proprioceptive losses would suggest corticospinal or medial lemniscus involvement on the opposite side.
educational_objective: Cerebellar pathway lesions cause ipsilateral limb ataxia/dysmetria.

question: A 36-year-old man comes to the physician because he has not urinated for the past 24 hours. He has a 3- day history of decreased urine output. He has had intermittent renal calculi during the past 5 years. His temperature is 36.9°C (98.4°F), pulse is 112/min, and blood pressure is 150/96 mm Hg. Physical examination shows no other abnormalities. Serum studies show: Na+ 138 mEq/L, Cl- 104 mEq/L, K+ 5.9 mEq/L, HCO3- 22 mEq/L, Creatinine 2 mg/dL. Ultrasonography of the abdomen shows bilateral hydronephrosis. Bilateral nephrostomy tubes are placed. Which of the following best predicts the most likely changes in urine output and urine potassium excretion that will occur during the next 24 hours?

options.B: Decreased urine output, no change in potassium
options.D: Increased urine output, no change in potassium

explanation: Relief of bilateral obstruction causes post-obstructive diuresis with natriuresis and kaliuresis (high urine volume and increased K excretion) as solute diuresis and impaired concentrating ability correct.
educational_objective: After relieving obstruction, expect post-obstructive diuresis with increased urine flow and K⁺ excretion.

question: A 56-year-old man is admitted to the hospital after an automobile collision that resulted in crush injuries to both legs. Thirty-six hours later he develops oliguria, hyperkalemia, and an increased serum urea nitrogen (BUN) concentration. Which of the following is the most likely cause of these findings?
explanation: Crush injury releases myoglobin, causing pigment nephropathy/ATN with oliguria, elevated BUN/Cr, and hyperkalemia. Contusion alone, fat emboli, or pyelonephritis do not explain these findings.
educational_objective: Crush injury leads to myoglobin-induced acute tubular necrosis.

question: A 2-year-old boy is brought to the physician because of increased thirst, urinary frequency, and failure to thrive. He appears frail. He is at the 5th percentile for length and 7th percentile for weight. His temperature is 38°C (100.4°F). Physical examination shows dehydration and decreased muscle tone. The diagnosis of Fanconi syndrome is made. Which of the following sets of changes in fractional reabsorption in the kidneys is most likely in this patient?

options.A: Amino Acids increased, Glucose increased, Phosphate decreased, HCO3- decreased
options.B: Amino Acids increased, Glucose decreased, Phosphate increased, HCO3- increased
options.C: Amino Acids decreased, Glucose increased, Phosphate increased, HCO3- increased
options.D: Amino Acids decreased, Glucose increased, Phosphate decreased, HCO3- decreased

explanation: Fanconi syndrome is a proximal tubule reabsorption defect causing loss of amino acids, glucose, phosphate, and bicarbonate in the urine (decreased reabsorption of each).
educational_objective: Fanconi syndrome causes global proximal tubular reabsorption defects (AA, glucose, phosphate, HCO₃⁻).

question: A 25-year-old primigravid woman at 42 weeks' gestation is admitted to the hospital for failure to begin spontaneous labor. She has no history of major medical illness. Pregnancy has been uncomplicated. Her vital signs are within normal limits. Physical examination shows a uterus consistent with a 42-week gestation. Intravenous infusion with oxytocin is initiated. Activation of which of the following signaling pathways most likely mediates the therapeutic effect of this drug for this patient?
explanation: Oxytocin acts via Gq–PLC–IP₃/Ca²⁺ to increase uterine contractions; among the listed choices, second-messenger options do not include the IP₃/Ca²⁺ pathway. (Of the provided options, gene transcription is least incorrect, though oxytocin's primary mechanism is Gq-mediated Ca²⁺ mobilization rather than cAMP/cGMP/tyrosine kinase.)
educational_objective: Oxytocin increases uterine contractions primarily via Gq–IP₃/Ca²⁺ signaling (not cAMP/cGMP/RTK).

question: Monoclonality of neoplastic cells in endometrial carcinoma can be best determined by analysis of which of the following?
explanation: In females, clonality can be assessed by X-linked isoenzyme (e.g., G6PD) patterns; monoclonal populations show a single X-linked isoenzyme variant. HLA subtypes, laminin receptors, or MMP activity are not clonality assays.
educational_objective: X-linked isoenzyme analysis can demonstrate tumor monoclonality in women.

question: A randomized clinical trial is conducted to compare wound healing and cosmetic differences between two surgical procedures for closing skin wounds following cesarean delivery. A total of 500 women undergoing cesarean delivery during a 6-month period are enrolled in the study. A research assistant is assigned to conduct outcome assessments of each participant at 4 weeks and 6 weeks following delivery. Both procedures require the expertise of surgical specialists who cannot be blinded to the procedure. Results show that Procedure A has a lower rate of wound infection compared with Procedure B (relative risk of 0.66 with a 95% confidence interval of 0.30 — 1.45). The two procedures also have similar cosmetic results 6 weeks after delivery. Which of the following statements most accurately represents the comparison between Procedure A and Procedure B in a clinical care setting?

options.A: Procedure A is superior to Procedure B
options.B: Procedure B is superior to Procedure A

explanation: The 95% CI for RR includes 1 (0.30–1.45), so there is no statistically significant difference in infection rates; cosmetic outcomes are similar.
educational_objective: If the confidence interval for RR includes 1, there is no significant difference between interventions.

question: A 24-year-old African American man comes to the physician because of a 3-month history of red bumps on his face and chin. He says that the bumps are itchy and painful. Physical examination shows hyperpigmented papules over the cheeks, jawline, and neck. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation: In men with tightly curled hair, chronic shaving trauma can lead to pseudofolliculitis and secondary keloidal papules/plaques (acne keloidalis barbae). Among choices, keloids best matches hyperpigmented, itchy papules along the beard area in a Black patient. Acne vulgaris and rosacea have different distributions; cutaneous lupus shows different morphology.
educational_objective: Repetitive follicular trauma from shaving can lead to keloidal scarring papules in the beard area.

question: Serum cholesterol concentrations are measured as part of a community study. The mean and standard deviation are given for women by age group: Age 45-49 years: 229 ± 47 mg/dL; Age 50-54 years: 246 ± 50 mg/dL; Age 55-59 years: 265 ± 46 mg/dL; Age 60-62 years: 244 ± 36 mg/dL. Assuming serum cholesterol concentrations follow a normal (gaussian) distribution, which of the following is the probability that a woman between the ages of 50 and 54 years has a serum cholesterol concentration greater than 296 mg/dL?
explanation: For the 50–54 group, 296 mg/dL is 1 SD above the mean (246 + 50). In a normal distribution, ~16% lie above +1 SD; among provided options, 5% is the closest tail probability offered (though the exact value is ~16%).
educational_objective: In a normal distribution, values >1 SD above the mean are ~16% (tail probability).

question: A 60-year-old man has two-pillow orthopnea, severe dyspnea, and edema of the lower extremities. The onset of these symptoms was preceded by an episode of prolonged substernal chest pain 5 days ago. Which of the following additional findings on examination of the neck is most consistent with these findings?

options.A: Carotid bruit best heard at the carotid bifurcation

explanation: Post-MI LV systolic dysfunction with low stroke volume can produce a low-amplitude, delayed carotid upstroke. Bifid pulse suggests HCM; cannon A waves point to AV dissociation; a carotid bruit localizes atherosclerosis but not LV failure.
educational_objective: Low-output LV failure can cause a weak, delayed carotid upstroke.

question: A 30-year-old man who completed a successful course of treatment for Hodgkin disease 2 months ago calls his physician on an increasingly frequent basis. He takes his temperature several times daily and contacts the office whenever it is above 37.2°C (99°F). He also has episodes of tingling of his fingers that last several seconds. Although evaluation has shown no evidence of recurrence, he is increasingly fearful that Hodgkin disease may not be detected rapidly enough for successful treatment. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation: Excessive anxiety and preoccupation following a clear stressor (recent cancer treatment), lasting <6 months and focused on that stressor, is consistent with adjustment disorder with anxiety. Illness anxiety disorder would involve persistent fear of serious illness without a proximate stressor (and typically >6 months across contexts).
educational_objective: Anxiety within 3 months of a stressor that impairs functioning suggests adjustment disorder with anxiety.

question: A 37-year-old woman has been having difficulty fastening buttons. She has weakness of the intrinsic muscles of the hands and loss of sensation in the little fingers. Which of the following is the most likely cause of these findings?

options.A: Compression of the radial nerve in the spiral groove
options.B: Compression of the ulnar nerve in the carpal tunnel

explanation: Ulnar neuropathy causes intrinsic hand weakness and sensory loss of the 5th digit; while the ulnar nerve actually traverses Guyon's canal at the wrist (not the median nerve's carpal tunnel), among choices this best captures ulnar entrapment rather than median or radial neuropathies.
educational_objective: Ulnar neuropathy at the wrist produces intrinsic hand weakness and 5th-digit sensory loss.

question: A 16-year-old student has uncontrollable sleepiness, falling asleep several times a day while sitting in class. The slightest noise or touch is enough to awaken him. Which of the following most likely characterizes the onset of his sleep at night?

options.A: Direct transition from wakefulness to Sleep stage 4
options.B: Gradual transition from wakefulness to sleep stage 1

explanation: Narcolepsy is characterized by sleep attacks, cataplexy (in some), and abnormal sleep architecture with sleep-onset REM periods (direct transitions from wakefulness to REM).
educational_objective: Narcolepsy shows sleep-onset REM periods.

question: A 30-year-old woman with multiple sclerosis comes to the physician because of a 2-week history of severe shooting pains in her right cheek. Each pain lasts less than 1 second. The pains sometimes occur spontaneously and sometimes are precipitated by a light touch to the right cheek. The most likely cause of this new finding is a plaque in which of the following locations?
explanation: Trigeminal neuralgia in MS typically arises from demyelination at the trigeminal root entry/primary sensory pathways in the brainstem; among choices, midbrain involvement (mesencephalic trigeminal nucleus/brainstem trigeminal pathways) best fits compared with hemisphere, thalamus, or spinal cord.
educational_objective: MS plaques in brainstem trigeminal pathways can cause trigeminal neuralgia.

question: A 50-year-old man is brought to the emergency department by his wife because of a 3-hour history of confusion and difficulty seeing. He says he is seeing flickering "snowflake-like white spots" that interfere with his vision. He has a 3-year history of alcohol use disorder. His wife says he has been drinking a commercial product containing methanol. He appears anxious, confused, and incoherent.
