explanation: Nephrogenesis depends on reciprocal induction between ureteric bud epithelium and metanephric mesenchyme (epithelial–mesenchymal, but specifically bidirectional).
educational_objective: Ureteric bud and metanephric mesenchyme direct each other's differentiation via reciprocal induction.

question: A 22-year-old woman comes to the physician 3 months after she noticed a painless, slowly enlarging mass on the left side of her neck. Physical examination shows a freely mobile, soft, cystic mass with a cutaneous surface opening. The physician explains that it is from incomplete fusion during embryonic development. Which of the following is the most likely location of the opening of the duct leading to the mass in this patient?
explanation: A branchial cleft sinus/cyst from incomplete obliteration of the 2nd branchial cleft typically lies along the anterior border of the SCM with a cutaneous opening. Midline openings suggest thyroglossal duct cyst; postauricular/submental do not match.
educational_objective: Branchial cleft anomalies present as cyst/sinus tracts along the anterior SCM border.

question: A 35-year-old woman undergoes flexible nasopharyngoscopy because of chronic episodes of bacterial sinusitis. Purulent discharge from the right sphenoethmoidal recess is noted during the procedure. Which of the following best describes the location of this structure?

options.C: Proximal to the fusion of the hard and soft palates

explanation: The sphenoethmoidal recess (drainage of the sphenoid sinus) lies superior to the superior nasal concha. It is not anterior to the nasolacrimal duct (inferior meatus), nor inferior to the hiatus semilunaris (middle meatus).
educational_objective: The sphenoethmoidal recess is above the superior turbinate.

question: Moving the forearm against resistance from palm-down to palm-up (supination) position requires the use of which of the following muscles?
explanation: The biceps brachii is the most powerful supinator, especially against resistance (radial tuberosity insertion). Brachialis is a pure elbow flexor; triceps extends the elbow; pronator teres pronates (opposite action).
educational_objective: Biceps brachii powerfully supinates the forearm against resistance.

question: Failure of normal differentiation of the endoderm in the embryonic lung bud is most likely to affect the development of which of the following?
explanation: Lung endoderm forms epithelium and glands of airways; cartilage, smooth muscle, capillaries, and tracheal rings are mesoderm-derived. None of the listed answers reflects endodermal derivatives.
educational_objective: Endoderm → airway epithelium; mesoderm → cartilage, smooth muscle, vessels.

question: A 55-year-old man comes to the physician because of a 2-month history of increasing difficulty swallowing and regurgitation of undigested food. He also has noticed unusual rumbling sounds in his voice that he feels originate in his neck. Physical examination shows halitosis. A videofluoroscopic swallowing study shows a 4-cm, posterior midline pouch protruding between the thyropharyngeus and cricopharyngeus portions of the inferior pharyngeal constrictor muscle. These muscles are most likely innervated by which of the following nerves?

options.B: Motor fibers from the vagus nerve
options.C: Sympathetic fibers from the superior cervical ganglion

explanation: Pharyngeal constrictors are innervated by CN X (pharyngeal plexus).
educational_objective: Inferior constrictor (thyropharyngeus/cricopharyngeus) is innervated by the vagus.

question: A 46-year-old man comes to the office because of a 1-year history of difficulty reading small print. He has no other history of vision difficulty. He has hypertension treated with hydrochlorothiazide. Pulse is 72/min, and blood pressure is 142/86 mm Hg; other vital signs are within normal limits. The pupils are 2 mm, equally round, and reactive to light and accommodation. Ocular movements are intact. On wall chart testing, visual acuity is 20/20 bilaterally. On handheld chart testing, he can read the 20/20 line only if he holds the card more than 14 inches away. Disc margins are sharp; there are no hemorrhages, exudates, or arteriolar narrowing. No other abnormalities are noted. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation: Correct: Presbyopia (loss of lens accommodation) causes difficulty with near vision while distance vision remains normal; holding material farther away improves focus. Incorrect: Hyperopia/myopia affect distance acuity; hypertensive retinopathy shows retinal changes.
educational_objective: Presbyopia is an age-related loss of accommodation causing difficulty with near tasks.

question: A newborn presents with continuous machinery-like murmur. Which embryologic structure failed to close?
explanation: PDA results from failure of ductus arteriosus closure.
educational_objective: Patent ductus arteriosus is due to persistence of ductus arteriosus.

question: A 2-year-old boy has a midline neck mass that moves with swallowing. Which embryologic remnant is responsible?
explanation: Thyroglossal duct cysts are midline and move with swallowing.
educational_objective: Thyroglossal duct cysts arise from persistence of thyroglossal duct.

question: A 25-year-old man has loss of sensation over the lateral forearm after fracture of the humerus. Which nerve is injured?
explanation: Musculocutaneous nerve injury → loss of lateral forearm sensation.
educational_objective: Musculocutaneous nerve supplies anterior arm muscles and lateral forearm sensation.

question: A newborn has cyanosis that worsens with crying. Echocardiogram shows failure of neural crest migration.
explanation: Persistent truncus arteriosus results from failed neural crest migration.
educational_objective: Neural crest cells contribute to aorticopulmonary septum formation.

question: A 45-year-old woman has hoarseness after thyroidectomy. Which nerve was injured?
explanation: Recurrent laryngeal nerve injury → hoarseness due to vocal cord paralysis.
educational_objective: Recurrent laryngeal nerve innervates intrinsic laryngeal muscles (except cricothyroid).

question: A 3-year-old boy has meconium discharge from the umbilicus. Which embryologic structure failed to involute?
explanation: Persistent vitelline duct → meconium discharge at umbilicus.
educational_objective: Vitelline duct connects yolk sac to midgut; persistence causes fistula.

question: A 60-year-old man has loss of abduction of the arm beyond 15°. Which nerve is injured?
explanation: Axillary nerve injury → deltoid paralysis → loss of abduction >15°.
educational_objective: Axillary nerve innervates deltoid and teres minor.

question: A newborn has polyhydramnios and vomiting after feeds. X-ray shows air in stomach but no gas in intestines.
explanation: Esophageal atresia with distal TEF → air in stomach, no distal gas.
educational_objective: TEF causes polyhydramnios, aspiration, and gastric air bubble.

question: A 35-year-old man has winged scapula after axillary lymph node dissection. Which nerve was injured?
explanation: Long thoracic nerve injury → serratus anterior paralysis → winged scapula.
educational_objective: Long thoracic nerve innervates serratus anterior, stabilizing scapula.

question: A newborn has cyanosis relieved by squatting. Which congenital heart defect is present?
explanation: Tetralogy of Fallot → cyanosis relieved by squatting (↑ SVR).
educational_objective: TOF results from anterior displacement of infundibular septum.

question: A 2-year-old boy has a right-sided scrotal mass that enlarges with crying. It is reducible. Which structure failed to close?
explanation: Patent processus vaginalis → indirect inguinal hernia.
educational_objective: Indirect inguinal hernia results from persistence of processus vaginalis.

question: A 30-year-old woman has loss of taste in the anterior two-thirds of the tongue. Which nerve is injured?
explanation: Chorda tympani (branch of CN VII) carries taste from anterior 2/3 of tongue.
educational_objective: Taste anterior 2/3 = CN VII (chorda tympani); posterior 1/3 = CN IX.

question: A newborn has a single umbilical artery. Which embryologic structure failed to form properly?
explanation: Single umbilical artery results from abnormal regression of one umbilical artery.
educational_objective: Normally, 2 umbilical arteries and 1 umbilical vein are present.

question: A 55-year-old man has difficulty abducting his arm above the horizontal plane. Which muscle is paralyzed?
explanation: Serratus anterior paralysis → inability to rotate scapula upward for abduction >90°.
educational_objective: Serratus anterior rotates scapula upward; innervated by long thoracic nerve.

question: A 1-day-old newborn has bilious vomiting. X-ray shows "double bubble" sign.
explanation: Duodenal atresia → double bubble sign; associated with Down syndrome.
educational_objective: Duodenal atresia results from failure of recanalization of duodenum.

question: A 40-year-old man has wrist drop after midshaft humeral fracture. Which artery is at risk?
explanation: Radial nerve and profunda brachii artery run in spiral groove of humerus.
educational_objective: Midshaft humeral fracture endangers radial nerve and profunda brachii artery.

question: A 3-year-old boy has recurrent urinary tract infections. Imaging shows urine reflux into ureters. Which embryologic defect is responsible?

options.A: Abnormal insertion of ureter into bladder
options.B: Failure of mesonephric duct to regress

explanation: Abnormal ureter insertion → vesicoureteral reflux.
educational_objective: Vesicoureteral reflux results from abnormal ureter insertion into bladder wall.

question: A 60-year-old man has loss of sensation over the posterior 1/3 of the tongue and impaired gag reflex. Which nerve is injured?
explanation: CN IX provides taste and sensation to posterior 1/3 of tongue and afferent gag reflex.
educational_objective: Glossopharyngeal nerve mediates posterior tongue sensation and gag reflex.

question: A newborn has imperforate anus. Which embryologic process failed?
explanation: Imperforate anus results from failure of cloacal membrane to break down.
educational_objective: Imperforate anus is due to abnormal development of cloacal membrane.

question: A 25-year-old man has loss of shoulder abduction from 0–15°. Which nerve is injured?
explanation: Suprascapular nerve injury → supraspinatus paralysis → loss of initial abduction.
educational_objective: Supraspinatus initiates abduction (0–15°); innervated by suprascapular nerve.

question: A 50-year-old man has difficulty climbing stairs and rising from a chair. Exam shows weakness of hip extension. Which muscle is affected?
explanation: Gluteus maximus extends the hip; innervated by inferior gluteal nerve.
educational_objective: Gluteus maximus is the primary hip extensor.

question: A newborn has cyanosis. Echocardiogram shows aorta arising from right ventricle and pulmonary artery from left ventricle.
explanation: Transposition results from failure of aorticopulmonary septum to spiral.
educational_objective: Transposition of great arteries causes cyanosis; requires shunt for survival.

question: A 35-year-old man has loss of sensation over the medial thigh and weakness in thigh adduction. Which nerve is injured?
explanation: Obturator nerve injury → loss of adduction and medial thigh sensation.
educational_objective: Obturator nerve innervates adductors and medial thigh sensation.

question: A 1-day-old newborn has bilious vomiting. Imaging shows apple-peel appearance of small intestine.
explanation: Jejunal atresia results from vascular accident → apple-peel deformity.
educational_objective: Jejunal/ileal atresia is due to vascular disruption, not recanalization failure.

question: A 40-year-old man has foot drop after fibular neck fracture. Which nerve is injured?
explanation: Common peroneal nerve injury → foot drop, loss of dorsiflexion/eversion.
educational_objective: Common peroneal nerve injury causes foot drop.

question: A 25-year-old woman has difficulty abducting her thigh. Which nerve is injured?
explanation: Superior gluteal nerve injury → loss of abduction (gluteus medius/minimus).
educational_objective: Superior gluteal nerve injury causes Trendelenburg gait.

question: A 60-year-old man has dysphagia and hoarseness after thyroid surgery. Which nerve is injured?
explanation: External branch of superior laryngeal nerve → cricothyroid paralysis → impaired pitch.
educational_objective: External branch of superior laryngeal nerve controls cricothyroid (tenses vocal cords).

question: A newborn has abdominal wall defect with herniated bowel loops not covered by peritoneum.
explanation: Gastroschisis = bowel herniation not covered by peritoneum.
educational_objective: Gastroschisis is due to failure of lateral fold closure.

question: A 45-year-old man has loss of sensation over the lateral leg and dorsum of foot. Which nerve is injured?
explanation: Superficial peroneal nerve injury → sensory loss dorsum of foot, weak eversion.
educational_objective: Superficial peroneal nerve supplies dorsum of foot sensation.

question: A 2-year-old boy has recurrent respiratory infections and situs inversus. Which embryologic defect is responsible?
explanation: Kartagener syndrome (primary ciliary dyskinesia) → situs inversus, infections.
educational_objective: Primary ciliary dyskinesia causes situs inversus and recurrent infections.

question: A 55-year-old man has loss of plantarflexion and Achilles reflex. Which nerve is injured?
explanation: Tibial nerve injury → loss of plantarflexion and Achilles reflex.
educational_objective: Tibial nerve innervates posterior leg muscles for plantarflexion.

question: A newborn has failure of septum primum and secundum to fuse.
explanation: ASD secundum is most common; due to failure of septa fusion.
educational_objective: ASD secundum is the most common atrial septal defect.

question: A 40-year-old man has medial knee pain and decreased patellar reflex. Which nerve is injured?
explanation: Femoral nerve injury → weak knee extension, ↓ patellar reflex.
educational_objective: Femoral nerve innervates quadriceps and provides anterior thigh sensation.

question: A 2-year-old boy has persistent urachus. What is the clinical presentation?
explanation: Persistent urachus → urine discharge from umbilicus.
educational_objective: Urachal fistula connects bladder to umbilicus.

question: A 45-year-old man has shoulder droop and difficulty shrugging. Which nerve is injured?
explanation: Spinal accessory nerve injury → trapezius weakness → shoulder droop.
educational_objective: Accessory nerve innervates trapezius and SCM.

question: A newborn has bilious vomiting and malrotation of midgut. Which embryologic process failed?
explanation: Midgut normally rotates 270° counterclockwise; failure → malrotation.
educational_objective: Midgut malrotation predisposes to volvulus and obstruction.

question: A 60-year-old man has loss of sensation over the lateral shoulder. Which nerve is injured?
explanation: Axillary nerve injury → sensory loss lateral shoulder.
educational_objective: Axillary nerve provides sensation over deltoid region.

question: A 35-year-old woman has difficulty swallowing and loss of gag reflex efferent limb. Which nerve is injured?
explanation: Vagus nerve mediates efferent gag reflex and swallowing.
educational_objective: CN X provides motor to pharynx and efferent gag reflex.

question: A newborn has failure of lateral body folds to close.
explanation: Gastroschisis results from failure of lateral fold closure.
educational_objective: Gastroschisis = bowel herniation without peritoneal covering.

question: A 45-year-old man has loss of wrist extension and sensory loss over dorsal hand after humeral fracture. Which nerve is injured?
explanation: Radial nerve injury → wrist drop, dorsal hand sensory loss.
educational_objective: Radial nerve innervates extensors of wrist/fingers.

question: A 65-year-old man has difficulty rising from a seated position. Which muscle is primarily responsible?
explanation: Gluteus maximus extends the hip, especially from seated position.
educational_objective: Gluteus maximus is the main hip extensor, innervated by inferior gluteal nerve.

question: A newborn has holosystolic murmur at left lower sternal border. Which defect is most likely?
explanation: VSD is most common congenital heart defect; holosystolic murmur at LLSB.
educational_objective: VSD causes left-to-right shunt; may progress to Eisenmenger.

question: A 40-year-old man has loss of sensation over the lateral thigh. Which nerve is injured?
explanation: Lateral femoral cutaneous nerve injury → meralgia paresthetica.
educational_objective: Lateral femoral cutaneous nerve supplies sensation to lateral thigh.

question: A 2-year-old boy has failure of processus vaginalis to close. What condition results?
explanation: Patent processus vaginalis → hydrocele (fluid accumulation).
educational_objective: Hydrocele results from persistent processus vaginalis.

question: A 55-year-old man has loss of sensation over posterior arm and forearm after humeral fracture. Which nerve is injured?
explanation: Radial nerve injury → sensory loss posterior arm/forearm.
educational_objective: Radial nerve supplies extensors and posterior arm/forearm sensation.

question: A newborn has failure of fusion of maxillary and medial nasal prominences.
explanation: Cleft lip results from failure of maxillary + medial nasal prominence fusion.
educational_objective: Cleft lip is due to abnormal facial prominence fusion.

question: A 30-year-old woman has loss of pronation and thenar muscle weakness. Which nerve is injured?
explanation: Median nerve injury → loss of pronation, thenar weakness.
educational_objective: Median nerve innervates pronators and thenar muscles.

question: A 1-day-old newborn has bilious vomiting and failure of neural crest migration in colon.
explanation: Hirschsprung disease = failure of neural crest migration → aganglionic colon.
educational_objective: Hirschsprung disease causes distal obstruction and megacolon.

question: A 45-year-old man has loss of medial forearm sensation. Which nerve is injured?
explanation: Ulnar nerve injury → sensory loss medial forearm/hand.
educational_objective: Ulnar nerve supplies medial forearm/hand sensation.

question: A newborn has cyanosis and boot-shaped heart on X-ray.
explanation: Tetralogy of Fallot → boot-shaped heart due to RV hypertrophy.
educational_objective: TOF is most common cyanotic heart defect in childhood.

question: A 70-year-old man has difficulty rising from a chair and climbing stairs. Which nerve is injured?
explanation: Inferior gluteal nerve injury → gluteus maximus weakness → impaired hip extension.
educational_objective: Inferior gluteal nerve innervates gluteus maximus, main hip extensor.

question: A newborn has cyanosis and echocardiogram shows pulmonary veins draining into right atrium.
explanation: Total anomalous pulmonary venous return (TAPVR) → pulmonary veins drain into RA.
educational_objective: TAPVR causes cyanosis; requires shunt for survival.

question: A 45-year-old man has wrist drop and loss of extension after humeral fracture. Which nerve is injured?
explanation: Radial nerve injury → wrist drop, loss of extension.
educational_objective: Radial nerve innervates extensors of wrist/fingers.

question: A 2-year-old boy has painless rectal bleeding. Meckel scan is positive.
explanation: Meckel diverticulum = vitelline duct remnant with ectopic gastric mucosa.
educational_objective: Meckel diverticulum causes painless rectal bleeding in children.

question: A 60-year-old man has loss of sensation over posterior thigh and leg. Which nerve is injured?
explanation: Sciatic nerve injury → sensory loss posterior thigh/leg.
educational_objective: Sciatic nerve supplies posterior thigh and leg.

question: A newborn has failure of fusion of palatine shelves.
explanation: Cleft palate results from failure of palatine shelf fusion.
educational_objective: Cleft palate is distinct from cleft lip (maxillary + medial nasal fusion).

question: A 35-year-old man has loss of thumb opposition. Which nerve is injured?
explanation: Median nerve injury → loss of thenar opposition.
educational_objective: Median nerve innervates thenar muscles (LOAF).

question: A newborn has failure of cloacal septation.
explanation: Imperforate anus results from cloacal septation failure.
educational_objective: Cloacal septation defects cause anorectal malformations.

question: A 40-year-old man has Trendelenburg gait. Which nerve is injured?
explanation: Superior gluteal nerve injury → gluteus medius/minimus weakness → Trendelenburg gait.
educational_objective: Superior gluteal nerve stabilizes pelvis during walking.

question: A 55-year-old man has uvula deviated to the left on phonation. Which nerve is injured?
explanation: Right vagus nerve lesion → uvula deviates away from lesion.
educational_objective: CN X lesion causes uvula deviation away from side of lesion.

question: A 45-year-old man has loss of sensation over the anterior thigh and medial leg. Which nerve is injured?
explanation: Femoral nerve injury → anterior thigh weakness, medial leg sensory loss.
educational_objective: Femoral nerve innervates quadriceps and provides anterior thigh/medial leg sensation.

question: A newborn has cyanosis that worsens with crying. Squatting improves symptoms.
explanation: Tetralogy of Fallot → cyanosis relieved by squatting.
educational_objective: TOF results from anterior displacement of infundibular septum.

question: A 30-year-old woman has loss of wrist flexion and thenar atrophy. Which nerve is injured?
explanation: Median nerve injury → loss of wrist flexion, thenar atrophy.
educational_objective: Median nerve innervates flexors and thenar muscles.

question: A 2-year-old boy has bilious vomiting. Imaging shows malrotation with volvulus. Which embryologic process failed?
explanation: Midgut normally rotates 270° counterclockwise; failure → malrotation.
educational_objective: Malrotation predisposes to volvulus and obstruction.

question: A 55-year-old man has shoulder abduction weakness from 15–90°. Which nerve is injured?
explanation: Axillary nerve injury → deltoid paralysis → loss of abduction 15–90°.
educational_objective: Axillary nerve innervates deltoid and teres minor.

question: A newborn has persistent truncus arteriosus. Which embryologic process failed?

options.D: Neural crest migration to aorticopulmonary septum

explanation: Neural crest migration failure → persistent truncus arteriosus.
educational_objective: Neural crest cells form aorticopulmonary septum.

question: A 40-year-old man has loss of sensation over the posterior leg and plantar foot. Which nerve is injured?
explanation: Tibial nerve injury → loss of plantar sensation and plantarflexion.
educational_objective: Tibial nerve innervates posterior leg and plantar foot.

question: A 25-year-old woman has difficulty swallowing and nasal regurgitation of liquids. Which nerve is injured?
explanation: Vagus nerve injury → dysphagia, nasal regurgitation.
educational_objective: CN X innervates pharyngeal muscles for swallowing.

question: A newborn has abdominal wall defect with bowel loops covered by peritoneum.
explanation: Omphalocele = bowel herniation covered by peritoneum.
educational_objective: Omphalocele results from failure of midgut return to abdomen.

question: A 60-year-old man has tongue deviated to the right on protrusion. Which nerve is injured?
explanation: Right hypoglossal nerve lesion → tongue deviates toward lesion.
educational_objective: Hypoglossal nerve innervates intrinsic tongue muscles.

question: A 40-year-old man has loss of sensation over the perineum and external anal sphincter weakness. Which nerve is injured?
explanation: Pudendal nerve injury → perineal sensory loss, sphincter weakness.
educational_objective: Pudendal nerve supplies perineum and external sphincters.

question: A newborn has cyanosis and echocardiogram shows failure of endocardial cushion fusion.
explanation: Endocardial cushion defect → ASD primum, VSD, AV valve abnormalities.
educational_objective: Endocardial cushions form atrioventricular septum and valves.

question: A 55-year-old man has loss of sensation over the lateral forearm. Which nerve is injured?
explanation: Musculocutaneous nerve injury → lateral forearm sensory loss.
educational_objective: Musculocutaneous nerve innervates anterior arm and lateral forearm sensation.

question: A 2-year-old boy has bilious vomiting and annular pancreas. Which embryologic process failed?

options.A: Fusion of dorsal and ventral buds

explanation: Annular pancreas = abnormal rotation of ventral pancreatic bud.
educational_objective: Annular pancreas encircles duodenum → obstruction.

question: A 60-year-old man has loss of dorsiflexion and toe extension. Which nerve is injured?
explanation: Deep peroneal nerve injury → loss of dorsiflexion, toe extension.
educational_objective: Deep peroneal nerve innervates anterior leg muscles.

question: A newborn has failure of neural crest migration into conotruncal region.
explanation: Persistent truncus arteriosus results from failed neural crest migration.
educational_objective: Neural crest cells form aorticopulmonary septum.

question: A 45-year-old man has scapular winging after axillary surgery. Which muscle is paralyzed?
explanation: Serratus anterior paralysis → winged scapula.
educational_objective: Serratus anterior stabilizes scapula; innervated by long thoracic nerve.

question: A 3-year-old boy has recurrent sinus infections and situs inversus.
explanation: Kartagener syndrome = primary ciliary dyskinesia → situs inversus, infections.
educational_objective: Primary ciliary dyskinesia causes situs inversus and recurrent infections.

question: A 50-year-old man has uvula deviated to the right on phonation. Which nerve is injured?
explanation: Left vagus nerve lesion → uvula deviates away from lesion.
educational_objective: CN X lesion causes uvula deviation away from side of lesion.

question: A newborn has abdominal wall defect with bowel loops not covered by peritoneum.
explanation: Gastroschisis = bowel herniation without peritoneal covering.
educational_objective: Gastroschisis results from failure of lateral fold closure.

question: A 55-year-old man has loss of sensation over the posterior arm and forearm with wrist drop. Which nerve is injured?
explanation: Radial nerve injury → wrist drop, posterior arm/forearm sensory loss.
educational_objective: Radial nerve innervates extensors and posterior arm/forearm sensation.

question: A newborn has cyanosis and echocardiogram shows failure of spiral septum formation.
explanation: Transposition of great arteries results from failure of spiral septum formation.
educational_objective: Aorticopulmonary septum must spiral for normal outflow tract.

question: A 40-year-old man has loss of thigh abduction and Trendelenburg gait. Which nerve is injured?
explanation: Superior gluteal nerve injury → gluteus medius/minimus weakness → Trendelenburg gait.
educational_objective: Superior gluteal nerve stabilizes pelvis during walking.

question: A 2-year-old boy has bilious vomiting and double bubble sign on X-ray.
explanation: Duodenal atresia → double bubble sign; associated with Down syndrome.
educational_objective: Duodenal atresia results from failure of recanalization.

question: A 60-year-old man has tongue deviated to the left on protrusion. Which nerve is injured?
explanation: Left hypoglossal nerve lesion → tongue deviates toward lesion.
educational_objective: Hypoglossal nerve innervates intrinsic tongue muscles.

question: A 45-year-old man has loss of plantar sensation and Achilles reflex. Which nerve is injured?
explanation: Tibial nerve injury → loss of plantar sensation and Achilles reflex.
educational_objective: Tibial nerve innervates posterior leg and plantar foot.

question: A newborn has failure of fusion of maxillary and medial nasal prominences.
explanation: Cleft lip results from failure of maxillary + medial nasal prominence fusion.
educational_objective: Cleft lip is due to abnormal facial prominence fusion.

question: A 35-year-old woman has hoarseness after thyroid surgery. Which nerve is injured?
explanation: Recurrent laryngeal nerve injury → hoarseness due to vocal cord paralysis.
educational_objective: Recurrent laryngeal nerve innervates intrinsic laryngeal muscles (except cricothyroid).

question: A 50-year-old man has foot drop and loss of dorsiflexion after fibular neck fracture. Which nerve is injured?
explanation: Common peroneal nerve injury → foot drop, loss of dorsiflexion/eversion.
educational_objective: Common peroneal nerve injury causes foot drop.

question: A newborn has cyanosis and boot-shaped heart on X-ray.
explanation: Tetralogy of Fallot → boot-shaped heart due to RV hypertrophy.
educational_objective: TOF is most common cyanotic heart defect in childhood.

question: A 3-year-old boy presents with a midline neck mass that moves upward with tongue protrusion. Which embryologic remnant is responsible?
explanation: Thyroglossal duct cysts are midline and move with swallowing or tongue protrusion.
educational_objective: Thyroglossal duct cysts arise from persistence of the thyroglossal duct, unlike branchial cleft cysts (lateral).

question: A 30-year-old man develops urinary incontinence 2 weeks after successful treatment of a fracture of the left pelvis that was sustained at work. He was pinned against a loading dock by a truck moving in reverse. Physical examination shows a distended bladder. Cystometrography shows absence of micturition reflexes. After the bladder fills to capacity, overflow of urine occurs through the urethra a few drops at a time. This patient most likely sustained additional injury to which of the following during his initial accident?
explanation: Overflow incontinence is due to impaired detrusor contraction and/or outlet obstruction, leading to chronic urinary retention with a distended bladder and dribbling when intravesical pressure exceeds outlet resistance. After pelvic trauma, injury to the pelvic parasympathetic nerves (pelvic plexus) impairs detrusor contraction and coordinated sphincter relaxation, causing overflow incontinence.
educational_objective: Pelvic parasympathetic nerves in the pelvic plexus excite the detrusor via muscarinic receptors; sympathetic fibers regulate the internal urethral sphincter via α1 receptors. Damage to the pelvic plexus disrupts detrusor contraction and sphincter relaxation, leading to overflow incontinence.

question: A 43-year-old woman has an absent right kidney on ultrasound; left kidney normal. What tissue failed to respond to the developmental stimulus from the ureteric bud?
explanation: The ureteric bud induces the surrounding metanephric mesenchyme to form mature renal tissue; failure of metanephros to respond causes renal agenesis.
educational_objective: During kidney development, reciprocal signaling between ureteric bud and metanephros is required; only the metanephros forms the definitive kidney.

question: A 32-year-old woman with intermittent chest pain and a midsystolic click at the left 5th intercostal space. Most likely cardiac abnormality?
explanation: Midsystolic click is classic for MVP, often due to myxomatous degeneration; may be associated with connective tissue disorders.
educational_objective: MVP involves abnormal leaflet displacement/thickening; classically presents with a midsystolic click and possible late systolic MR murmur.

question: A 3-year-old boy with developmental delay, microcephaly, smooth philtrum, ptosis; history of cleft palate. Maternal substance most likely responsible?
explanation: Alcohol causes fetal alcohol syndrome: neurodevelopmental impairment and characteristic facial/structural anomalies.
educational_objective: Alcohol is a teratogen causing FAS with intellectual disability, developmental delay, and facial/organ malformations.

question: A 12-year-old boy with polyuria, polydipsia, low urine specific gravity and osmolality; which hypothalamic nucleus is involved?
explanation: Central diabetes insipidus arises from impaired ADH production in paraventricular/supraoptic nuclei; leads to inability to concentrate urine.
educational_objective: Supraoptic (and paraventricular) nuclei make ADH; deficiency causes dilute urine and hyperosmolality, treated with desmopressin.

question: A 16-year-old boy with type 1 diabetes and poor control; best question to explore reluctance to self-inject insulin?

options.A: "I get the feeling you have not been taking your insulin regularly. Would you like me to arrange some training for you by our nurses?"
options.B: "It's been my experience that most poorly controlled diabetics have trouble giving themselves insulin. Do you have this problem?"
options.C: "You are clearly having difficulty with insulin injections. Would you like to arrange for a family member to give you your shots?"
options.D: "You seem to have missed your shots. How often has this happened?"

explanation: Use nonjudgmental, open-ended questions to elicit barriers and strengthen alliance; avoid accusatory or presumptive wording.
educational_objective: Effective responses to suspected nonadherence assume barriers and use open-ended questions (motivational interviewing principles).

question: A 6-week-old male infant with persistent umbilical stump discharge containing intestinal fluid; which GI segment is the fistula connected to?
explanation: Persistent vitelline duct (Meckel) can form an umbilical fistula; Meckel diverticulum is typically in the ileum.
educational_objective: Meckel diverticulum results from vitelline duct persistence and may connect ileum to umbilicus causing enteric discharge.

question: An 18-year-old woman with fever, weight loss, retinal hemorrhage, carotid bruits, diminished/absent radial pulses; labs show anemia, leukocytosis, high ESR; type of vasculitis on carotid histology?
explanation: Takayasu arteritis is a large-vessel vasculitis in young women with pulselessness; histology shows granulomatous inflammation and intimal fibrosis.
educational_objective: Takayasu arteritis causes granulomatous inflammation and stenosis of the aortic arch/proximal branches; diagnosed by angiography; treated with steroids/immunomodulators.

question: A 30-year-old couple with one daughter with isolated VSD; both parents normal; risk of another child with CHD?
explanation: Isolated VSD risk is multifactorial with de novo mutations; population baseline ~2–3% in otherwise normal parents.
educational_objective: Baseline VSD incidence is ~2–3%; many cases are non-Mendelian and not due to a single-gene inheritance in unaffected parents.

question: 27-year-old male weightlifter on synthetic androgens has scalp hair loss, mild testicular atrophy; mechanism of decreased testicular size?

options.A: Downregulation of pituitary luteinizing hormone receptors
options.B: Downregulation of testicular follicle-stimulating hormone receptors
options.D: Increased negative feedback on gonadotropin secretion

explanation: Exogenous androgens suppress GnRH → ↓LH/FSH → ↓Leydig stimulation → ↓intratesticular testosterone → testicular atrophy.
educational_objective: Testicular atrophy from anabolic steroids or TRT is due to hypothalamic-pituitary suppression and reduced LH-driven testosterone synthesis.

question: 2-month-old boy with hypotonia, poor feeding, large fontanels, midface hypoplasia, hepatomegaly; very-long-chain fatty acids, phytanic acid, pipecolic acid elevated; which organelle absent in hepatocytes?
explanation: Zellweger syndrome: peroxisome biogenesis disorder → accumulation of VLCFA and related substrates; severe neonatal neuro-hepatic features.
educational_objective: Peroxisomes metabolize VLCFA and phytanic acid; their absence causes characteristic metabolic buildup and multisystem disease.

question: 5-year West Nile infection study describing 25 CDC-confirmed patients with demographics and sources; study design?
explanation: Descriptive report of a group of cases without controls or hypothesis testing is a case series.
educational_objective: Case series describe clinical features/natural history in small groups without implying causality.

question: 10-year-old boy with anemia, thrombocytopenia, renal failure; normal PT/PTT; smear with schistocytes; most likely diagnosis?
explanation: Triad of MAHA, thrombocytopenia, and AKI after diarrheal illness is classic for HUS.
educational_objective: HUS is often due to Shiga toxin–producing E. coli; platelet-rich microthrombi shear RBCs and injure kidneys; coag tests are normal.

question: Full-term newborn with symmetrically enlarged neck mass of endothelial-lined cystic spaces (cystic hygroma); likely disorder?
explanation: Cystic hygroma (lymphangioma) is classically associated with Turner syndrome (45,XO).
educational_objective: Turner syndrome can present with webbed neck/cystic hygroma due to lymphatic maldevelopment.

question: 58-year-old woman post-PCI has rise in CK-MB and troponin; mechanism?

options.D: Protease inactivation by cytoplasmic free calcium ions

explanation: Reperfusion injury generates ROS → lipid peroxidation, protein/DNA damage → membrane injury and myocyte necrosis releasing enzymes.
educational_objective: Reperfusion after ischemia causes ROS-mediated injury with lipid peroxidation and cellular necrosis.

question: Male newborn with right-sided aortic arch, full cheeks, low-set ears, small chin, hypocalcemia; most likely site of malformations?
explanation: DiGeorge syndrome (22q11 deletion) → failure of 3rd/4th pouches (thymus and parathyroids) → hypocalcemia, immune defects, cardiac anomalies.
educational_objective: Third pouch forms thymus/inferior parathyroids; fourth forms superior parathyroids; failure leads to classic DiGeorge features.

question: 3-year-old girl after petting zoo with anemia, thrombocytopenia, AKI, schistocytes; in addition to platelet aggregates, what causes small renal vessel occlusion?
explanation: HUS features platelet-fibrin microthrombi causing vascular occlusion and RBC shearing.
educational_objective: HUS forms fibrin-rich platelet thrombi in microvasculature leading to MAHA and renal injury.

question: A 29-year-old woman is brought to the emergency department 1 hour after a motor vehicle collision. CT shows only a small amount of intraperitoneal fluid. After 6 hours, exploratory laparotomy reveals sudden massive hemorrhage when the surgeon slides a hand behind the liver. BP becomes undetectable within 1 minute. Which lesion is most likely?

options.A: Avulsion of hepatic veins from the inferior vena cava
options.C: Traumatic transection of the hepatic artery
options.D: Traumatic transection of the portal vein

explanation: Avulsion of hepatic veins from the IVC causes occult bleeding posterior to the liver. Supine positioning may tamponade bleeding until liver manipulation triggers exsanguination.
educational_objective: Hepatic veins and IVC lie posterior to the liver. Blunt trauma can cause avulsion, leading to hidden hemorrhage that may erupt during surgery.

question: A 36-year-old man with HIV infection has been treated with a combination of antiretroviral drugs, including zidovudine (AZT), for 3 years. Laboratory studies show a marked increase in his plasma HIV viral load during the past 3 months. Viral resistance to zidovudine is suspected. A mutation in which of the following is most likely to explain the resistance to zidovudine in this patient?
explanation: RNA-dependent DNA polymerase (HIV reverse transcriptase) mutations are most likely to account for this patient's resistance to zidovudine (AZT). AZT is an NRTI, and selective pressure can lead to thymidine analog mutations (TAMs) in reverse transcriptase.
educational_objective: HIV medications that inhibit the RNA-dependent DNA polymerase (HIV reverse transcriptase) are either NRTIs or NNRTIs. Monotherapy can induce resistance via mutation of reverse transcriptase, which is mitigated by combination regimens.

question: A 38-year-old woman has had a slowly enlarging pink papule on her left cheek for 1 year. A photomicrograph of a biopsy specimen of the papule is shown. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation: Basal cell carcinoma presents as pink, pearly papules with rolled borders and central ulceration. Histology shows basaloid blue islands of cells with peripheral palisading and stromal retraction.
educational_objective: Basal cell carcinoma is a malignant proliferation of basal keratinocytes extending into the dermis. Pathologic features include basaloid islands with palisading and retraction. Treated with surgical modalities like Mohs surgery

question: A 36-year-old man comes to the physician because of fever and frequent slimy stools for 2 weeks. He recently emigrated from Ecuador. His temperature is 38.2°C (100.8°F). Abdominal examination shows mild tenderness of the right upper quadrant. Examination of the stool shows mucus. Colonoscopy shows multiple flask-shaped ulcers that have undermined and destroyed large areas of the intestinal epithelium. Which of the following is the most likely causal organism?
explanation: Entamoeba histolytica causes amoebic dysentery via fecal-oral transmission. Trophozoites invade colonic mucosa, forming flask-shaped ulcers and may cause hepatic abscesses. Diagnosis includes stool microscopy and PCR.
educational_objective: Entamoeba histolytica is an amoebic parasite transmitted via contaminated water. It invades the colon and may cause hepatic abscesses.

question: A 43-year-old woman comes to the physician because of a 4-week history of intermittent episodes of severe abdominal pain, especially after eating fatty foods. Physical examination shows no abnormalities. Abdominal ultrasonography shows several 3- to 4-mm gallstones contained within the gallbladder. The patient declines surgery. A drug with which of the following mechanisms of action is most appropriate for this patient?
explanation: Ursodiol inhibits biliary cholesterol secretion, reducing cholesterol content in bile and preventing gallstone formation. It is second-line therapy for biliary colic when surgery is declined.
educational_objective: Ursodiol decreases cholesterol in bile and prevents cholesterol gallstones. It is used when cholecystectomy is declined in biliary colic.

question: A 40-year-old woman who is a construction worker comes to the physician because of pain in her shoulder that developed after she lifted a heavy beam. Physical examination shows weakness and pain only during external rotation of the arm at the shoulder. There is muscle wasting inferior to the spine of the scapula. Which of the following muscles is most likely injured?
explanation: Weakness in external rotation and muscle wasting below the scapular spine indicate infraspinatus injury, a rotator cuff muscle responsible for external rotation.
educational_objective: Rotator cuff injuries present with weakness in the direction of motion controlled by the affected muscle. Infraspinatus controls external rotation.

question: A 74-year-old woman is admitted to the hospital to undergo a cholecystectomy. During the operation, she becomes acutely hypotensive. The hypotension persists for 5 minutes despite administration of appropriate pressor agents. Which of the following morphologic lesions is most likely to occur in this patient as a result of this incident?

options.B: Lacunar infarcts of the basal ganglia

explanation: The hippocampus is highly susceptible to hypoxic injury due to its metabolic demands. Cytotoxic edema causes neuronal enlargement.
educational_objective: The hippocampus is vulnerable to hypoxia, leading to cytotoxic edema and neuronal swelling.

question: A 7-year-old girl is brought to the physician because of a 2-week history of painful swelling under her right arm, which has become increasingly severe during the past 3 days. Physical examination shows a 2 x 1-cm, tender, right axillary lymph node and a small papule on the dorsum of the right hand. A silver-stained biopsy specimen of the papule shows pleomorphic bacilli. Which of the following is the most likely causal organism?
explanation: Bartonella henselae causes cat scratch disease, presenting with lymphadenitis and a papule at the inoculation site. Histology shows necrotizing granulomas with stellate abscesses.
educational_objective: Cat scratch disease is caused by Bartonella henselae and presents with lymphadenitis and characteristic histologic findings.

question: A 68-year-old man with Parkinson disease is being treated with levodopa and carbidopa. He is doing well and has few adverse effects. Concurrent therapy with levodopa and carbidopa is useful because of which of the following characteristics of carbidopa?

options.A: Does not cross the blood-brain barrier
options.B: Enhances activity of the transporter for levodopa

explanation: Carbidopa does not cross the BBB and inhibits peripheral dopa decarboxylase, increasing levodopa delivery to the brain and reducing peripheral dopamine adverse effects (eg, nausea, vomiting).
educational_objective: Carbidopa cannot cross the blood-brain barrier and therefore increases the bioavailability of levodopa without inhibiting the conversion of levodopa to dopamine in the brain. Carbidopa also decreases peripheral dopamine concentrations, reducing the likelihood of dopamine-related side effects such as nausea.

question: A 58-year-old woman comes to the office for a follow-up examination 2 days after she noticed a lump in her left breast on self-examination. Menopause occurred 6 years ago. Physical examination shows a 1-cm, poorly circumscribed, nodular mass in the left periareolar tissue. Mammography shows an ill-defined density suspicious for malignancy. A needle biopsy specimen is nondiagnostic. Microscopic examination of the excised mass shows a large dilated space lined by glandular epithelium and surrounded by a dense lymphoplasmacytic inflammatory infiltrate; the associated lumen is filled with lipid-laden macrophages and amorphous debris. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation: Periareolar mass in a peri/postmenopausal woman with duct dilation, inflammation, and lipid-laden macrophages is characteristic of mammary duct ectasia.
educational_objective: Mammary duct ectasia often occurs in perimenopausal women when a lactiferous duct becomes blocked and accumulating lipid and debris cause dilation to occur.

question: A 20-year-old man is brought to the physician because of a 4-hour history of abdominal pain, nausea, and vomiting. He says that he had been drinking ethanol heavily all weekend, and he took three doses of acetaminophen within 2 hours after the onset of a severe headache Monday morning. This patient is at increased risk for liver injury because of which of the following actions of ethanol?

options.C: Induction of cytochrome P450 enzymes that activate acetaminophen to a hepatotoxic metabolite
options.D: Metabolic acidosis due to an increased NADH:NAD+ ratio

explanation: Ethanol induces CYP enzymes that convert acetaminophen to NAPQI, increasing toxic metabolite formation in overdose.
educational_objective: Alcohol leads to the induction of P450 enzymes that convert acetaminophen to N-acetyl-p-benzoquinoneimine (NAPQI), a toxic metabolite that causes hepatotoxicity in the setting of acetaminophen overdose.

question: A 34-year-old man has a herniated lumbar intervertebral disc. Laminectomy and removal of the herniated fragment are scheduled. Which of the following labeled sites on the normal lumbar axial CT scan shown is the most appropriate location for surgical entrance to the neural canal?
explanation: Laminectomy enters via the lamina to access the spinal canal and decompress the herniated disc.
educational_objective: Injury to the spinal column involving bony, ligament, or disc disruption can lead to compression of neural elements. This presents as acute neurologic symptoms such as pain, weakness, and change in sensation in a dermatomal and myotomal distribution. The lamina serves as the most appropriate location for surgical entrance to the spinal canal to access the herniated disc.

question: A 70-year-old woman comes to the physician for advice after her husband of 45 years suddenly dies of cardiac arrest. She wants to donate $1,000,000 to a small city's department of public health to decrease the number of sudden cardiac deaths. She asks the physician to recommend the most effective way to put this money to use. She says, "I want to see the results of my donation over the next 1 to 2 years." The patient is most likely to accomplish her goal if she contributes to which of the following?

options.A: Creation of a citywide aerobic exercise program
options.B: Fortification of the water supply with aspirin
options.C: Placement of external automatic defibrillators in public spaces throughout the city
options.D: Provision of free HMG-CoA reductase inhibitor drugs to everyone in town over the age of 50 years

explanation: Public AED deployment shortens time to defibrillation for VF/VT arrests in public settings, reducing sudden cardiac deaths in the near term.
educational_objective: AED placement in public areas such as shopping centers, airports, and train stations is an effective intervention that decreases sudden cardiac death as a result of the decreased time from event to initiation of treatment.

question: A 33-year-old man with HIV infection comes to the physician because of a 3-day history of headaches, intolerance to light, and severe neck stiffness. His temperature is 39.5°C (103.1°F). Physical examination shows photophobia and nuchal rigidity. Analysis of cerebrospinal fluid obtained on lumbar puncture shows cryptococci. Initial therapy with combination antifungal medication, including fluconazole, successfully resolves the symptoms. Fluconazole most likely impaired or inhibited which of the following fungal targets in this patient?
explanation: Fluconazole inhibits CYP450-dependent demethylation from lanosterol to ergosterol, disrupting fungal cell membrane synthesis.
educational_objective: Cryptococcus neoformans is an encapsulated, nondimorphic yeast and common opportunistic pathogen in immunocompromised patients. Cryptococcal meningitis presents with headache, nuchal rigidity, photophobia, nausea and vomiting, and progressive encephalopathy. Treatment is with antifungal agents, typically a combination of amphotericin B with high-dose oral fluconazole. Fluconazole inhibits the production of ergosterol by inhibiting the cytochrome P450 (CYP450)-dependent reaction that synthesizes ergosterol from lanosterol.

question: A 32-year-old nulligravid woman comes to the office because she has been unable to conceive during the past 2 months. She and her husband have had sexual intercourse three times weekly during this time. Menarche was at the age of 13 years. Menses are light and occur at regular 30-day intervals. Her last menstrual period was 7 days ago. She has no personal or family history of major medical illness, and her only medication is a prenatal vitamin. She does not smoke, drink alcoholic beverages, or use illicit drugs. She is 155 cm (5 ft 1 in) tall and weighs 75 kg (165 lb); BMI is 31 kg/m2. Vital signs are within normal limits. Physical examination, including pelvic examination, shows no abnormalities. Her serum follicle-stimulating hormone concentration is 75 mIU/mL, luteinizing hormone concentration is 30 mIU/mL, and estradiol concentration is 75 pg/mL (N=30–400). Which of the following is the most likely explanation for these laboratory findings?
explanation: Moderately increased FSH and LH with FSH>LH indicates mid-follicular phase before the LH surge.
educational_objective: At the start of the follicular phase of the menstrual cycle, just after menses occurs, follicle-stimulating hormone (FSH) increases to support a developing ovarian follicle. Unlike the 14-day luteal phase, the length of the follicular phase is variable. Ovulation is accompanied by a rapid surge in FSH and luteinizing hormone; this marks the transition from the follicular phase to the luteal phase.

question: A 37-year-old woman is brought to the emergency department 20 minutes after injuring her right arm when she fell down the stairs in her home. Examination of the right upper extremity shows tenderness and deformity over the humerus. Sensation to light touch is absent over the area indicated by the oval in the diagram of the patient's right hand shown. An x-ray of the right upper extremity shows a fracture of the humerus. Further examination of this patient's right hand will most likely show impairment of which of the following movements?
explanation: Humeral fracture can injure the radial nerve in the spiral groove, causing deficits in wrist/digit extensors and impaired thumb extension.
educational_objective: Fracture of the humerus places the radial nerve at greatest risk for injury as it courses within the spiral groove of the humerus. Extension of the thumb is primarily controlled by the extensor pollicis brevis and extensor pollicis longus, both of which are innervated by the posterior interosseous nerve, a branch of the radial nerve.

question: A 48-year-old woman comes to the emergency department 2 hours after the sudden onset of severe flank pain. She also has a 2-month history of mild exacerbation of her baseline constipation. She has had no fever, chills, pain with urination, or increased urinary frequency. She has a history of infrequent urinary tract infections, with the most recent occurring more than 5 years ago. She has no personal or family history of renal calculi. Her pulse is 92/min, and blood pressure is 138/88 mm Hg. Physical examination shows no other abnormalities. Laboratory studies show: Serum Na+ 144 mEq/L; K+ 3.8 mEq/L; Cl− 100 mEq/L; HCO3− 27 mEq/L; Ca2+ 10.6 mg/dL; Urea nitrogen 19 mg/dL; Creatinine 0.8 mg/dL; Phosphorus 2.9 mg/dL. Urine blood 2+. Which of the following is the most likely cause of these findings?
explanation: Primary hyperparathyroidism causes hypercalcemia with hypophosphatemia and predisposes to nephrolithiasis and constipation.
educational_objective: Primary hyperparathyroidism presents with symptoms of hypercalcemia, including recurrent nephrolithiasis, bone pain from osseous resorption, polyuria, dehydration, constipation, and psychiatric disturbances. Parathyroid chief cell adenoma is the most common cause.

question: A 22-year-old man comes to the physician because of a2-month history of foul-smelling, watery diarrhea with significant flatulence; he also has had a4.5-kg (10-lb) weight loss during this period. He recently returned from a trip to rural Indonesia, where he did not always have access to clean water. He appears thin. Physical examination shows a soft, mildly distended abdomen with active bowel sounds. A photomicrograph of a stool specimen is shown. The most appropriate pharmacotherapy has which of the following mechanisms of action?
explanation: The photomicrograph displays a flagellated, pear-shaped trophozoite with two large central nuclei and a median axostyle, consistent with the appearance of Giardia lamblia. G. lamblia is a flagellated, parasitic organism that causes giardiasis. Giardiasis is usually acquired through the ingestion of cysts in contaminated water, which then mature into trophozoites in the small bowel. Parasitic overgrowth of the small bowel leads to intestinal malabsorption. Giardiasis presents with persistent diarrhea that is foul-smelling and fatty, as well as abdominal pain, bloating, cramping, and weight loss. Diagnosis is made with stool culture, microscopy, or stool antigen testing. Metronidazole is the first line treatment and asserts its antimicrobial effect through the formation of destructive free radicals.
educational_objective: Metronidazole is the first line treatment of giardiasis and enacts its antimicrobial effect through the formation of destructive free radicals.

question: A 1-year-old boy is brought to the physician by his parents because of a 4-week history of progressive generalized tonic-clonic seizures and a strange odor to his urine. He has a history of delayed development. He was adopted from an orphanage in Russia at the age of 6 months. Physical examination shows fair skin and blond hair. His phenylalanine hydroxylase gene is homozygous for a point mutation (GT→AT) in intron 12 of the affected gene that causes skipping of exon 12. Which of the following is the most likely explanation for exon skipping in this patient's affected gene?
explanation: After DNA is transcribed into pre-messenger RNA (pre-mRNA), processing occurs to form the finished mRNA product. One element of this processing is the splicing out of introns, non-coding portions of the genetic material which do not contribute to the final protein, leaving behind only exons. From a single pre-mRNA, several unique proteins may be made if splicing variations occur. Correct splicing is dependent on the spliceosome recognizing a splice site at the start of an intron, which typically consists of base pairs G-U-A-A-G. A point mutation in DNA changing a guanine to an adenine, as in this case, may mask a splice site and either cause an intron to remain in the final mRNA product erroneously or cause a larger region of pre-mRNA to be spliced, leading to the removal of an exon. In this case, incorrect removal of exon 12 has created a defective version of phenylalanine hydroxylase and led to the condition phenylketonuria. Patients with phenylketonuria do not have the ability to convert phenylalanine to tyrosine. Accumulation of phenylalanine leads to physical manifestations including a musty odor, impaired neurologic development, and seizures.
educational_objective: Before a strand of mRNA is mature, splicing of the introns must occur, which requires specific splice sites to be recognized by the spliceosome. If a splice site is masked, an intron may be inappropriately retained, or an exon may be erroneously removed.

question: A 22-year-old man comes to the physician because of a 2-week history of itching and pain to the right of his umbilicus. Physical examination shows a rash that extends posterolaterally to the right from the patient's umbilicus. A diagnosis of herpes zoster is made. The viral infection is most likely located in which of the following dorsal root ganglia?
explanation: Shingles typically results in a vesicular rash in a dermatomal distribution as a result of reactivation of the varicella-zoster virus from a dorsal root ganglion. This most often occurs in the setting of immunosuppression or physiologic stress. This patient's rash that extends posterolaterally from the right of his umbilicus is consistent with a rash along a dermatome. A dermatome is one of the components of the embryonic somite, a paired segment of paraxial mesoderm. When fully developed, the dermatome is an area of skin whose afferent fibers travel within a single spinal nerve. Herpes zoster is often dermatomal because the virus replicates in the dorsal root ganglion of a single spinal nerve. The T10 dermatome correlates with the area of skin that extends in an antero-posterior pattern at the level of the umbilicus and mid back.
educational_objective: Shingles typically results in a vesicular rash in a dermatomal distribution as a result reactivation of the varicella-zoster virus from a dorsal root ganglion. A dermatome is an area of skin whose afferent fibers travel within a single spinal nerve. The T10 dermatome correlates with the area of skin that extends in an antero-posterior pattern at the level of the umbilicus and mid back.

question: A 41-year-old woman is evaluated because of increasingly severe headaches for 6 weeks. Her blood pressure is 160/100 mm Hg while standing and supine. A bruit is heard over the left costovertebral angle. Urinalysis shows no abnormalities. An angiogram of the left renal artery shows alternating areas of stenosis and aneurysmal dilatation ("string of beads" sign). Which of the following conditions of the renal artery is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation: Fibromuscular dysplasia is a non-inflammatory and non-atherosclerotic angiopathy of medium-sized arteries (eg, renal, carotid), that results in multifocal fibrous and muscular thickening of the arterial wall. The resultant stenosis causes secondary hypertension due to abnormal stimulation of the juxtaglomerular apparatus from low afferent blood flow leading to excessive production of renin and angiotensin. It can lead to severe hypertension in an otherwise healthy, young patient with no medical comorbidities or laboratory abnormalities. Physical examination findings often include signs of left ventricular hypertrophy such as S4 gallop and a renal artery bruit auscultated lateral to the umbilicus. Angiography may reveal a bead-like appearance of the renal artery. ACE inhibitors can be considered for unilateral stenosis but can lead to acute renal failure in the setting of significant bilateral renal artery stenosis.
educational_objective: Fibromuscular dysplasia is a non-inflammatory and non-atherosclerotic angiopathy of medium-sized arteries that can lead to renal artery stenosis and secondary hypertension due to the excessive production of renin and angiotensin. It commonly presents in a young patient with no medical comorbidities or abnormal laboratory findings.

question: A 58-year-old woman comes to the office because of a 1-month history of fatigue, fever, shortness of breath, and joint pain; she also has had a 3.2-kg (7-lb) weight loss during this period. Her temperature is 37.6°C (99.7°F), and respirations are 34/min. Physical examination shows tenderness to palpation over the maxillary sinus, nasal ulcerations, and a bulging, red left tympanic membrane. Laboratory studies show: Erythrocyte sedimentation rate 65 mm/h Serum C-reactive protein 8.2 mg/L (N=0.08–3.1) Urine Blood 2+ Protein 2+ Histologic examination of a biopsy specimen of affected lung tissue shows granulomata and vasculitis. An autoantibody is most likely directly binding which of the following cell types in this patient?
explanation: Granulomatosis with polyangiitis (GPA, formerly Wegener granulomatosis) is a systemic necrotizing granulomatous vasculitis that affects small and medium vessels. It is associated with the development of cytoplasmic antineutrophil cytoplasmic antibodies (c-ANCA) targeting neutrophils. GPA primarily affects the sinopulmonary tract, kidneys, and skin. Patients typically present with constitutional symptoms, such as fever, weight loss, and fatigue, with additional symptoms based on specific organ involvement. Sinopulmonary manifestations include recurrent sinusitis, otitis media, mastoiditis, nasal ulcerations with epistaxis, hemoptysis, cough, and dyspnea. The kidneys are typically involved, and patients often present with hematuria with an increased risk for developing rapidly progressive glomerulonephritis and renal failure. When the skin is involved, patients may exhibit purpura.
educational_objective: Granulomatosis with polyangiitis (GPA) is a systemic necrotizing granulomatous vasculitis that affects small and medium vessels. It is associated with the development of cytoplasmic antineutrophil cytoplasmic antibodies (c-ANCA). GPA primarily affects the sinopulmonary tract, kidneys, and skin. GPA may present with sinusitis, otitis media, mastoiditis, nasal ulcerations with epistaxis, hemoptysis, cough, hematuria with an increased risk for developing rapidly progressive glomerulonephritis, and renal failure.

question: A 65-year-old woman with stage I estrogen receptor-positive breast carcinoma undergoes a mastectomy and radiation therapy. After completion of the chemotherapy, she begins treatment with tamoxifen. The initial site of binding of this agent to its receptor most likely occurs in which of the following areas of the tumor cells?
explanation: Tamoxifen is a selective estrogen receptor modulator that is used in the treatment of breast cancer. It acts as an estrogen receptor antagonist in the breast but an estrogen receptor agonist in the endometrium and bone. Estrogen is a steroid hormone and is consequently lipophilic. Its receptor is located in the cytosol. Following binding to the receptor, the receptor-ligand complex translocates to the nucleus, where it binds to DNA to exert its effects. Because of tamoxifen's unopposed estrogen stimulation of the endometrium, it increases the risk for endometrial hyperplasia, with the potential for atypia and consequent endometrial cancer. Other risks of tamoxifen use include deep venous thrombosis and pulmonary embolism, because of the hypercoagulability caused by alterations in the coagulation system. It decreases the risk for recurrent invasive breast cancer in bilateral breasts by approximately 30 to 50%, although it results in little difference in overall mortality.
educational_objective: Steroid hormones commonly bind to intracellular receptors. Most steroid hormones (eg, estrogen, androgens, glucocorticoids) bind the receptor in the cytosol, after which it moves to the nucleus where it acts as a transcription factor at the level of the DNA. Other similar hormones (eg, thyroid hormone) bind their receptor in the nucleus, at which time it binds to DNA to exert its effects.

question: A 20-year-old man comes to the physician because of a 2-month history of recurrent headaches. Funduscopic examination shows papilledema and a small retinal lesion consistent with a retinal hemangioblastoma. An MRI of the brain shows a lesion in the cerebellar midline. A CT scan of the abdomen shows cystic lesions in the pancreas. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation: This patient with a retinal hemangioblastoma, cerebellar lesion, and cystic lesions of the pancreas likely has von Hippel-Lindau disease. Von Hippel-Lindau disease is a heritable neurocutaneous disorder that presents with multiple benign and malignant tumors. Many tumors originate from the vasculature, including hemangioblastomas of the retina and cerebellum and angiomatosis of the skin and mucosa. Additional tumors include renal clear cell carcinomas, pancreatic masses, and pheochromocytomas. Diagnosis occurs by genetic testing that shows the pathogenic variant of the VHL gene, which is typically inherited in an autosomal dominant fashion. Management involves surgical excision of the tumors.
educational_objective: Von Hippel-Lindau disease is an autosomal dominant neurocutaneous disorder that presents with multiple benign and malignant tumors. Many tumors originate from the vasculature, including hemangioblastomas of the retina and central nervous system, and angiomatosis of the skin and mucosa. Tumors of the kidney and pancreas also occur.

question: Numerous cross-sectional studies in different populations have shown a significant relationship between the use of tanning beds and the development of melanoma. The odds ratios of these studies range from 3.2 to 7.1. In these studies, the number of hours of tanning bed use was highly correlated with an increase in the size and number of dysplastic nevi. Which of the following is the greatest limitation in establishing causality from these studies?
explanation: A cross-sectional study seeks to identify the prevalence of a condition at a particular point in time. In this scenario, these studies examine the use of tanning beds and the development of melanoma at a single cross-section of time. Thus, the risk factor (tanning beds) and the outcomes (melanoma) are measured simultaneously. Cross-sectional studies do not follow patients over time. All information is collected at a single point, so causation cannot be determined because the temporal sequence of events cannot be examined. In these studies, the development of melanoma may have preceded the use of tanning beds. Cross-sectional studies can, however, determine correlation. Correlation relates the trends of two variables together and is quantified by the Pearson correlation coefficient (r). It represents the increase, decrease, or absence, or absence of change in one variable with changes in the other. In cases where variables trend together (both increase), the r value is positive. The closer the value of the correlation coefficient to 1.0, the stronger the trend between the two variables. Negative r values suggest that data trend in opposing fashion; as one variable increases, the other decreases. Uncorrelated data will have a correlation coefficient near zero, which indicates that changes in one variable are not associated with any trend in the other variable. Correlation should not be confused with causation.
educational_objective: A cross-sectional study seeks to identify the prevalence of a condition at a particular point in time. Because the risk factor and the outcomes are measured at the same time, the temporal sequence of events cannot be determined. This inhibits the ability to infer causality. Biologic plausibility, consistent findings, a strong dose response, and a strong association increase the likelihood of causality but do not prove it.

question: A 52-year-old woman comes to the office for a follow-up examination. She began treatment with gentamicin 10 days ago for treatment of pyelonephritis caused by a highly resistant pathogen. She has no other history of serious illness and takes no other medications. At her last visit 1 week ago, serum trough concentration of gentamicin was 1 μg/mL (target <2). Vital signs are within normal limits. Physical examination shows no abnormalities. Serum trough concentration of gentamicin now is 10 μg/mL. Which of the following best explains the increased serum gentamicin concentration in this patient?
explanation: Gentamicin is renally cleared; acute kidney injury decreases clearance, causing a supratherapeutic trough.
educational_objective: Gentamicin is cleared by the kidneys and renal function should be monitored throughout treatment. Aminoglycoside usage may be complicated by nephrotoxicity, ototoxicity, neuromuscular damage, and teratogenic effects. Nephrotoxicity can cause decreased clearance of gentamicin, therefore causing supratherapeutic concentrations of the antibiotic.

question: A 22-year-old man is brought to the emergency department 30 minutes after a friend found him unconscious on the floor. A drug overdose is suspected. His pulse is 120/min, respirations are 4/min with apparent low tidal volumes, and blood pressure is 120/100 mm Hg. Physical examination shows mild cyanosis. He is intubated and mechanically ventilated with positive pressure ventilation (rate = 12/min; VT = 7 mL/kg) using 10 cm H2O positive end-expiratory pressure (PEEP). Which of the following sets of findings best describes the effects of the mechanical ventilation with PEEP on this patient's alveolar (PA) and intrapleural (P ip) pressures?
explanation: With positive-pressure ventilation plus PEEP, peak inspiratory and end-tidal alveolar and intrapleural pressures remain positive relative to atmosphere.
educational_objective: Modern mechanical ventilation utilizes a positive pressure system to drive air into the lungs. This is in contrast to normal, spontaneous breathing, in which outward expansion of the chest wall generates negative intrapleural and alveolar pressures relative to atmosphere, creating a pressure gradient for the movement of air into the lung.

question: A 58-year-old man comes to the physician because of a 2-week history of severe chest pain when climbing stairs. He does not have chest pain at rest. The diagnosis of angina pectoris is made. Nitroglycerin is prescribed for this patient because of which of the following mechanisms of action?
explanation: Nitroglycerin releases NO, activates guanylate cyclase, increases cGMP → MLCP activation → smooth muscle relaxation/vasodilation.
educational_objective: Nitroglycerin is used in the treatment of angina pectoris for its vasodilatory effect, which is mediated by increased cGMP in smooth muscle cells.

question: An 82-year-old woman is brought to the physician by her son because of a 1-year history of increasing word-finding difficulty and a 3-year history of increasing forgetfulness. She has hypertension and hypercholesterolemia. Her medications are lisinopril and atorvastatin. Her blood pressure is 120/80 mm Hg. Physical examination shows no abnormalities. On mental status examination, she is alert and attentive. She recalls one of five parts of a name and address after 5 minutes, and does not recognize the remaining parts when given clues for each. She recalls zero of three figures 5 minutes after copying them. She cannot name the point of a pen or the band of a watch. Degeneration of which of the following is the most likely cause of this patient's memory changes?
explanation: Prominent anterograde memory impairment reflects hippocampal degeneration in the mesial temporal lobe, typical of Alzheimer-type dementia.
educational_objective: The hippocampus is a key center for learning and memory processing and is located within the mesial temporal lobe. The hippocampus forms anterograde, declarative memories (eg, memories about facts) and consolidates these memories into long-term memories.

question: A 53-year-old woman is brought to the emergency department because of a 1-week history of severe chest pain and cough productive of moderate amounts of thick yellow sputum. She currently takes no medications. She is not in acute respiratory distress. Her temperature is 37.6°C (99.6°F), pulse is 95/min, respirations are 32/min, and blood pressure is 120/80 mm Hg. A chest x-ray shows consolidation of the right lower lobe of the lung. Culture of sputum grows Streptococcus pneumoniae. Treatment with antibiotics is started. This patient is most likely to sustain injury to normal pulmonary tissue by inflammatory cells releasing which of the following mediators?
explanation: Neutrophil respiratory burst (NADPH oxidase) generates ROS that kill bacteria but also damage host tissues (lipids, proteins, DNA).
educational_objective: Inflammation is the response to harmful stimuli such as infection, with direct microbial killing resulting from the leukocyte production of reactive oxygen species and antimicrobial peptides. Inadvertent host tissue damage can occur from exposure to reactive oxygen species, which result in structural damage to DNA, RNA, enzymes, and the cellular lipid membrane.

question: A 25-year-old man who immigrated to the USA from Pakistan 2 months ago comes to the physician for a follow-up examination. He was diagnosed with hepatitis C at the age of 5 years but has had no symptoms or clinical signs of this condition. Physical examination shows no abnormalities. Serum studies done today show an AST activity of 68 U/L, ALT activity of 100 U/L, and hepatitis C virus RNA of 1.5 million IU/mL. A photomicrograph of the liver biopsy specimen is shown. Which of the following characteristic features of virus-induced histopathology is seen in this patient?
explanation: Councilman bodies are eosinophilic apoptotic hepatocytes seen in viral hepatitis.
educational_objective: Councilman bodies are eosinophilic hepatocytes with a nuclear fragment that represent cells undergoing apoptosis. They are frequently seen in both acute and chronic hepatitis.

question: A 55-year-old man comes to the physician because of a 4-month history of cough and chest pain. He has smoked 1 pack of cigarettes daily for 30 years. Physical examination shows no abnormalities. A chest x-ray shows a 3-cm mass in the right lower lobe of the lung. It is most appropriate for the physician to begin to communicate the x-ray findings in which of the following manners?

options.A: "I'm afraid I have bad news; the chest x-ray showed an abnormality in your lung that concerns me."
options.B: "I'm sorry, but you are almost certainly going to need an operation and chemotherapy."
options.C: "Let's make an appointment for you and your wife next week so I can tell you both the results at that time."
options.D: "We need to do more tests before I can give you the final results of your x-ray."

explanation: Deliver bad news promptly, honestly, and in manageable pieces; acknowledge concern directly before detailing next steps.
educational_objective: Bad news should be delivered honestly, directly, in a timely manner, and using small pieces of information at a time.

question: A 10-year-old boy is brought to the physician by his parents because of increased urinary frequency and progressive fatigue during the past 3 weeks. Physical examination shows no abnormalities. His fasting serum glucose concentration is 350 mg/dL. Urinalysis shows 4+ glucose. Which of the following mechanisms in the proximal tubule is the most likely cause of the glycosuria in this patient?

options.A: Inhibition of the sodium/glucose cotransporter-1 (SGLT-1) carrier protein
options.B: Saturation of the glucose transporter protein-1 (GLUT-1) carrier protein
options.C: Saturation of glucose transporter protein-2 (GLUT-2) carrier protein
options.D: Saturation of the sodium/glucose cotransporter-1 (SGLT-1) carrier protein

explanation: Filtered glucose exceeds the reabsorptive capacity of SGLT transporters in the proximal tubule; when serum glucose is markedly elevated (≈180 mg/dL threshold), SGLT proteins saturate and glucose spills into urine.
educational_objective: Filtered glucose is reclaimed by the nephron through the action of sodium-glucose cotransporter proteins. When serum glucose concentrations exceed approximately 180 mg/dL, these transporters begin to saturate and some filtered glucose cannot be recovered from the tubular filtrate, resulting in glycosuria.

question: A 50-year-old man comes to the physician because of a 2-week history of progressive shortness of breath while climbing stairs to his office every morning. He reports no other problems, but he is concerned because his father had a major myocardial infarction at the age of 52 years. His pulse is 110/min and regular, respirations are 16/min, and blood pressure is 135/95 mm Hg. The lungs are clear to auscultation. Cardiac examination shows normal heart sounds with a physiologic split of S2. Stress echocardiography shows hypokinesis of the posterior left ventricle with increasing activity levels. Which of the following is the most likely cause of the posterior left ventricular findings in this patient?

options.A: Extravascular compression of the coronary arteries
options.D: Stenosis of the right coronary artery

explanation: In most individuals the RCA (via the PDA) supplies the posterior LV; a flow-limiting RCA stenosis causes exercise-induced regional hypokinesis on stress echocardiography.
educational_objective: In a majority of people, the RCA supplies the posterior left ventricle via the PDA. In patients with CAD and a flow-limiting stenosis, stress echocardiography can demonstrate hypokinesis of the region of myocardium supplied by the affected artery.

question: A 60-year-old man comes to the physician because of the gradual onset of muscle weakness during the past 5 years. He takes no medications. Physical examination shows no skin lesions or rashes. There is marked weakness of the distal muscles. Corticosteroids are administered. At a follow-up examination 6 weeks later, his condition has not improved. His serum creatine kinase concentration is increased. The results of assays for antinuclear antibody and U1 ribonucleoprotein are negative.
