The set point will determine the fraction of patients who are true or false positive and true or false negative and should be chosen to optimize the sensitivity and specificity of the test. Point A would result in the majority of persons with type 2 diabetes mellitus being identified as positive; therefore, the number of false negatives would be low, and the number of true positives would be high. Moving the cut point from point A to point B (raising the threshold) would result in fewer people with the disease being identified, thereby increasing the number of false negatives and reducing the number of false positives, which would decrease sensitivity and increase specificity.
educational_objective: Raising the threshold for a positive test to diagnose patients with a disease decreases sensitivity and increases specificity of the test by increasing the number of false negatives and decreasing the number of false positives.

question: A 29-year-old man comes to the physician with his 27-year-old wife because they have been unable to conceive for 1 year. Previous examination of the wife showed no abnormalities. Physical examination shows normal genitalia. His serum testosterone and luteinizing hormone concentrations are within the reference ranges and serum follicle-stimulating hormone concentration is increased. Semen analysis shows decreased sperm count. A decreased serum concentration of which of following is the most likely in this patient?
explanation: Sertoli-cell –only syndrome, also known as germinal cell aplasia, is a rare disorder in which only Sertoli cells line the seminiferous tubules, indicating an absence of germ cells and spermatogonia with resultant failure in spermatogenesis. The cause is not completely understood but is thought to have an underlying genetic cause in at least some cases. Under normal conditions, the seminiferous tubules are lined by spermatogonia, which generate the primary spermatocytes that will ultimately become sperm. Sertoli cells are also present within the seminiferous tubules and are required to support spermatogenesis. Pulsatile gonadotropin-releasing hormone produced by the hypothalamus causes the pituitary gland to secrete follicle-stimulating hormone (FSH) and luteinizing hormone (LH). LH acts on the Leydig cells, located adjacent to the seminiferous tubules, and causes them to secrete testosterone. FSH acts on the Sertoli cells, leading them to produce androgen-binding protein and promote sperm development. Additionally, Sertoli cells provide negative feedback on hypothalamic FSH secretion by producing inhibin B. Inhibin B concentration correlates directly with sperm count and is typically decreased or undetectable in patients with Sertoli-cell–only syndrome. The diagnosis of Sertoli-cell–only syndrome is suggested by normal testosterone and LH concentrations, increased FSH concentration, and azoospermia (lack of sperm) on semen analysis, although testicular biopsy is required to confirm the absence of germ cells.
educational_objective: Sertoli-cell–only syndrome is a rare disorder in which only Sertoli cells line the seminiferous tubules, indicating an absence of germ cells and spermatogonia with resultant failure in spermatogenesis. Patients exhibit abnormally reduced inhibin B production by Sertoli cells due to the absence of spermatogonia. The diagnosis of Sertoli-cell–only syndrome is suggested by normal testosterone and luteinizing hormone concentrations, increased follicle-stimulating hormone concentration, and azoospermia (lack of sperm) on semen analysis, although testicular biopsy is required to confirm the absence of germ cells.

question: A 21-year-old man comes to the physician because of a lump in his scrotum for 3 months. Physical examination shows a 1-cm nontender nodule in the right scrotum. Transillumination shows a solid, noncystic structure. An operation to remove the testis is done. After incision of the skin and subcutaneous tissue, the next fascial layer to be incised in this patient is a direct extension of which of the following abdominal layers?
explanation: From superficial to deep, the layers of the scrotum include the skin, the Dartos muscle and fascia, the external spermatic fascia, the cremaster muscle and fascia, the internal spermatic fascia, and the tunica vaginalis. Each of these layers is derived from a layer of the abdominal wall because the fetal testes originated in the abdomen. Early in the third trimester the testes begin to migrate through the inguinal canal and into the scrotum, carrying with them the abdominal wall coverings. While the structures are contiguous, they are named differently in the abdomen and scrotum. In this case, the skin and next layer, the Dartos muscle and fascia (subcutaneous tissue), have been incised. The following layer is the external spermatic fascia which is derived from the external abdominal oblique muscle aponeurosis.
educational_objective: Each layer of the testes is derived from a layer of the abdominal wall (listed in parentheses). From superficial to deep, the layers of the scrotum include the skin (skin), the dartos muscle and fascia (Scarpa fascia), the external spermatic fascia (external abdominal oblique muscle and fascia), the cremaster muscle and fascia (internal abdominal oblique muscle), the internal spermatic fascia (transversalis fascia), and tunica vaginalis (peritoneum).

question: A previously healthy 32-year-old man is brought to the emergency department because of a 1-day history of intermittent flashing spots and blurred vision, vomiting, confusion, and difficulty walking. He is a painter and says that yesterday he cleaned up a spilled bottle of paint thinner. Ophthalmologic examination shows dilated pupils with hyperemia of the optic disc and retinal edema. Physical examination shows tachypnea. Serum studies show an anion gap metabolic acidosis. The most appropriate pharmacotherapy for this patient is most likely to inhibit the activity of which of the following?
explanation: Methanol is commonly used as paint thinner or as an additive in paint thinner. Methanol can be absorbed into the body via ingestion, inhalation, and skin or eye contact. Once absorbed, methanol can be converted by alcohol dehydrogenase to formaldehyde, which is then converted by aldehyde dehydrogenase into formic acid, a toxic metabolite that can cause visual disturbances, retinal edema, optic disc hyperemia, gastrointestinal distress (eg, abdominal pain, nausea, vomiting), putaminal hemorrhage, and neurologic depression (eg, confusion, ataxia). The production of formic acid results in the development of an anion gap metabolic acidosis with a compensatory respiratory alkalosis, manifesting as tachypnea. Treatment requires the administration of fomepizole, which inhibits alcohol dehydrogenase and blocks the conversion of methanol to its toxic metabolites. Severe methanol toxicity resulting in refractory metabolic acidosis, refractory electrolyte abnormalities, visual disturbances, or deteriorating vital signs may require dialysis.
educational_objective: Methanol can be metabolized to formic acid, a toxic metabolite that can cause visual disturbances, retinal edema, optic disc hyperemia, gastrointestinal distress, putaminal hemorrhage, and neurologic depression. Fomepizole inhibits alcohol dehydrogenase and thus blocks the conversion of methanol to its toxic metabolites.

question: A 25-year-old man sustains perforation of the large bowel in the area of the cecum during a motor vehicle collision. An exploratory operation is planned to resect the affected bowel. To prevent excessive intraoperative hemorrhage in this patient, it is most appropriate to ligate the terminal branch of which of the following arteries?
explanation: The superior mesenteric artery (SMA) supplies arterial blood to the distal duodenum, jejunum, and ileum, as well as the large bowel including the cecum, ascending colon, and proximal two-thirds of the transverse colon. The arterial blood supply to the cecum is supplied by the ileocolic artery, a branch of the SMA. The ileocolic artery can be ligated during exploratory abdominal surgery and repair of perforating cecal injuries to prevent excessive intraoperative hemorrhage.
educational_objective: The cecum derives its arterial blood supply from the ileocolic artery, which is a branch of the SMA. The ileocolic artery may be ligated during surgical repair of cecal trauma to prevent excessive intraoperative bleeding.

question: A 48-year-old man with renal artery stenosis undergoes stent placement. Femoral access is used to place the stent. After entrance into the aorta, the guide wire should be advanced superiorly just beyond which of the following structures to approach the right renal artery in this patient?
explanation: Testicular arteries arise just inferior to the renal arteries (≈L2); advancing just above them places the catheter at the level of the renal arteries to enter the right renal artery.
educational_objective: To access the renal arteries from the femoral artery approach, the catheter should be advanced to the area just superior to the takeoff of the testicular artery.

question: A 53-year-old man has had progressive difficulty swallowing for the past 3 months. He has a 10-year history of heartburn with esophageal regurgitation of gastric contents. Tissue obtained on biopsy of the lower third of the esophagus is shown. Which of the following best describes the nature of this lesion?

options.B: Malignant transformation of epithelium into squamous carcinoma

explanation: Chronic GERD leads to intestinal (columnar with goblet cells) metaplasia replacing squamous epithelium—Barrett esophagus.
educational_objective: Barrett esophagus develops in individuals with chronic GERD and is histologically characterized by intestinal metaplasia whereby the normal squamous epithelium is replaced by columnar epithelium. Over time, dysplasia can develop, predisposing to esophageal adenocarcinoma.

question: A 35-year-old man is brought to the emergency department 30 minutes after fainting while at work. He is conscious and is able to state his name and what he was doing before the episode. He says that he has had fatigue during the past 3 weeks. He has no history of major medical illness and takes no medications. His mother died of ovarian cancer at the age of 40 years. His maternal grandfather died of colon cancer at the age of 49 years. The patient does not smoke or drink alcoholic beverages. He appears pale. His temperature is 37.5°C (99.5°F), pulse is 110/min, respirations are 20/min, and blood pressure is 95/55 mm Hg. Physical examination shows no other abnormalities. Laboratory studies show a hemoglobin concentration of 6.2 g/dL and hematocrit of 19%. Test of the stool for occult blood is positive. Colonoscopy shows an isolated right-sided mass. Examination of a biopsy specimen of the mass shows a poorly-differentiated adenocarcinoma with mucinous features. Immunohistochemistry of the biopsy specimen is most likely to show loss of expression of which of the following proteins?
explanation: Lynch syndrome tumors show loss of DNA mismatch repair proteins (eg, MSH2) with microsatellite instability.
educational_objective: Inherited defects in DNA mismatch repair genes are the cause of Lynch syndrome, an autosomal dominant disorder characterized by a high risk for colorectal cancer, along with endometrial, ovarian, gastric, hepatobiliary, pancreas, brain, and skin cancer. Patients with Lynch syndrome should undergo screening colonoscopy every 1 to 2 years beginning at age 25, or 5 years before the first age of diagnosis in the family, and then annually beginning at age 35. Additional treatment options include prophylactic colectomy, hysterectomy, and bilateral salpingo-oophorectomy.

question: A 34-year-old woman comes to the office because of a 6-month history of progressive swelling of her hands and feet. Her blood pressure is 140/89 mm Hg. Physical examination shows 1+ edema of the hands and 2+ edema of the feet. Serum studies show a potassium concentration of 3.3 mEq/L, decreased aldosterone concentration and plasma renin activity, and increased cortisol:cortisone ratio. After questioning, it is found that the patient has been consuming a nutritional supplement she obtained from the Internet during the past 10 months. Serum studies obtained after the patient stops using the supplement are within the reference ranges. The supplement this patient consumed most likely inhibited the activity of which of the following enzymes?
explanation: Glycyrrhetinic acid in licorice inhibits 11β-HSD2, increasing cortisol activity at mineralocorticoid receptors → HTN, hypokalemia, low renin/aldosterone, ↑cortisol:cortisone.
educational_objective: Glycyrrhetinic acid, or enoxolone, is the active ingredient in licorice and primarily inhibits 11β-hydroxysteroid dehydrogenase type II, which is responsible for the conversion of cortisol to cortisone. With increased concentrations of cortisol, downstream mineralocorticoid effects are observed, which cause inhibition of the renin-angiotensin-aldosterone pathway and decreased serum concentrations of its associated hormones.

question: A study of 10 patients with severe emphysema who were treated with oral theophylline for 12 weeks found no improvement in the exercise ability of these patients after treatment. Which of the following best describes this study design?
explanation: Descriptive, nonanalytic report of a series of patients with the same condition/intervention (no randomization, no control group).
educational_objective: A case series is a descriptive study that describes the history, possible exposures, clinical findings, and treatment results of a group of patients with a similar diagnosis. Case series studies are useful for studying the outcomes or natural history of a particular group, procedure, or treatment.

question: A 70-year-old man comes to the physician because of intense pain in his left great toe for 2 hours. He was successfully treated with colchicine for acute arthritis in the same toe 6 months ago. Physical examination shows redness, mild swelling, warmth, and exquisite tenderness of the first metatarsophalangeal joint. The effectiveness of colchicine in the treatment of this condition is most likely the result of which of the following pharmacologic effects?

options.A: Decreased local proliferation of neutrophils and monocytes
options.B: Decreased proliferation of synovial lining cells
options.C: Increased histamine release from local mast cells
options.D: Increased renal excretion of uric acid

explanation: Colchicine inhibits microtubule polymerization, impairing neutrophil chemotaxis/degranulation and leukocyte migration into the joint.
educational_objective: Gout occurs as a result of the precipitation of monosodium urate crystals in a joint. It typically presents with acute, atraumatic single-joint pain, erythema, and swelling. Treatment of acute gout includes NSAIDs, colchicine, and/or corticosteroids. Colchicine inhibits microtubule polymerization, which decreases leukocyte motility and infiltration into the joint.

question: A 3-year-old boy is brought to the physician because of a 6-month history of a sway back when standing. His brother had a history of muscle weakness and died of pneumonia at the age of 12 years. Physical examination shows hip girdle weakness. His serum creatine kinase concentration is markedly increased. This patient's symptoms are most likely caused by the accumulation of a defective protein in which of the following locations in muscle cells?
explanation: Duchenne muscular dystrophy is due to dystrophin, a cytoplasmic protein linking actin to the sarcolemma; dysfunction leads to myonecrosis.
educational_objective: Duchenne muscular dystrophy is an X-linked recessive condition that is caused by mutations in the DMD gene encoding dystrophin, a cytoplasmic protein that plays an important role in anchoring muscle actin filaments to the plasma membrane. Duchenne muscular dystrophy results in progressive proximal muscle weakness after a period of relatively normal development. Symptoms include an inability to rise from a squatting position and weakness of the lower limb girdle. Late complications include dilated cardiomyopathy and respiratory insufficiency.

question: A 22-year-old woman is brought to the emergency department in a semicomatose condition after collapsing near the end of running a marathon. Her prerace weight was 47 kg (103 lb). She now weighs 50 kg (110 lb). Her pulse is 115/min, respirations are 15/min, and blood pressure is 90/50 mm Hg. Physical examination shows cool, dry skin. She is responsive to painful stimuli. Laboratory studies show: Serum Na+ 116 mEq/L; K+ 4.8 mEq/L; Cl− 89 mEq/L; HCO3− 22 mEq/L. Urea nitrogen 22 mg/dL. Glucose 101 mg/dL. Creatinine 1 mg/dL. This patient's condition is most likely due to which of the following?
explanation: Acute hypervolemic hyponatremia from excessive free-water intake during endurance exercise causes cerebral edema and CNS symptoms.
educational_objective: Acute hyponatremia is associated with central nervous system symptoms such as headache, nausea, vomiting, confusion, delirium, weakness, seizures, and coma. Excessive fluid intake can lead to hypervolemic hyponatremia and cerebral edema.

question: A prospective study is done to assess the relative efficacy of two different antihypertensive medications, both of which were shown to be efficacious in placebo-controlled trials. In the study, patients with hypertension were randomly assigned to receive one of two antihypertensive medications. At the conclusion of the study, some participants reported inconsistent adherence to their medication regimen, while others reported discontinuing their study medication altogether before the primary outcome (blood pressure measurement after 30 days) was obtained. A few of these patients who discontinued their study medication were prescribed the other group's study medication by their primary care physician and were taking it at the time of the primary outcome measurement. In their primary analysis, which of the following methods should the investigators use to analyze data from the patients who were not adherent to the medication regimen?

options.A: Exclude the outcome for only those who reported stopping the medication altogether
options.B: Include the outcome for each participant in the group to which he or she was randomized
options.C: Include the outcome for those who took more than a prespecified fraction of medication doses

explanation: Use intention-to-treat: analyze participants in their originally randomized groups to preserve randomization despite nonadherence/crossover.
educational_objective: Intention-to-treat analysis groups patients as initially randomized regardless of the actual occurrence of treatment within the study. This analysis strategy preserves randomization but may dilute the true effects of the intervention.

question: A 68-year-old man is diagnosed with metastatic prostate cancer. The most appropriate treatment should include a drug with which of the following mechanisms of action?
explanation: Continuous GnRH agonist (eg, leuprolide) desensitizes pituitary GnRH receptors → ↓LH/FSH → medical castration (↓testosterone).
educational_objective: Leuprolide, a gonadotropin-releasing hormone agonist, is used in prostate cancer as a form of medical castration. Continuous administration of leuprolide decreases luteinizing hormone release by the pituitary gland and subsequently decreases the production of testosterone by the Leydig cells.

question: A 45-year-old man comes to the office because of a 2-week history of malaise and lethargy. He has HIV infection and chronic hepatitis B and C. Current medications include antiretroviral therapy. Blood pressure is 144/88 mm Hg. Physical examination shows 1+ pitting edema of all extremities. Results of laboratory studies are shown: Serum Creatinine 2.6 mg/dL; Albumin 2.8 g/dL; Total cholesterol 278 mg/dL. Urine total protein 3725 mg/24 h. Pathologic examination of a renal biopsy specimen shows nonlobulated glomeruli with uniform thickening of capillary walls, subepithelial electron dense deposits, and granular IgG immunofluorescent deposits along the glomerular basement membrane. Which of the following is the most likely cause of these findings?

options.A: Focal segmental glomerulosclerosis secondary to HIV infection
options.B: Membranous glomerulonephritis secondary to chronic hepatitis B and C
options.D: Type II membranoproliferative glomerulonephritis secondary to chronic hepatitis B and C

explanation: Nephrotic syndrome with diffuse capillary wall thickening, granular IgG along GBM, and subepithelial deposits—membranous nephropathy, here secondary to chronic hepatitis.
educational_objective: Membranous nephropathy is the most common nephrotic syndrome in Caucasian patients and is characterized by proteinuria (>3g/day), edema, hypoalbuminemia, and hypercholesterolemia. It can be primary or secondary to conditions such as Hepatitis B or C virus. Classically, biopsy shows diffuse thickening of the glomerular capillary wall, immunofluorescence shows IgG deposition along the glomerular basement membrane, and electron microscopy shows subepithelial deposits.

question: A 24-year-old man who is comatose is admitted to the hospital because of a drug overdose and pneumonia. On admission, he is intubated and mechanically ventilated. While receiving a tidal volume of 500 mL, the patient's end-expiratory pressure is +5 cm H2O, and his end-inspiratory airway pressure is +25 cm H2O. An esophageal balloon is inserted, and an end-inspiratory pleural pressure of +20 cm H2O is measured. Which of the following best represents this patient's respiratory system compliance?
explanation: Compliance = ΔV/ΔP = 500 mL ÷ (25−5 cm H2O) = 25 mL/cm H2O.
educational_objective: Compliance is the measure of the change in volume of a system in response to a change in pressure. The respiratory system compliance, in the setting of mechanical ventilation, can be determined by dividing the tidal volume delivered by the difference between the end-expiratory and end-inspiratory pressures.

question: A 44-year-old woman comes to the physician because of a 3-week history of severe headache. She is 157 cm (5 ft 2 in) tall and weighs 86 kg (190 lb); BMI is 35 kg/m2. Funduscopic examination shows papilledema. An MRI of the brain shows no abnormalities. A lumbar puncture is done. Cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) analysis shows an opening pressure of 32 cm H2O. In addition to recommendations regarding dietary changes and weight loss, treatment with acetazolamide is begun. This drug will most likely improve the patient's symptoms by which of the following mechanisms?

options.A: Decreased venous pressure around the arachnoid granulations
options.B: Increased permeability of tight junctions (zonulae occludentes) between endothelial cells
options.C: Increased sodium permeability of the ependyma
options.D: Increased water transport by astrocyte end-foot processes

explanation: Acetazolamide (carbonic anhydrase inhibitor) lowers ICP by reducing CSF production at the choroid plexus.
educational_objective: Pseudotumor cerebri is an idiopathic disorder of increased ICP that is most common in obese women of childbearing age that presents with headache and physical examination findings of increased ICP. Acetazolamide can decrease CSF production by the choroid plexus, thereby decreasing ICP.

question: A 5-year-old girl is brought to the physician because of a 4-day history of stumbling gait, muscle rigidity, slurred speech, and decreased cognitive function. Ophthalmologic examination shows decreased visual acuity and inability to discern colors. Assays of isolated muscle mitochondria show decreased ability to oxidize NADH but normal FADH2 oxidation. Which of the following electron transport chain complexes is most likely impaired in this patient?
explanation: Decreased NADH oxidation with normal FADH2 points to Complex I (NADH dehydrogenase) dysfunction (eg, LHON).
educational_objective: Complex I, NADH oxireductase, transfers electrons from NADH to ubiquinone while also generating a proton gradient. For every two electrons transferred from NADH, four protons are pumped across the membrane. Mutations in genes encoding complex I are commonly implicated in the pathogenesis of Leber Hereditary Optic Neuropathy, a mitochondrial-inherited condition that results in degeneration of the optic nerve and retina.

question: A 30-year-old woman has diarrhea and crampy abdominal pain. Which of the following historical features most strongly suggests that the cause is inflammatory bowel disease rather than irritable bowel syndrome?

options.B: More than three bowel movements daily
options.C: Nighttime awakening caused by pain and diarrhea

explanation: Nocturnal pain/diarrhea suggests organic disease (eg, IBD), not functional IBS.
educational_objective: Both inflammatory bowel disease and irritable bowel syndrome can present with abdominal pain and diarrhea. Features that are suggestive of an underlying disease rather than irritable bowel syndrome include occult blood or melena, nocturnal diarrhea, worsening abdominal pain, weight loss, and a family history of inflammatory bowel disease or colon cancer.

question: A 34-year-old woman is brought to the emergency department 30 minutes after being involved in a motor vehicle collision. Sensation to pain is decreased over the left lower extremity. Which of the following labeled regions on the diagram of the spinal cord shown is most likely damaged in this patient?
explanation: Pain/temperature fibers decussate near entry and ascend contralaterally in the lateral spinothalamic tract; left-leg loss implies right tract injury (region D).
educational_objective: The lateral spinothalamic tract carries ascending sensory fibers for pain and temperature. As a result of the immediate decussation of these sensory nerves in the spinal cord, sensations of pain and temperature from the left side of the body ascend in the lateral spinothalamic tract on the contralateral right side of the spinal cord.

question: A 26-year-old man comes to the physician because of a 1-week history of temperatures to 38.3°C (101°F), chills, and chest and back pain. Two weeks ago, he returned from a trip to Costa Rica, where he had been performing ecologic studies of bats in their cave habitats. He reports exposure to bat urine and feces during his studies. Today, his temperature is 38.1°C (100.6°F). Physical examination shows no other abnormalities. A complete blood count and serum chemistry studies are within the reference ranges. A chest x-ray shows bilateral reticulonodular infiltrates. The virulence of the most likely infectious agent in this patient depends on which of the following?

options.B: Invasion of host tissues and vasculature
options.C: Phenotypic switching from yeast to hyphae in the host

explanation: Histoplasma capsulatum survives/replicates within nonactivated macrophages, aiding immune evasion.
educational_objective: Histoplasmosis is an endemic fungal infection caused by Histoplasma capsulatum. The organism is able to evade detection by the immune system through residing and replicating within macrophages, contributing to its virulence.

question: An 18-year-old man has had temperatures to 38.3°C (101°F), a sore throat, and cervical lymph node enlargement for 8 days. A latex agglutination test result for Epstein-Barr virus antibody is positive. Atypical cells with abundant lacey cytoplasm in the peripheral blood smear are most likely derived from which of the following types of cells?
explanation: Atypical lymphocytes in mono are reactive CD8+ T cells responding to EBV-infected B cells.
educational_objective: Infectious mononucleosis is a viral illness caused most often by infection with Epstein-Barr virus (EBV). While EBV infects B lymphocytes through CD21, the atypical lymphocytes seen on peripheral blood smear are cytotoxic CD8+ T lymphocytes reacting to the viral infection.

question: An 84-year-old man is brought to the emergency department 30 minutes after an episode of syncope. Transthoracic echocardiography shows a 4-cm myxoma occupying the majority of the left atrium. The tumor will be excised using a robotically assisted operation via an oblique right atriotomy and transection of the interatrial septum. When making the incision into the left atrium to remove the myxoma, which of the following regions of the interatrial septum should be avoided in order to prevent injury to the cardiac conduction system?

options.B: Posteroinferior region above the opening of the coronary sinus
options.C: Superoanterior region above the limbus of the fossa ovalis
options.D: Superoposterior region posterior to the fossa ovalis

explanation: The AV node lies in the posteroinferior interatrial septum (Koch's triangle) above the coronary sinus; incisions here risk AV block.
educational_objective: Electrical impulses originate from the sinoatrial node, located in the right atrium, and reach the atrioventricular (AV) node, located in the interatrial septum, before being carried to the ventricles via the His-Purkinje system. When transecting the interatrial septum for access to the left atrium, care must be taken to avoid injuring the cardiac conduction system, most importantly, the AV node, which is located in the posteroinferior region of the septum above the opening of the coronary sinus.

question: A 50-year-old man has had progressive dyspnea on exertion over the past 6 months. He now has dyspnea at rest. He has had a persistent dry cough since having an upper respiratory tract bacterial infection 1 year ago. Examination of lung tissue obtained on biopsy shows chronic inflammation and fibrous thickening of the alveolar septa. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation: Usual interstitial pneumonitis (UIP) pattern with interstitial fibrosis/honeycombing fits progressive dyspnea, dry cough, and fibrous septal thickening.
educational_objective: Pulmonary fibrosis results from chronic inflammation of the pulmonary interstitium, classically presenting with dyspnea and a nonproductive cough. Idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis demonstrates a usual interstitial pneumonitis pattern on both imaging and histology.

question: A 62-year-old man is admitted to the intensive care unit after having a myocardial infarction. During the next 36 hours, his serum creatinine concentration increases to 3.9 mg/dL and his urine output decreases. Three days later, he develops polyuria. At the time of discharge from the hospital, his serum creatinine concentration is 2.6 mg/dL. Which of the following is the most likely cause of this patient's episode of acute kidney injury?

options.B: Atheroembolic renal disease with acute renal infarction

explanation: Ischemic injury from cardiogenic shock → ATN with initial oliguria followed by polyuria; proximal tubules are most vulnerable.
educational_objective: Acute tubular necrosis frequently results from ischemic injury to the nephron and is characterized by damage to the proximal convoluted tubule. Sloughing of tubular cells leads to the formation of muddy brown casts. Acute tubular necrosis presents initially with oliguria before progressing to polyuria when the cells regenerate.

question: A 70-year-old man has angiodysplasia of the ascending colon. Which of the following is the most likely complication?
explanation: Fragile, dilated mucosal vessels in angiodysplasia commonly rupture, causing lower GI bleeding.
educational_objective: Angiodysplasia is a common disorder found in older adults and patients with hereditary defects of blood vessel growth and formation (eg, hereditary hemorrhagic telangiectasia). The major complication is bleeding.

question: An 11-year-old boy has had persistent pain in his right knee since he twisted it in a soccer game 3 weeks ago. Physical examination shows a tender area in the distal femur but no perceptible mass. An x-ray of the femur shows an osteolytic mass that has eroded through the cortex and elevated the periosteum; the mass is surrounded by reactive bone in some areas. Biopsy of the mass shows atypical cells with hyperchromatic pleomorphic nuclei. The cells are surrounded by an eosinophilic matrix, some of which is calcified. This tumor is most likely to spread first to which of the following areas?
explanation: Osteosarcoma metastasizes hematogenously with a strong predilection for the lungs.
educational_objective: Osteosarcoma is the most common malignancy of bone. It is an aggressive malignancy that occurs in a bimodal distribution in children and in older adults. It commonly metastasizes to the lungs.

question: A 60-year-old man comes to the emergency department because of swelling of his right elbow that began after he struck it against the edge of a file cabinet earlier that day. On physical examination, the tip of the olecranon is obscured by a golf ball-sized fluctuant mass with well-defined borders. The mass is swollen, mildly tender, and smooth. Range of motion of the elbow is normal. Which of the following structures was most likely injured in this patient?
explanation: Post-traumatic fluid collection over the olecranon reflects olecranon bursitis (inflamed bursa).
educational_objective: Olecranon bursitis is a common orthopedic condition that occurs secondary to trauma to or infection of the bursa. In this condition, fluid collects in the bursa, resulting in a fluctuant, tender mass.

question: A 67-year-old man who is a retired coal miner comes to the physician because of a 2-year history of progressive shortness of breath. He also has had a 23-kg (50-lb) weight loss during this period. He appears cachectic. He is 175 cm (5 ft 9 in) tall and now weighs 54 kg (120 lb); BMI is 18 kg/m2. His temperature is 36.8°C (98.2°F), pulse is 100/min, respirations are 22/min, and blood pressure is 137/83 mm Hg. Physical examination shows symmetric air entry with no crackles or wheezes. A chest x-ray and photomicrograph of lung tissue obtained on biopsy are shown. The structure indicated by the arrow in the photomicrograph most likely represents which of the following?
explanation: Silicotic nodules have a central, concentrically layered collagen core with surrounding inflammatory cells.
educational_objective: Silicosis is an interstitial lung disease caused by inhalation of crystalline silica dust particles, which are deposited in the terminal bronchioles and alveoli. Silicotic nodules are characterized by a central hyaline core made of concentrically layered collagen fibers, surrounded by a less organized zone of inflammatory cells and loose collagen.

question: A 47-year-old woman comes to the physician for a follow-up examination. She has a strong family history of type 2 diabetes mellitus and was diagnosed with this disease 3 months ago. At that time, she began a diet and exercise regimen, which resulted in a 2.7-kg (6-lb) weight loss. She is 165 cm (5 ft 5 in) tall and now weighs 100 kg (220 lb); BMI is 37 kg/m2. Hemoglobin A1c is 9%; 3 months ago, it was 8%. The physician believes that pharmacotherapy is indicated. When he tells the patient that she needs to start an oral medication, the patient says, "I'll take it, but I want to get off of it as soon as possible. How long do you think it will take to get my diabetes under control so I won't have to take the medication anymore?" Which of the following is the most appropriate response by the physician?

options.A: "It sounds as if the idea of taking medication is troubling to you. Tell me more about your concerns regarding your diabetes and our treatment plan."
options.B: "It's important that you take this medication to get your glucose under control. I'll see you in about a month to see how it's working."
options.C: "We don't know how you will respond to the medication. Let's wait and see how you do and take it from there."
options.D: "We've tried managing this with diet and exercise, but now you need the medication."

explanation: First explore and validate emotions with an open-ended invitation before giving facts/education.
educational_objective: After a patient expresses emotional distress about an aspect of medical care, the physician should initially focus on feelings rather than facts and encourage the patient to elaborate on emotions in an open-ended way. If the patient expresses significant distress, the physician should briefly screen for psychiatric disorders (eg, adjustment disorder, major depressive disorder).

question: A 12-year-old girl is brought to the physician by her parents because of a 2-day history of dizziness and headache. She is intelligent and does well in school. Her mother had a cerebellar tumor removed during childhood and is concerned that her daughter might have a similar condition. A normal reaction to which of the following physical examination maneuvers is most likely to rule out a cerebellar tumor in this patient?
explanation: Normal rapid alternating movements argue against cerebellar dysfunction (dysdiadochokinesia indicates cerebellar disease).
educational_objective: The inability to perform rapid alternating movements indicates cerebellar dysfunction. The cerebellum mediates motor learning and calculates movement course changes in response to sensory input.

question: A 31-year-old man comes to the physician 1 day after he noticed that the right side of his face was lower than the left while shaving. On physical examination, he is unable to grimace his right cheek or elevate his right eyebrow. Neurologic examination shows impaired facial expression and loss of taste in the anterior two thirds of the tongue. Which of the following additional neurologic findings is most likely in this patient?
explanation: Facial nerve palsy can involve stapedius paralysis, leading to hyperacusis on the affected side.
educational_objective: Bell palsy refers to isolated facial nerve palsy that is typically secondary to the reactivation of herpes simplex virus. Patients present with complete ipsilateral facial weakness that involves the forehead and can also experience taste and hearing abnormalities.

question: A 68-year-old woman with a 20-year history of hypertension is brought to the emergency department 30 minutes after the sudden onset of right-sided weakness. Her speech is dysarthric. Physical examination shows drooping of the right side of the face. Visual field testing shows no deficits. Muscle strength is 4/5 in the right upper extremity and 3/5 in the right lower extremity. Deep tendon reflexes are 2+ in the upper extremities and left lower extremity and 3+ in the right lower extremity. Sensation is intact throughout. Babinski sign is present on the right. Mental status examination shows no abnormalities. Which of the following is the most likely cause of this patient's condition?

options.A: Embolism of the right anterior cerebral artery
options.B: Lacunar infarct of the internal capsule
options.C: Ruptured aneurysm of the circle of Willis
options.D: Thrombus of the left posterior cerebral artery

explanation: Pure motor hemiparesis from long-standing HTN is typical of a lacunar infarct of the internal capsule.
educational_objective: Lacunar infarcts are ischemic strokes that occur in small penetrating arteries, most commonly involving the basal ganglia or internal capsule. Lacunar strokes of the internal capsule typically result in contralateral hemiparesis.

question: A 55-year-old woman is scheduled to undergo transvaginal hysterectomy and oophorectomy for dysfunctional uterine bleeding. During the procedure, the uterus must be separated from all surrounding pelvic structures. Identification and incision of which of the following structures that attaches to the cervical region and extends posteriorly is most appropriate in this patient?
explanation: The uterosacral ligaments run from the cervix to the sacrum and must be divided during hysterectomy.
educational_objective: The uterosacral ligament is a paired structure that extends bilaterally from the cervical region to the sacrum, helping to support the uterus in the pelvis.

question: A 57-year-old man comes to the physician because of increasingly severe joint pain and weakness during the past 2 months. Physical examination shows pallor. Laboratory studies show: Hemoglobin 8 g/dL; Hematocrit 25%; Leukocyte count 150,000/mm3 (myeloid cells [immature and mature] 90%); Platelet count 50,000/mm3; Philadelphia (Ph1) chromosome present. A chimeric growth-promoting protein with which of the following activities is most likely encoded in this patient due to the presence of this chromosome?
explanation: The t(9;22) Philadelphia chromosome creates BCR-ABL with constitutive tyrosine kinase activity.
educational_objective: CML is a neoplasm of the myeloid cell line that is defined by the presence of the Ph chromosome resulting in constitutive activation of the ABL1 tyrosine kinase. Typical findings include hyperleukocytosis with a diverse array of myeloid lineage cells present on the peripheral smear.

question: A 45-year-old woman has had progressive fatigue and mild shortness of breath with exertion during the past 3 months. She thinks she had rheumatic fever at the age of 10 years. A grade 2/6, rumbling, diastolic murmur is heard at the fifth left intercostal space in the midclavicular line. A lateral x-ray of the chest shows mild posterior displacement of the esophagus. Which of the following cardiovascular structures is most likely responsible for the esophageal displacement?
explanation: Mitral stenosis causes left atrial enlargement; the LA lies anterior to the esophagus and can displace it posteriorly.
educational_objective: Rheumatic fever commonly affects the mitral valve, potentially leading to mitral stenosis later in life and subsequent left atrial enlargement. The left atrium and esophagus have a close anatomic relationship and left atrial enlargement can displace the esophagus posteriorly.

question: A 20-year-old woman comes to the physician because her menstrual period is 1 week late. Menses had occurred at regular 28-day intervals. She had unprotected sexual intercourse with her boyfriend 20 days ago. A urine pregnancy test result is positive. Which of the following best describes the stage of development of the embryo at this time?

options.A: Gastrulation is complete, but there are only two germ layers
options.B: The neural plate is present, but the neural tube is not yet complete
options.C: Placental development is complete, but the embryo is resistant to teratogens
options.D: The sclerotome cells have begun migrating, but the somites have not yet formed

explanation: Around day 20, the neural plate is present (post-gastrulation); neural tube closure occurs in week 4.
educational_objective: In the third week of embryogenesis, gastrulation has occurred, and the neural plate is present. The neural tube will form during week four. The embryo is highly sensitive to teratogens at this time.

question: A study is done to determine the relationship between use of oral contraceptives and cervical cancer. Study subjects include 50,000 women who are using oral contraceptives and 50,000 women who have had a tubal ligation. After 2 years of follow-up, the rate of in situ cervical cancer is 18 per 10,000 women among users of oral contraceptives and 3 per 10,000 among sterilized women (p<0.05). Which of the following is the design of this study?
explanation: Subjects are grouped by exposure and followed for incident disease → prospective cohort study.
educational_objective: A cohort study follows patients over time, either retrospectively or prospectively, and seeks to investigate the impact of exposures or risk factors on an outcome of interest.

question: A 3-month-old girl is brought to the physician by her mother for a well-child examination. Her mother says that the infant can lift her head when lying prone. The patient is eating well and recently started sleeping about 6 uninterrupted hours through the night. The mother adds that the baby does not yet smile in response to human faces and has not started to coo or gurgle with attention. The patient is at the 25th percentile for length and weight and 10th percentile for head circumference. Physical examination shows no other abnormalities. Which of the following best describes this infant's development?
explanation: Motor skills are appropriate, but social and verbal/cognitive milestones are delayed (no smile or coo).
educational_objective: By age 3 months, infants are typically able to hold their head up, grasp toys, smile socially, and babble or coo.

question: A 25-year-old woman comes to the physician because of a 3-year history of irregular menses. Menarche was at the age of 14 years. Puberty began at the age of 12 years and progressed normally. Her blood pressure is 116/62 mm Hg. Physical examination shows increased hair growth on the face and chest. Pelvic examination shows clitoromegaly and a normal-appearing uterus. Serum studies show increased concentrations of 17-hydroxyprogesterone and androstenedione. This patient most likely has a deficiency of which of the following enzyme activities?
explanation: Nonclassic 21-hydroxylase deficiency shunts precursors to androgens → virilization with elevated 17-hydroxyprogesterone/androstenedione.
educational_objective: CAH results from adrenal enzyme deficiencies in the synthesis of cortisol with variable effects on mineralocorticoids and androgens. 21-Hydroxylase deficiency, the most common form, classically presents in genetic females with virilization and hypoaldosteronism during infancy. However, a nonclassic form can present in young adulthood with virilization only.

question: A 45-year-old man comes to the office because of a 2-week history of malaise and lethargy. He has HIV infection and chronic hepatitis B and C. Current medications include antiretroviral therapy. Blood pressure is 144/88 mm Hg. Physical examination shows 1+ pitting edema of all extremities. Results of laboratory studies are shown: Serum Creatinine 2.6 mg/dL Albumin 2.8 g/dL Total cholesterol 278 mg/dL Urine total protein 3725 mg/24 h Pathologic examination of a renal biopsy specimen shows nonlobulated glomeruli with uniform thickening of capillary walls, subepithelial electron dense deposits, and granular IgG immunofluorescent deposits along the glomerular basement membrane. Which of the following is the most likely cause of these findings?

options.A: Focal segmental glomerulosclerosis secondary to HIV infection
options.B: Membranous glomerulonephritis secondary to chronic hepatitis B and C
options.D: Type II membranoproliferative glomerulonephritis secondary to chronic hepatitis B and C

explanation: Nephrotic syndrome with diffuse capillary wall thickening, granular IgG along GBM, and subepithelial deposits—membranous nephropathy from chronic hepatitis.
educational_objective: Membranous nephropathy is the most common nephrotic syndrome in Caucasian patients and is characterized by proteinuria (>3g/day), edema, hypoalbuminemia, and hypercholesterolemia. It can be primary or secondary to conditions such as Hepatitis B or C virus. Classically, biopsy shows diffuse thickening of the glomerular capillary wall, immunofluorescence shows IgG deposition along the glomerular basement membrane, and electron microscopy shows subepithelial deposits.

question: A 14-year-old boy is brought to the physician by his parents because of increasingly severe left knee pain during the past week. The pain is exacerbated by running or kneeling. He plays multiple sports and is currently in the middle of soccer season. There has been no recent trauma to the area or related sports injuries. Physical examination shows full range of motion of both lower extremities. There is a discrete area of swelling just below the left patella over the proximal portion of the tibia. Palpation of the area produces pain. Pain is also reproduced when he does a full squat. Examination of the right knee shows no abnormalities. Which of the following is the most likely cause of this patient's condition?
explanation: Osteochondrosis/traction apophysitis of the tibial tubercle in athletic adolescents causes focal tenderness over an enlarged tibial tubercle and pain with activities that tension the patellar tendon; managed with rest, ice, NSAIDs.
educational_objective: Apophysitis of the tibial tubercle, known as Osgood-Schlatter disease, is a common cause of knee pain at the insertion of the patellar tendon in young athletes. It presents with focal pain and tenderness that is worse with the application of tension to the tibial tubercle.

question: A 68-year-old man comes to the physician because of a 6-month history of progressive shortness of breath. He also has a 1-month history of nonproductive cough. He has a long history of joint pain treated with prednisone. He does not smoke cigarettes, but he was raised in a coal mining community. Vital signs are within normal limits. Physical examination shows no jugular venous distention or edema. There are small painless nodules along the extensor surface of both forearms, ulnar deviation, and swan neck deformities of the fingers. Bilateral diffuse crackles are heard on auscultation of the chest. A chest x-ray shows a diffuse fibronodular infiltrate with a right pleural effusion. A thoracentesis is done, and pleural fluid analysis shows straw-colored fluid containing 200 leukocytes/mm³ and a glucose concentration of 12 mg/dL (N=70). Which of the following is the most likely underlying cause of his current condition?
explanation: Autoimmune synovitis with extra-articular manifestations (rheumatoid nodules, pleural effusions with very low glucose) is characteristic of rheumatoid arthritis.
educational_objective: Rheumatoid arthritis (RA) is an autoimmune disease characterized by joint destruction, periarticular bone loss, synovial hypertrophy, rheumatoid nodules, and can be complicated with development of pleural effusions. Patients present with symmetric arthritis of the wrists and hands and are positive for rheumatoid factor, as well as anti–cyclic citrullinated peptide antibodies. Tumor necrosis factor is key in the pathophysiology of RA and is targeted by disease-modifying agents.

question: A previously healthy 42-year-old Asian woman is brought to the emergency department because of a 24-hour history of nausea, vomiting, and progressive lethargy. She has smoked 1 pack of cigarettes daily for 25 years and drinks four glasses of wine daily. She uses high-dose acetaminophen daily for headaches. She does not use illicit drugs. She is 155 cm (5 ft 1 in) tall and weighs 50 kg (110 lb); BMI is 21 kg/m². She is responsive to painful stimuli. Initial laboratory studies show increased hepatic aminotransferase. Which of the following effects of alcohol most likely contributed to this patient's condition?
explanation: Chronic ethanol induces CYP450, increasing conversion of acetaminophen to the hepatotoxic metabolite NAPQI and causing liver injury at high doses.
educational_objective: Chronic ethanol ingestion leads to the induction of cytochrome P450. Cytochrome P450 is responsible for the generation of the toxic acetaminophen metabolite NAPQI. Patients with a history of chronic ethanol ingestion are at an increased risk of hepatotoxicity when consuming high doses of acetaminophen.

question: A 45-year-old man comes to the physician because of a 4-week history of mild confusion, memory difficulties, generalized muscle aching, and intermittent tingling of his lips and fingers. He says he has been sleeping more than usual, and that he feels "down in the dumps." Vital signs are normal. Physical examination shows no abnormalities except for dry, scaly skin and dry hair. Tapping with a reflex hammer over the left side of the face just anterior to the ear causes left facial muscle contractions. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation: Chvostek sign and paresthesias indicate hypocalcemia due to low PTH from hypoparathyroidism.
educational_objective: Hypoparathyroidism can result in hypocalcemia, which can present with confusion, memory difficulties, myalgias, perioral and/or peripheral paresthesias, and facial muscle spasm upon tapping the facial nerve on examination.

question: A 29-year-old woman comes to the physician because of a 6-day history of rash, joint pain, and fatigue. Her temperature is 37.4°C (99.4°F), and blood pressure is 150/90 mm Hg. Physical examination shows a raised, erythematous, blotchy malar rash and mild peripheral edema. There is tenderness and swelling of several joints. Laboratory studies show: Leukocyte count 3200/mm3 (segmented neutrophils 62%, eosinophils 3%, lymphocytes 29%, monocytes 6%); Platelet count 74,000/mm3; Serum albumin 2.8 g/dL; Antinuclear antibody positive; Antibody to double-stranded DNA positive; Urine protein 3+; RBC casts 2+. Which of the following serologic studies is most likely to produce a false-positive result in this patient?
explanation: Anticardiolipin antibodies in SLE can cause false-positive RPR tests; confirm with treponemal testing.
educational_objective: Patients with SLE also commonly have antiphospholipid antibodies. The RPR test for syphilis evaluates for the presence of antibodies against specific syphilis antigens to which anticardiolipin antibodies react, resulting in a false positive RPR.

question: A 3-year-old boy is brought to the emergency department by his parents because of a 1-hour history of constant cough that began while he was eating a snack. He is actively coughing. Pulmonary examination discloses dullness to percussion and decreased breath sounds in the right lower lung field. Chest x-ray shows a foreign body in the right bronchus with opacification of the right lower lobe. Which of the following is the most likely explanation for the findings in this patient?
explanation: Airway obstruction from aspirated material causes collapse of distal alveoli (obstructive atelectasis) with lobar opacification.
educational_objective: Atelectasis refers to the partial or complete collapse or incomplete expansion of pulmonary parenchyma. However, it can also be seen in patients who have aspirated, causing an obstruction and resultant collapse of alveoli.

question: A 23-year-old woman has a grade 3/6 systolic murmur. Cardiac catheterization shows: Pressure (mm Hg) / O2 Saturation (%) — Right atrium 6 / 75; Right ventricle 30/5 / 80; Pulmonary artery 30/20 / 80; Left atrium 10 / 96; Left ventricle 110/10 / 96; Aorta 110/70 / 96. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation: Step-up in RV O2 saturation with elevated right-sided pressures indicates a left-to-right shunt at the ventricular level (VSD).
educational_objective: Ventricular septal defects are among the most common congenital heart abnormalities. The shunting of oxygenated blood from the high-pressure left ventricle to the right ventricle results in increased right-side pressures, which can be observed through hemodynamic monitoring.

question: Fracture of the humerus places the radial nerve at greatest risk of damage. Which of the following functions would be affected by an injury to this nerve?
explanation: The radial nerve innervates the posterior compartment (extensors) of the forearm; injury impairs extension of the wrist, fingers, and thumb (eg, thumb extension).
educational_objective: Within the forearm, radial nerve innervates the muscles of the posterior compartment (eg, extensor digitorum and extensor pollicis longus/brevis) and supplies sensation to the dorsal lateral hand. Patients with radial nerve injury typically present with weakness in wrist extension ("wrist drop"), finger and thumb extension, and extension and abduction of the thumb.

question: A 48-year-old woman returns to the office because of recurrent episodes of intense flank pain. During the most severe of these episodes, she was evaluated in the emergency department. Urinalysis showed microscopic hematuria. The stone she passed there was 2 mm in diameter and contained calcium oxalate. Serum studies show a calcium concentration of 11.8 mg/dL and a phosphate concentration of 2.9 mg/dL. Which of the following is the most likely cause of this patient's condition?
explanation: Primary hyperparathyroidism causes hypercalcemia with hypophosphatemia and promotes hypercalciuria, predisposing to calcium oxalate stones.
educational_objective: Primary hyperparathyroidism results in hypercalcemia and hypophosphatemia. Increased parathyroid hormone (PTH) levels lead to increased calcium release from bone and calcium reabsorption in the kidneys as well as increased excretion of phosphate in the kidneys. These effects result in hypercalciuria, which predisposes patients to the formation of calcium oxalate kidney stones.

question: A 22-year-old man comes to the physician because of a 1-week history of foul-smelling watery diarrhea and abdominal pain. He just returned from a service trip to rural Indonesia. A photomicrograph of this patient's stool is shown. Which of the following best represents the mechanism of action of the most appropriate pharmacotherapeutic agent for this parasite?
explanation: Metronidazole treats Giardia by generating nitro radicals that damage DNA and lead to cell death in anaerobic/protozoal organisms.
educational_objective: Metronidazole is a nitroimidazole antibiotic used in the treatment of both protozoal infections (eg, Giardia lamblia) and anaerobic bacterial infections (eg, C. difficile). Its mechanism of action relates to the generation of toxic free radicals by its metabolism, which cause damage to DNA and ultimately result in cell death.

question: A 1-year-old boy is brought to the emergency department because of seizures and a foul-smelling odor to the urine. He is lethargic and has poor muscle tone. DNA analysis shows a point mutation (GT→AT) in intron 12 of the affected gene that causes skipping of exon 12. Which of the following is the best explanation for the observed genetic findings?
explanation: A mutation at the conserved splice donor site leads to abnormal pre-mRNA splicing with exon skipping (splice-site defect).
educational_objective: RNA processing defects (eg, splice site mutations) can cause exon skipping during mRNA maturation, resulting in a shorter mRNA and truncated protein with loss of function.

question: A 22-year-old man comes to the student health center because of a scalp rash and blisters that developed 5 days ago and are intermittently painful. He also reports a rash that extends posterolaterally from the right of his umbilicus. The neurons involved in this condition are most likely located in which of the following dorsal root ganglia?
explanation: The umbilicus corresponds to the T10 dermatome; herpes zoster reactivation causes dermatomal vesicular eruption due to involvement of neurons in the corresponding dorsal root ganglion.
educational_objective: The T10 dermatome contains the skin surrounding the umbilicus. Varicella-zoster virus reactivation causes pain and vesicular eruptions along a single dermatome due to inflammation of sensory neurons in dorsal root ganglia.

question: A 41-year-old woman comes to the physician because of increasing systolic hypertension. She has no other medical problems. On physical examination, blood pressure is 150/85 mm Hg. A renal angiogram shows alternating areas of stenosis and dilatation ("string of beads" sign). Which of the following conditions is the most likely cause of this patient's hypertension?
explanation: Alternating stenosis and aneurysmal dilatation of medium-sized arteries producing a "string of beads" angiographic appearance is classic for fibromuscular dysplasia causing renovascular hypertension.
educational_objective: Fibromuscular dysplasia is a nonatherosclerotic process caused by fibroplasia within the wall of medium-sized arteries (most commonly renal), leading to alternating areas of stenosis with intervening aneurysmal dilation ("string of beads") and secondary hypertension.

question: A 58-year-old woman develops fever and malaise. She also has sinus tenderness, nasal ulcers, left tympanic membrane bulging, and urinary findings of 2+ blood and 2+ protein. A biopsy of the sinuses shows granulomata and vasculitis involving blood vessels of various sizes. An autoantibody is most likely directly binding which of the following cell types in this patient?
explanation: Granulomatosis with polyangiitis is associated with c-ANCA (anti-PR3) autoantibodies that target neutrophils, promoting neutrophil activation and small-vessel vasculitis.
educational_objective: Granulomatosis with polyangiitis (Wegener) is a small- and medium-sized vessel necrotizing vasculitis associated with cytoplasmic-antineutrophil cytoplasmic antibodies (c-ANCA) directed against proteinase-3 in neutrophils.

question: A 65-year-old woman is diagnosed with stage I infiltrating ductal carcinoma of the breast. Immunohistologic staining of the tumor is positive for estrogen receptor. She undergoes mastectomy followed by chemotherapy and begins taking tamoxifen to prevent recurrence. The initial site of binding of this agent to its receptor most likely occurs in which of the following areas of the cell?
explanation: Estrogen receptors are intracellular; tamoxifen (a SERM) binds the estrogen receptor in the cytosol, and the ligand–receptor complex then translocates to the nucleus to regulate transcription.
educational_objective: Steroid hormones commonly bind to intracellular receptors. Most steroid hormones (eg, estrogen, androgens, glucocorticoids) bind the receptor in the cytosol, after which it moves to the nucleus where it acts as a transcription factor at the level of the DNA. Other similar hormones (eg, thyroid hormone) bind their receptor in the nucleus, at which time it binds to DNA to exert its effects.

question: A 22-year-old man is brought to the emergency department 30 minutes after a friend found him unconscious on the floor. A drug overdose is suspected. His pulse is 120/min, respirations are 4/min with apparent low tidal volumes, and blood pressure is 120/100 mm Hg. Physical examination shows mild cyanosis. He is intubated and mechanically ventilated with positive pressure ventilation (rate = 12/min; VT = 7 mL/kg) using 10 cm H2O positive end-expiratory pressure (PEEP). Which of the following sets of findings best describes the effects of the mechanical ventilation with PEEP on this patient's alveolar (PA) and intrapleural (P ip) pressures? \n Peak Inspiratory PA End-Tidal PA Peak Inspiratory P ip End-Tidal P ip
explanation: With positive-pressure ventilation and PEEP, both alveolar and intrapleural pressures remain positive relative to atmosphere at peak inspiration and end expiration.
educational_objective: Modern mechanical ventilation utilizes a positive pressure system to drive air into the lungs. This is in contrast to normal, spontaneous breathing, in which outward expansion of the chest wall generates negative intrapleural and alveolar pressures relative to atmosphere, creating a pressure gradient for the movement of air into the lung.

question: A 29-year-old woman is brought to the emergency department 1 hour after being injured in a motor vehicle collision. Abdominal examination shows tenderness with rebound. Vital signs are stable. A CT scan of the abdomen shows no abnormalities except for a small amount of intraperitoneal fluid. After 6 hours of observation, an exploratory laparotomy is done because of continuing severe abdominal pain. No abnormalities are seen until the surgeon gently slides his hand behind the liver; there is a sudden massive hemorrhage from the region of the hand, and the patient's blood pressure becomes undetectable within 1 minute. Which of the following underlying lesions is most likely associated with the hemorrhage?

options.A: Avulsion of hepatic veins from the inferior vena cava
options.C: Traumatic transection of the hepatic artery
options.D: Traumatic transection of the portal vein

explanation: Posterior liver hemorrhage suggests avulsion of hepatic veins from the IVC, which can auto-tamponade until mobilized.
educational_objective: The hepatic veins and IVC lie posterior to the liver and blunt traumatic injury such as in a motor vehicle collision can cause avulsion of the hepatic veins from the IVC, leading to intraperitoneal hemorrhage posterior to the liver.

question: A 48-year-old man comes to the physician because of an episode of fever, cough, chills, and shortness of breath 5 days ago that began several hours after he helped a friend bale and store hay on a farm. The symptoms resolved within 2 days, but he is concerned about what could have caused the incident. He takes no medications and does not smoke cigarettes. His temperature is 37°C (98.6°F), and respirations are 12/min. The lungs are clear to auscultation of the chest. Which of the following conditions is the most likely cause of this patient's acute episode of respiratory symptoms?
explanation: This patient's presentation and exposure history are suggestive of hypersensitivity pneumonitis. Moldy hay is associated with hypersensitivity pneumonitis secondary to the inhalation of dust and mold spores.

question: A previously healthy 6-month-old boy is brought to the physician because of a cough for 1 week. Initially he had a low-grade fever, sneezing, congestion, and runny nose. He then developed a dry intermittent cough. The parents now note that with any startle the baby chokes and gasps. He has not had any immunizations. Physical examination shows paroxysms of "machine gun" -like coughing with a forced expiratory grunt at the end of coughing. Leukocyte count is 30,000/mm3 (70% lymphocytes). Neutrophil chemotaxis and oxidative metabolism are defective due to increased activity of which of the following enzymes?
explanation: Episodes of severe paroxysmal coughing in the setting of a respiratory illness is concerning for pertussis. Pertussis toxin is a major virulence factor that inactivates the Gi subunits of G protein-coupled receptors, leading to uninhibited adenylyl cyclase activity and increased intracellular cAMP.

question: A 14-year-old boy is brought to the emergency department by his friend because of palpitations. His friend says the symptoms began shortly after he "snorted" cocaine. He is found to have tachycardia and increased mean arterial pressure. Which of the following mechanisms is the most likely cause of these adverse effects?

options.A: Agonist action at ligand-gated Na+–K+ channels

explanation: Cocaine blocks the presynaptic reuptake of dopamine, serotonin, and norepinephrine, increasing their concentrations in the synaptic cleft and causing tachycardia and hypertension via adrenergic effects.

question: A 41-year-old man comes to the physician because of a 6-week history of numbness of his right hand. He works in construction. Sensation to pinprick is decreased in the thumb and over a portion of the anterior forearm. The physician suspects that there is compression of the C5 and C6 spinal nerves as they exit the spinal canal. Weakness of which of the following movements on the right is most likely to confirm the diagnosis?
explanation: The C5 and C6 nerve roots innervate deltoid and rotator cuff muscles responsible for shoulder abduction; compression at these roots causes weakness of upper extremity abduction.

question: A 6-year-old boy is admitted to the hospital because of an 8-hour history of fever, headache, and nausea. Administration of intravenous (IV) fluids and empiric antibiotics is started pending culture results. A lumbar puncture is done, and a photomicrograph of a Gram stain of cerebrospinal fluid is shown. During the next24 hours, he develops bleeding from his gums and from all IV puncture sites. He is intubated for respiratory failure, and norepinephrine is administered for blood pressure support. The most likely cause of this patient's new symptoms is which of the following infection-related complications?
explanation: Findings are consistent with meningococcemia complicated by DIC and Waterhouse-Friderichsen syndrome, which causes bilateral adrenal hemorrhage and adrenal insufficiency.

question: A 72-year-old man with multiple myeloma agrees to participate in an investigational chemotherapy clinical trial. Prior to enrollment in the study, peripheral blood B and T lymphocytes are isolated and undergo Southern blot analysis of lymphoid cell-specific genes. Using a single B-lymphocyte J-region probe, analysis of the B-lymphocyte DNA shows a 1.5-kb band. Analysis of the T-lymphocyte DNA using the same J-region probe shows a 6-kb band. The 6-kb band most likely signifies which of the following?
explanation: A 6-kb band with a J-region probe in T cells indicates an unrearranged immunoglobulin (germline) configuration; B cells show a single smaller band after V(D)J rearrangement.

question: A 6-week-old male infant has a persistent discharge from a swollen umbilical stump. If the discharge contains intestinal fluid, to which of the following portions of the gastrointestinal tract is the fistula most likely connected?
explanation: Persistent vitelline duct can form a fistula connecting the umbilicus to the ileum (Meckel diverticulum region), leading to intestinal discharge at the umbilicus.

question: An 18-year-old woman comes to the physician because of a 3-week history of intermittent double vision and transient vision loss. She also has had a 9-kg (20-lb) weight loss during the past 5 months due to decreased appetite. She is 152 cm (5 ft) tall and now weighs 51 kg (112 lb); BMI is 22 kg/m2. Her temperature is 38°C (100.5°F), and blood pressure is 146/88 mm Hg. Funduscopic examination shows a recent retinal hemorrhage of the left eye. Cardiac examination shows bilateral carotid bruits. Radial pulses are diminished on the right side and absent on the left side. Laboratory studies show: Hemoglobin 10.5 g/dL Hematocrit 32% Mean corpuscular volume 95 µm3 Leukocyte count 13,250/mm3 with normal differential Erythrocyte sedimentation rate 84 mm/h Serum IgA 650 mg/dL IgG 3100 mg/dL IgM 852 mg/dL Antinuclear antibodies weakly positive Rheumatoid factor weakly positive. Histologic examination of a carotid artery in this patient will most likely show which of the following types of vasculitis?
explanation: Young woman with diminished pulses, carotid bruits, systemic symptoms, and elevated ESR is consistent with Takayasu arteritis; biopsy shows granulomatous inflammation and intimal fibrosis.

question: A 30-year-old woman and her 35-year-old husband come to the physician for genetic counseling prior to conception. They have a 2-year-old daughter with an isolated ventricular septal defect. The wife's sister had a heart defect, for which she underwent operative repair. Previous evaluation of the couple, including echocardiography, showed no abnormalities. Which of the following best represents this couple's risk for having another child with a congenital heart defect?
explanation: In offspring of phenotypically normal parents, isolated VSD risk approximates the baseline population incidence (~2%–3%) due to heterogeneous, often non-Mendelian causes.
educational_objective: The baseline population VSD incidence is approximately 2% to 3%, with inheritance patterns that do not follow conventional Mendelian patterns apart from those associated with known genetic syndromes.

question: A 27-year-old man who is a weightlifter comes to the physician for a routine examination. He has been taking a synthetic androgen for the past year to increase his muscle mass. Examination shows increased scalp hair loss and mild testicular atrophy. Which of the following is most likely responsible for the decreased size of this patient's testicles?

options.A: Downregulation of pituitary luteinizing hormone receptors
options.B: Downregulation of testicular follicle-stimulating hormone receptors
options.D: Increased negative feedback on gonadotropin secretion

explanation: Exogenous androgens increase negative feedback on GnRH → ↓LH/FSH, reducing Leydig cell stimulation and intratesticular testosterone, causing testicular atrophy.
educational_objective: Testicular atrophy is primarily caused by decreased testicular testosterone synthesis as a result of the absence of stimulation by luteinizing hormone. This commonly occurs in the setting of anabolic steroid use or testosterone replacement therapy, as these exogenous androgens provide excessive negative feedback upon the hypothalamus, thereby causing the decreased production of GnRH and, subsequently, LH.

question: A 2-month-old boy is brought to the physician because of hypotonia and poor feeding since birth. Physical examination shows large fontanels, midface hypoplasia, hepatomegaly, and cryptorchidism. Serum studies show increased concentrations of very-long-chain fatty acids, phytanic acid, and pipecolic acid. If this patient's hepatocytes were analyzed using electron microscopy, results would most likely show the absence of which of the following organelles?
explanation: Zellweger syndrome causes absence of peroxisomes, leading to accumulation of VLCFA, phytanic acid, and pipecolic acid with hypotonia, seizures, and hepatomegaly.
educational_objective: Zellweger syndrome is caused by a genetic absence of peroxisomes and presents classically with seizures, intellectual disability, hypotonia, hepatomegaly, kidney disease, cataracts, hearing loss, and craniofacial abnormalities. Laboratory evaluation will demonstrate increased VLCFA, phytanic acid, and pipecolic acid.

question: An investigator is studying patients with West Nile virus infection. During a 5-year period, data are collected on 25 patients diagnosed with this condition as confirmed by testing at the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention. Demographic information on the patients is reported (age, gender, and ethnicity), as well as information about likely sources of infection. Which of the following best describes this study design?
explanation: A case series describes consecutive or nonconsecutive patients with a disease/treatment in detail; it is observational and does not imply causality.
educational_objective: A case series includes a small number of patients and seeks to describe the course of a disease or treatment. It does not imply a causal relationship. It is observational in nature and is useful in describing a disease or treatment with limited numbers of patients.

question: A full-term female newborn is born with a symmetrically enlarged neck. The swelling is composed of a mass of endothelial cell-lined, cystically dilated spaces filled with lymph. The intervening stroma is scanty, and there are occasional lymphoid aggregates. Which of the following disorders is most likely in this newborn?
explanation: Cystic hygroma (lymphangioma) of the neck in a newborn is classically associated with Turner syndrome (45,X).
educational_objective: Turner Syndrome (45, XO) can present with a cystic hygroma, which is a lymphangioma or cystically dilated space filled with lymph fluid caused by obstruction of the lymphatic system. It is lined with endothelium and does not contain a significant amount of connective tissue.

question: A 58-year-old woman is brought to the emergency department because of a 2-hour history of shortness of breath and chest pain that radiates to her back between the shoulder blades. Her respirations are 28/min. Physical examination shows diaphoresis. An ECG shows no abnormalities. Coronary angiography shows occlusion of the marginal branch of the left anterior descending coronary artery. A percutaneous coronary revascularization is done. Subsequent to the stent's placement, her serum concentrations of myocardial creatine kinase (CK-MB) and troponin I are increased. Which of the following mechanisms best explains these laboratory findings?

options.D: Protease inactivation by cytoplasmic free calcium ions

explanation: Reperfusion injury generates free oxygen radicals that cause membrane lipid peroxidation and protein/DNA damage, leading to release of CK-MB and troponin.
educational_objective: Reperfusion injury occurs when tissue oxygenation is restored following a period ischemia. This occurs because of the generation of free oxygen radicals and peroxides which result in lipid peroxidation, protein modification, and DNA strand breaks.

question: A male newborn is delivered at term with a right-sided aortic arch. Physical examination shows full cheeks, low-set ears, and a small chin. Serum studies show a decreased calcium concentration. Which of the following is the most likely site of the malformations in this patient?
explanation: DiGeorge syndrome (22q11 deletion) causes failure of development of the third and fourth pharyngeal pouches (thymus and parathyroids), leading to hypocalcemia and craniofacial/cardiac anomalies.
educational_objective: The third branchial pouch gives rise to the thymus and inferior parathyroid glands, and the fourth branchial pouch to the superior parathyroid glands. Abnormalities involving development of these pouches typically stem from a deletion of chromosome 22q11, which presents as DiGeorge syndrome or velocardiofacial syndrome.

question: A 25-year-old woman comes to the physician because of a 7-year history of 5- to 10-minute episodes of increased heart rate, sweating, trembling, dizziness, derealization, and intense fear that occur almost daily. She feels well between attacks except for apprehension about when the next attack will occur. Physical examination and laboratory studies show no abnormalities. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation: Recurrent, unexpected panic attacks with autonomic symptoms (eg, palpitations, sweating, trembling, dizziness) and persistent worry about future attacks indicate panic disorder.
educational_objective: Panic attacks feature acute fear or anxiety that peaks within minutes and is associated with symptoms of sympathetic hyperactivity such as tachycardia, heart palpitations, sweating, and trembling along with shortness of breath, chest pain, dizziness, gastrointestinal distress, and paresthesias. Panic disorder is characterized by recurrent panic attacks that are unexpected and associated with worry about future panic attacks or avoidance of panic attack triggers.

question: An 1814-g (4-lb) female newborn is delivered in the hospital at 24 weeks' gestation to a 25-year-old primigravid woman via a spontaneous vaginal delivery. Examination of the newborn shows no peripheral cyanosis. There is a grade 3/6, continuous murmur over the left midclavicular, second intercostal space. At the age of 2 days, the newborn develops respiratory distress. Echocardiography shows a failure of a vascular structure to close. The embryologic origin of this anomaly is most likely which of the following aortic arches?
explanation: Patent ductus arteriosus derives from the sixth aortic arch; failure to close causes a continuous murmur and respiratory distress.
educational_objective: The sixth aortic arch gives rise to the ductus arteriosus, a structure that allows shunting of placental oxygenated blood from the pulmonary artery to the systemic circulation during development in utero but closes shortly after birth. Persistence of this structure is called a patent ductus arteriosus (PDA). Symptoms are dependent upon the size of the PDA and the degree of left-to-right shunting, with severe shunts causing right-sided heart failure and pulmonary hypertension.
