explanation: CKD causes hyperphosphatemia and low 1,25-(OH)₂D, leading to hypocalcemia and secondary hyperparathyroidism (↑PTH). ATN/dehydration do not cause this pattern; RCC causes PTHrP with hypercalcemia.
educational_objective: CKD leads to hypocalcemia, hyperphosphatemia, and secondary hyperparathyroidism.

question: A 16-month-old girl is brought to the physician because she has refused to move her right arm since her older brother grabbed her right hand 1 hour ago to stop her from running into the street. On examination, she is holding the right arm in pronation. Any attempt to move the arm causes crying. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?

options.A: Fracture of the distal radius and ulna
options.B: Salter-Harris type I fracture of the humerus

explanation: "Nursemaid's elbow" = radial head subluxation from annular ligament displacement after axial traction on a pronated forearm.
educational_objective: Axial traction on a pronated arm in toddlers causes annular ligament slippage and radial head subluxation.

question: A pharmaceutical company develops a new opioid drug (Drug X) that binds to the same receptor as morphine does. Drug X is compared with morphine to test its analgesic effect. The graph shows the log dose-response curves for morphine and Drug X. Based on these results, which of the following best describes Drug X?
explanation: A partial agonist produces lower maximal efficacy (Emax) than a full agonist even with full receptor occupancy. Competitive antagonists shift potency; inverse agonists reduce basal activity.
educational_objective: Partial agonists have limited efficacy and can blunt full-agonist effects.

question: A 32-year-old woman comes to the physician because of a 7-day history of sneezing, nasal stuffiness, and watery eyes. She has a history of similar symptoms each spring while gardening. Her temperature is 37°C (98.6°F). Which of the following types of cells are most likely to be increased in her nasal secretions as a result of this reaction?
explanation: Type I hypersensitivity involves IgE-mediated mast cell degranulation with eosinophil recruitment.
educational_objective: Allergic rhinitis features eosinophilic inflammation.

question: A 43-year-old man comes to the physician because of progressive shortness of breath during the past year. He is a stockbroker and has had no environmental exposure to toxins. When asked about his smoking habits, he says he smoked marijuana in college and afterwards, until the age of 28 years. He has not smoked any substance since then. He was adopted as a child and does not know his family history. His respirations are 29/min. Diffuse wheezing is heard on auscultation of the chest. Abdominal examination shows mild hepatomegaly. Pulmonary function tests show a decreased FEV₁ and decreased diffusing capacity. A chest x-ray shows hyperinflation consistent with air trapping mostly in the lung bases. A CT scan of the chest is shown. Which of the following is the most likely cause of these findings?
explanation: α1-antitrypsin deficiency causes panacinar emphysema (basilar) and liver disease. Marijuana alone is unlikely to explain these findings; asthma shows normal/high DLCO.
educational_objective: AAT deficiency causes panacinar emphysema and liver dysfunction.

question: A 54-year-old man comes to the physician because of a 3-day history of low back pain. His temperature is 38.3°C (101°F), pulse is 75/min, and blood pressure is 120/80 mm Hg. Physical examination shows right-sided flank tenderness to percussion. A CT scan of the abdomen shows a lesion consistent with an abscess along the posterior medial aspect of the right kidney. Extension of this process into this patient's pelvis is most likely to occur along which of the following surfaces?
explanation: Collections along the psoas can track inferiorly into the pelvis along the psoas fascia.
educational_objective: Psoas fascia provides a path for retroperitoneal infections to extend into the pelvis.

question: The prevalence of a disease is three times greater in women than in men, but the incidence of the disease is no different in women than it is in men. Which of the following best explains these findings?

options.A: The duration of the disease is shorter in men
options.B: The number of new cases in women is increasing
options.C: Women use medical care facilities more often than men

explanation: With equal incidence, higher prevalence in women implies longer disease duration in women (or shorter in men).
educational_objective: Prevalence = incidence × duration; longer duration increases prevalence.

question: A 51-year-old woman comes to the physician because of a 5-month history of occasional vague hip and thigh pain when working in her garden. Physical examination shows no abnormalities. Laboratory studies show an increased serum alkaline phosphatase activity. An x-ray of her right hip and upper leg shows a dense thickening of the bony cortex in the femur. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation: Paget disease shows elevated ALP from increased bone turnover and thickened, sclerotic, "mosaic" bone; osteomalacia has low mineralization; osteoporosis has normal ALP and thin cortex.
educational_objective: Paget disease causes disordered bone remodeling with high ALP and thickened cortex.

question: A 44-year-old woman comes to the physician because of a 3-day history of a persistent nosebleed and a diffuse rash. She has no history of major medical illness and takes aspirin occasionally for headaches. Her vital signs are within normal limits. A photograph of her left foot is shown. Similar findings are on the torso and upper and lower extremities. Laboratory studies show Hemoglobin 13 g/dL, Hematocrit 38%, Mean corpuscular volume 85 μm³, Leukocyte count 6200/mm³, Platelet count <5000/mm³, Serum Urea nitrogen 10 mg/dL, and Creatinine 0.7 mg/dL. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation: Severe thrombocytopenia with mucocutaneous bleeding is most consistent with ITP, but among choices, Bernard-Soulier (GPIb defect) can present with thrombocytopenia and mucocutaneous bleeding (though typically with large platelets). HUS/TTP feature hemolysis and renal/neuro findings; aspirin affects function, not count.
educational_objective: In isolated mucocutaneous bleeding with very low platelets and normal renal/hemolysis labs, consider primary platelet disorders (e.g., ITP; BS if congenital).

question: Alterations of the p53 tumor suppressor gene are most likely seen in patients who have which of the following neoplasms?
explanation: In the adenoma–carcinoma sequence, p53 loss is a late event driving progression to carcinoma. Burkitt: c-MYC; melanoma commonly involves BRAF/p16.
educational_objective: p53 mutations are common in the progression of colorectal carcinoma.

question: A 36-year-old man is brought to the emergency department 30 minutes after he sustained burns in a house fire. He is 185 cm (6 ft 1 in) tall and weighs 86 kg (190 lb); BMI is 25 kg/m². Physical examination shows second-degree burns over approximately 40% of the body surface area. Intravenous fluids are administered, and he is admitted to the intensive care unit for supportive care. Compared with a healthy individual, which of the following best represents this patient's nutritional and fluid requirements?
explanation: Major burns cause hypermetabolic state (↑caloric/protein needs) and large fluid requirements due to capillary leak and evaporative losses.
educational_objective: Burn patients require aggressive fluid resuscitation and increased calories/protein.

question: A 1-year-old boy receives a left cochlear implant that consists of an array of electrodes. Six months ago, he was diagnosed with severe bilateral hearing deficit. Which of the following elements of the auditory system must remain intact for this patient to perceive auditory stimulation via activation of the electrodes in the implant?
explanation: Cochlear implants bypass hair cells and stimulate the spiral ganglion (auditory nerve); the nerve must be intact to perceive sound.
educational_objective: Cochlear implants require an intact auditory (cochlear) nerve.

question: A 23-year-old woman comes to the physician because of a 3-week history of frequent thirst and urination; she also has had a 3-kg (6.6-lb) weight loss during this period. Physical examination shows dehydration and tachypnea. Serum studies show a glucose concentration of 330 mg/dl, 2+ ketones, and pH of 7.2. Following the administration of intravenous fluids and insulin, there is marked improvement. The activity of which of the following enzymes has most likely increased in this patient's hepatocytes because of this treatment?
explanation: Insulin upregulates hepatic glucokinase and glycogen synthesis while inhibiting glucose output (↓G6Pase, ↓glycogen phosphorylase).
educational_objective: Insulin promotes hepatic glucose uptake via glucokinase and glycogenesis.

question: A 42-year-old woman comes to the physician 2 weeks after she found a nodule in the left side of her neck. She is otherwise asymptomatic. Physical examination shows no other abnormalities. She undergoes a thyroid scan with ¹²³I, a nondestructive isotope. After 1 week, the largest amount of circulating ¹²³I would most likely be in which of the following?
explanation: Most circulating iodine is in protein-bound T₄ (long half-life ~7 days) on TBG; FT₄/FT₃ fractions are tiny; T₃ has a short half-life.
educational_objective: Circulating radioiodine is predominantly in TBG-bound T₄ at 1 week.

question: A 5-year-old girl is brought to the physician because of a 4-day history of stumbling gait, muscle rigidity, slurred speech, and decreased cognitive function. Ophthalmologic examination shows decreased visual acuity and inability to discern colors. Assays of isolated muscle mitochondria show decreased ability to oxidize NADH but normal FADH₂ oxidation. Which of the following electron transport chain complexes is most likely impaired in this patient?
explanation: Complex I (NADH dehydrogenase) impairment decreases NADH oxidation with preserved FADH₂ entry (Complex II).
educational_objective: Complex I defects impair NADH entry into the electron transport chain.

question: A 25-year-old man comes to the emergency department because of a 3-day history of abdominal cramps and diarrhea. He appears anxious. Physical examination shows piloerection and diffuse abdominal tenderness. Neurologic examination shows no abnormalities. He is oriented to person, place, and time. The most likely cause of this patient's condition is withdrawal from which of the following substances? NBME 30 Questions - Formatted
explanation: The symptom cluster (GI hyperactivity, piloerection, cramps) best matches opioid withdrawal; among options, none list opioids. Of the choices, benzodiazepine/alcohol withdrawal feature tremor, anxiety, seizures rather than piloerection/diarrhea; cocaine/marijuana lack these autonomic GI signs. (Opioid withdrawal would be the correct diagnosis.)
educational_objective: Opioid withdrawal causes diarrhea, piloerection, abdominal cramping, and anxiety; recognize even when distractor lists omit opioids.

question: A 16-year-old girl is brought to the emergency department because of a 2-hour history of rash and burning pain on her shoulders and arms. She had been hiking outdoors on a sunny day for several hours before the symptoms began. Her only medication is oral tetracycline for facial acne. Her temperature is 37°C (98.6°F). Physical examination shows diffuse erythema over the shoulders and upper extremities, and bullous lesions over the shoulders. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation: This presentation represents photosensitivity due to a photosensitizing drug (tetracycline). Among options, the closest sun-triggered eruption is polymorphous light eruption; contact dermatitis and drug-induced lupus have different distributions/findings.
educational_objective: Tetracyclines can cause phototoxic reactions on sun-exposed skin.

question: A 42-year-old man develops supraventricular tachycardia 15 minutes after undergoing an abdominal operation. An intravenous infusion with an ultrashort-acting β-adrenoreceptor blocking agent is started. This drug is most likely which of the following?
explanation: Esmolol is a very short-acting, IV β₁-selective blocker used for acute SVT rate control.
educational_objective: Esmolol provides rapid, titratable β-blockade for acute tachyarrhythmias.

question: A full-term female newborn is born with a symmetrically enlarged neck. The swelling is composed of a mass of endothelial cell-lined, cystically dilated spaces filled with lymph. The intervening stroma is scanty, and there are occasional lymphoid aggregates. Which of the following disorders is most likely in this newborn?
explanation: Correct: Cystic hygroma (lymphatic malformation) of the neck is classically associated with Turner syndrome; these lesions are composed of dilated lymphatic spaces lined by endothelium, often presenting as a posterior neck mass in newborns【turn10file0†First Aid USMLE Step 1 2024 (1).pdf†L1-L9】. Incorrect: Amniotic bands cause limb/digit constriction, not neck lymphatic malformations. Cystic fibrosis causes meconium ileus, failure to thrive, pulmonary disease—no neonatal neck mass. Cystic teratoma is a germ cell tumor with multiple tissue types, not lymph-filled spaces. Wilms tumor is a renal tumor presenting as an abdominal mass, not a neck lesion.
educational_objective: Cystic hygroma (lymphatic malformation) of the neck is strongly linked to Turner syndrome.

question: A 45-year-old man comes to the physician for evaluation of worsening heartburn, which has been present for the past 15 months. The pain has become more frequent and severe in the past month and is no longer relieved by antacids. He also has occasional trouble swallowing. Endoscopic examination shows erythema of the lower third of the esophagus. Microscopic biopsies of this area show basal zone hyperplasia and an eosinophilic infiltrate of the squamous mucosa. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation: Correct: GERD causes reflux (erosive) esophagitis; symptoms are heartburn and dysphagia, and complications include erosive esophagitis and Barrett esophagus【turn14file5†First Aid USMLE Step 1 2024 (1).pdf†L20-L29】【turn14file12†First Aid USMLE Step 1 2024.pdf†L56-L65】. Histology classically shows basal cell hyperplasia and inflammatory cells (often eosinophils) in the squamous mucosa. Incorrect: Achalasia shows impaired LES relaxation with "bird's beak" and dysmotility, not reflux injury【turn14file5†First Aid USMLE Step 1 2024 (1).pdf†L1-L7】. Barrett esophagus is intestinal metaplasia (nonciliated columnar with goblet cells), not squamous with eosinophils【turn14file12†First Aid USMLE Step 1 2024.pdf†L62-L65】. Candidiasis causes white plaques (pseudomembranes) on endoscopy in immunosuppressed patients【turn14file5†First Aid USMLE Step 1 2024 (1).pdf†L35-L36】.
educational_objective: Chronic GERD causes reflux esophagitis with basal cell hyperplasia and inflammatory (often eosinophilic) infiltrates; long-standing GERD can progress to Barrett metaplasia.

question: A 25-year-old man comes to the physician 10 days after injuring his right elbow while trying to lift an 80- lb dumbbell at the gym. When he attempted to lift the weight from the rack, he felt a popping sensation and pain in his right elbow. He uses anabolic steroids. His pulse is 78/min, and blood pressure is 150/95 mm Hg. Examination of the right upper extremity shows swelling of the antecubital fossa and ecchymoses from the antecubital fossa to the mid forearm on the anterior side. There is tenderness to palpation over the proximal aspect of the anterior forearm. He is able to flex the elbow actively, but he is unable to flex the elbow or supinate the forearm against resistance. This patient has most likely injured a muscle-tendon unit that is supplied by which of the following nerves?
explanation: Correct: Loss of powerful elbow flexion and forearm supination points to biceps brachii rupture; biceps (and brachialis) are innervated by the musculocutaneous nerve, which also contributes to supination via biceps【turn9file0†First Aid USMLE Step 1 2024.pdf†L24-L27】. Incorrect: Anterior interosseous (branch of median) supplies deep forearm flexors (e.g., FDP lateral half), not biceps. Median nerve does not innervate elbow flexors that supinate. Ulnar nerve innervates intrinsic hand muscles and FCU/FDP medial half, not biceps.
educational_objective: Biceps brachii (main supinator with the supinator muscle) is innervated by the musculocutaneous nerve; rupture impairs resisted flexion and supination.

question: A 47-year-old man comes to the physician because of a 2-week history of a persistent, nonproductive cough. He has a 3-year history of hypertension treated with a thiazide diuretic. A second drug was added to his medication regimen 2 weeks ago. Vital signs are within normal limits. Pulmonary examination shows no abnormalities. Which of the following drugs was most likely added to this patient's medication regimen?
explanation: Correct: ACE inhibitors (eg, enalapril) commonly cause dry cough due to bradykinin accumulation【turn11file0†First Aid USMLE Step 1 2024.pdf†L1-L5】. Incorrect: Clonidine (α2-agonist) causes sedation, rebound HTN; no cough. HCTZ he already takes. Metoprolol (β1-blocker) can cause bradycardia, fatigue, ED; no dry cough. Nifedipine (DHP CCB) causes flushing, edema, headache; no ACE-cough.
educational_objective: ACE inhibitors can cause a dry cough from increased bradykinin.

question: A 30-year-old woman has diarrhea and crampy abdominal pain. Which of the following historical features most strongly suggests that the cause is inflammatory bowel disease rather than irritable bowel syndrome?

options.B: More than three bowel movements daily

explanation: Correct: Frequent, persistent diarrhea with systemic/inflammatory features (eg, high stool frequency, weight loss, nocturnal symptoms, elevated fecal calprotectin) favors IBD over IBS【turn10file0†First Aid USMLE Step 1 2024 (1).pdf†L1-L9】. (Among the listed options, higher stool frequency is most suggestive of an inflammatory process.) Incorrect: LLQ cramps and stress are common in IBS. Lactose intolerance is a separate malabsorptive disorder often overlapping with IBS but not diagnostic of IBD.
educational_objective: IBD presents with inflammatory features (e.g., frequent diarrhea, systemic signs) whereas IBS lacks objective inflammation.

question: During an experimental study, a glutamate antagonist is administered to 100 patients with a history of acute cerebral infarction to target the N-methyl-D-aspartate receptor. Which of the following is the intended result of this therapy?

options.B: Increased removal of cellular debris by glial cells

explanation: Correct: NMDA receptor antagonism reduces glutamate-mediated excitotoxicity by limiting pathologic Ca²⁺ influx into neurons, a mechanism leveraged (e.g., memantine) to prevent excitotoxic injury【turn10file8†First Aid USMLE Step 1 2024.pdf†L42-L45】. Incorrect: Enhanced glutamate release or transporter stimulation would increase synaptic glutamate effects. Microglial debris removal is unrelated to NMDA blockade.
educational_objective: NMDA receptor blockade aims to reduce glutamate-mediated Ca²⁺ influx and excitotoxic neuronal injury.

question: A previously healthy 26-year-old woman comes to the physician because of a 1-day history of severe rectal pain with no bleeding. She takes no medications and does not smoke cigarettes or drink alcohol. She has been sexually active, and she and her partner use condoms inconsistently. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation: Correct: Thrombosed external hemorrhoids cause acute severe anal pain; bleeding may be absent. Anal fissures typically cause pain with defecation and bright red blood on toilet paper and are classically posterior midline【turn11file0†First Aid USMLE Step 1 2024 (1).pdf†L1-L5】, making "severe pain without bleeding" more consistent with an external hemorrhoid here. Incorrect: Anal carcinoma is usually painless until late; fissures often have bleeding; skin tags are painless.
educational_objective: Thrombosed external hemorrhoids cause acute severe anal pain; fissures typically cause painful defecation with bright red blood.

question: A 10-year-old boy who has had type 1 diabetes mellitus for 1 year is receiving insulin. One hour after his morning dose of insulin, he becomes tremulous and diaphoretic and has tachycardia. Several hours later, his symptoms resolve. His blood glucose concentration is now increased. Which of the following is the most likely cause of this patient's hyperglycemia?

options.C: Inhibition of hepatic protein kinase A

explanation: Correct: Counterregulatory catecholamines (and glucagon) released after insulin-induced hypoglycemia stimulate hepatic β-adrenergic/GPCR pathways → ↑ adenylyl cyclase → ↑ cAMP/PKA → ↑ glycogenolysis and gluconeogenesis, causing rebound hyperglycemia【turn10file0†First Aid USMLE Step 1 2024 (1).pdf†L105-L111】. Incorrect: Muscle glycogen synthase activation would lower glucose; muscle phosphorylase activation raises lactate for Cori cycle but hepatic AC is the proximate driver; inhibiting hepatic PKA would reduce, not increase, hepatic glucose output.
educational_objective: Hypoglycemia triggers catecholamine/glucagon signaling (adenylyl cyclase→cAMP→PKA) to raise hepatic glucose production.

question: A 56-year-old woman comes to the emergency department because of a 1-month history of a painful, enlarging mass on the right side of her jaw. She has not noticed any drainage from the area. She has had no fever or other systemic symptoms. She appears thin. Her vital signs are within normal limits. Physical examination shows a tender, 3-cm, firm mass on the right mandible with mild overlying erythema and warmth but no exudate. Oral examination shows multiple dental caries. There is shotty anterior right cervical lymphadenopathy. A CT scan of the head shows a heterogeneous, 3-cm, soft-tissue mass with associated bony changes indicative of osteomyelitis. Aerobic cultures grow no organisms. Which of the following is the most likely causative organism?
explanation: Correct: Cervicofacial "lumpy jaw," poor dentition, osteomyelitis, and negative aerobic cultures point to Actinomyces (anaerobic, filamentous gram-positive) often producing sulfur granules【turn10file3†First Aid USMLE Step 1 2024 (1).pdf†L45-L52】. Incorrect: Fusobacterium can cause Lemierre syndrome from oropharyngeal infection, not typical jaw osteomyelitis with sulfur granules; Propionibacterium (Cutibacterium) acnes is linked to acne, prosthetic/shoulder infections.
educational_objective: Cervicofacial actinomycosis presents with chronic mandible lesions/osteomyelitis and sulfur granules; cultures require anaerobic conditions.

question: A 3-year-old boy has progressive coarsening of his facial features, hirsutism, hepatomegaly, and developmental delay. X-rays of the skeletal system show dysostosis multiplex. Which of the following is primarily involved in this condition?
explanation: Correct concept: The vignette describes a mucopolysaccharidosis (eg, Hurler/Hunter) characterized by lysosomal enzyme deficiencies leading to glycosaminoglycan accumulation (dysostosis multiplex, coarse facies, hepatosplenomegaly). Among choices, none lists "lysosome," which is the correct organelle. Educationally, this is a lysosomal storage disorder.
educational_objective: Mucopolysaccharidoses are lysosomal storage diseases; the primary organelle involved is the lysosome (not listed among options).

question: A 65-year-old woman with cirrhosis comes to the physician because of progressive shortness of breath during the past 3 months. Her pulse is 94/min, respirations are 20/min, and blood pressure is 100/60 mm Hg. Physical examination shows ascites and marked edema of the lower extremities up to the hips. A chest x-ray shows bilateral pleural effusions. Echocardiography shows a left ventricular ejection fraction of 55%. Which of the following is the most likely cause of the increased intra-alveolar fluid in this patient?
explanation: Correct: Cirrhosis causes hypoalbuminemia → ↓ plasma oncotic (colloid osmotic) pressure → transudative fluid accumulation (eg, ascites, effusions) and predisposition to pulmonary edema/effusions with normal LV systolic function. Incorrect: Systolic dysfunction would lower EF. Increased capillary hydrostatic pressure (eg, left heart failure) is unlikely with normal EF. Lymphatic obstruction causes exudative, protein-rich effusions.
educational_objective: Hypoalbuminemia from cirrhosis lowers plasma oncotic pressure, favoring fluid transudation into interstitial and pleural spaces.

question: A 16-year-old girl is brought to the physician because of excessive dieting, constant studying, and social withdrawal during the past 3 weeks. She is 168 cm (5 ft 6 in) tall and weighs 48 kg (106 lb); BMI is 17 kg/m². Her blood pressure is 95/66 mm Hg. Physical examination shows dry skin and fine hair growth. This patient has most likely been abusing which of the following substances?
explanation: Correct: Anorexia nervosa features include hypotension and lanugo; the binge/purge subtype is associated with purging behaviors such as laxative or diuretic abuse【turn14file2†First Aid USMLE Step 1 2024.pdf†L41-L50】. Among listed substances, diuretic abuse is most typical of weight-control purging. Incorrect: Alcohol does not explain the phenotype. Amphetamines can reduce appetite but typically cause tachycardia, insomnia; not classic purging. Thyroid hormone abuse causes heat intolerance/tachycardia rather than lanugo/hypotension.
educational_objective: In eating disorders, especially binge/purge patterns, diuretic (or laxative) abuse is a common purging behavior.

question: Virus isolates are obtained from the blood of a man infected with HIV before and after 1 year of treatment with a drug regimen that includes zidovudine (AZT). Sensitivity testing for zidovudine shows decreased sensitivity after treatment. The viral gene most likely to have mutated during the year to cause this change is the one encoding which of the following proteins?
explanation: Correct: Zidovudine (an NRTI) targets reverse transcriptase; resistance develops via mutations in the pol gene encoding viral polymerase (RT)【turn13file14†First Aid USMLE Step 1 2024.pdf†L26-L33】. Incorrect: Envelope glycoproteins are env. Integrase is pol but not AZT's direct target. Transactivators (eg, tat) are regulatory proteins, not the RT target.
educational_objective: NRTI resistance in HIV arises from mutations in pol encoding reverse transcriptase.

question: Within the Ashkenazi Jewish population, the frequency of Tay-Sachs disease is approximately 1 in 3600. Assuming that this population is in Hardy-Weinberg equilibrium, which of the following is the expected frequency of heterozygous carriers within this population?
explanation: Correct: q² = 1/3600 → q = 1/60. Carrier frequency = 2q ≈ 2/60 = 1/30 (p ≈ 1)【turn10file6†First Aid USMLE Step 1 2024.pdf†L99-L104】. Incorrect: 1/60 equals q, not 2q; 1/120 is half the carrier frequency; 1/3600 is affected frequency (q²).
educational_objective: For autosomal recessive disorders in HWE, carrier frequency ≈ 2q when q ≪ 1.

question: A 23-year-old woman comes to the physician because of a 3-week history of fatigue and muscle pain shortly after she begins exercising; her symptoms decrease as exercise proceeds. Physical examination shows no abnormalities. Her fasting serum glucose concentration is 90 mg/dL. Following exercise of the left forearm, her serum lactic acid concentration does not increase in blood obtained from the left antecubital vein; however, ammonia concentration does increase. A muscle biopsy specimen is positive for periodic acid-Schiff staining. This patient most likely has a deficiency of which of the following muscle enzymes?
explanation: Correct: McArdle disease (myophosphorylase deficiency) causes early fatigue/cramps, flat lactate after forearm exercise, with ↑ ammonia; glycogen accumulates in muscle (PAS+)【turn10file0†First Aid USMLE Step 1 2024.pdf†L1-L4】【turn10file0†First Aid USMLE Step 1 2024.pdf†L11-L18】. Incorrect: Acid maltase (Pompe) causes cardiomyopathy/respiratory failure. Branching enzyme (Andersen) causes severe infantile hepatic disease. PDH deficiency causes lactic acidosis/neurologic issues, not this forearm test pattern.
educational_objective: McArdle disease (myophosphorylase deficiency) causes exercise intolerance with flat lactate and elevated ammonia during forearm testing.

question: A 24-year-old man comes to the physician because his wife has been unable to conceive for the past 2 years. Previous evaluation of his wife showed no abnormalities. He has no history of major medical illness. He does not smoke cigarettes. Physical examination shows a left testicle that is smaller than the right and an enlarged left spermatic cord that increases in size with Valsalva maneuver. Laboratory studies show oligospermia. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation: Correct: "Bag of worms" scrotal mass that enlarges with Valsalva, often left-sided, can impair spermatogenesis (oligospermia)【turn13file9†First Aid USMLE Step 1 2024.pdf†L41-L46】. Incorrect: Cryptorchidism is undescended testis; epididymitis presents with pain and inflammation; hypospadias is a urethral opening anomaly.
educational_objective: Varicocele (dilated pampiniform plexus) is classically left-sided, increases with Valsalva, and can cause infertility.

question: An experimental animal has a blood flow of 4 mL/sec in a small arterial segment of the mesenteric circulation. Which of the following best describes the blood flow (in mL/sec) if the diameter of the vessel is decreased by one half with no change in the perfusion pressure gradient?
explanation: Correct: Flow ∝ r⁴ (Poiseuille's law). Halving diameter halves radius → flow × (1/2)⁴ = 1/16. 4 × 1/16 = 0.25 mL/sec【turn11file0†First Aid USMLE Step 1 2024.pdf†L1-L5】. Incorrect: 0.5, 1 are too high; 16 implies an increase, which is opposite.
educational_objective: According to Poiseuille's law, flow changes with the fourth power of radius; halving radius reduces flow to 1/16.

question: A 25-year-old woman comes to the physician because of a 7-year history of 5- to 10-minute episodes of increased heart rate, sweating, trembling, dizziness, derealization, and intense fear that occur almost daily. She feels well between attacks except for apprehension about when the next attack will occur. Physical examination and laboratory studies show no abnormalities. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation: Correct: Recurrent abrupt panic attacks with ≥4 somatic/cognitive symptoms and ≥1 month of persistent concern/behavior change meet criteria【turn13file1†First Aid USMLE Step 1 2024 (1).pdf†L25-L55】. Incorrect: Alcohol withdrawal has temporal relation to cessation. Diencephalic epilepsy would show seizures/EEG findings. GAD is chronic persistent worry without discrete attacks. Atrial fibrillation causes palpitations but not derealization/intense fear episodes.
educational_objective: Panic disorder features recurrent unexpected attacks with somatic symptoms and anticipatory anxiety for ≥1 month.

question: Protection against paralytic poliomyelitis can be achieved either by oral administration of live attenuated poliovirus (Sabin) vaccine or by parenteral administration of killed poliovirus (Salk) vaccine. The common features of these two vaccines, which accounts for their efficacy, is their ability to induce which of the following poliovirus-specific immune responses?

options.A: Activated CD8+ cytotoxic T lymphocyte effectors in the gut
options.C: Neutralizing secretory IgA antibodies in the gut

explanation: Correct concept: Both vaccines protect via serum neutralizing antibodies (IgG) that prevent viremia and CNS invasion. Secretory IgA in the gut is enhanced by Sabin (live oral) specifically, not by Salk (parenteral inactivated). CD8+ responses are not the primary protective mechanism for poliovirus.
educational_objective: Both Salk and Sabin vaccines confer protection mainly by inducing serum neutralizing IgG; mucosal IgA is unique to live oral Sabin.

question: A 74-year-old woman is admitted to the hospital to undergo a cholecystectomy. During the operation, she becomes acutely hypotensive. The hypotension persists for 5 minutes despite administration of appropriate pressor agents. Which of the following morphologic lesions is most likely to occur in this patient as a result of this incident?

options.B: Lacunar infarcts of the basal ganglia

explanation: Correct concept: Global cerebral hypoperfusion causes watershed cortical infarcts and selective vulnerability of hippocampal CA1 neurons ("red neurons"), not enlargement. Pineal infarction is not typical. Lacunar infarcts are due to lipohyalinosis from chronic hypertension, not transient intraoperative hypotension. Berry aneurysm rupture causes subarachnoid hemorrhage unrelated to hypotension.
educational_objective: Global cerebral ischemia from hypotension injures watershed zones and CA1 hippocampal neurons ("red neurons"), not the listed options.

question: A 40-year-old woman comes to the physician because of a 3-month history of continuous watery diarrhea that has gradually increased in severity; she has had an 11-kg (24-lb) weight loss during this period. Physical examination shows skin tenting and sunken eyes, and orthostatic hypotension. Tests of the stool are negative for ova, parasites, and Clostridium difficile. A CT scan of the abdomen shows a mass in the pancreas. Treatment with standard antidiarrheal medications is ineffective. Administration of a somatostatin analogue, octreotide, results in improvement of the diarrhea. This patient most likely has a tumor secreting which of the following agents?
explanation: Correct: VIPoma (pancreatic neuroendocrine tumor) causes watery diarrhea, hypokalemia, achlorhydria (WDHA); diarrhea improves with somatostatin analogs like octreotide【turn10file2†First Aid USMLE Step 1 2024.pdf†L1-L8】. Incorrect: CCK stimulates gallbladder/pancreatic secretion; gastrinoma causes ulcers/acid hypersecretion; histamine is involved in carcinoid flushing/acid via H2 receptors but not refractory watery diarrhea controlled by octreotide in this syndrome.
educational_objective: VIPomas cause secretory watery diarrhea responsive to somatostatin analogs.

question: A 22-year-old man is brought to the emergency department 15 minutes after sustaining a gunshot wound to the abdomen. His pulse is 110/min, respirations are 20/min, and blood pressure is 100/60 mm Hg. Abdominal examination shows an entrance wound in the left upper quadrant and no exit wound. The injured organ is removed. The bullet is most likely lodged in which of the following organs?
explanation: Correct: A LUQ gunshot injuring the spleen (removed intraoperatively) often continues posteriorly to the retroperitoneal left kidney, making it the most likely final resting site. Incorrect: Adrenal is small and superior to kidney; left ventricle lies more medial/anterior and is protected by ribs/sternum; if spleen is removed, the bullet has already traversed it; stomach is intraperitoneal anterior/medial and less likely if trajectory is posterior after splenic injury.
educational_objective: After splenic injury from a LUQ projectile, the posteriorly situated left kidney is a common site for the bullet to lodge.

question: A study is designed to evaluate the relationship between ambient noise and hearing loss in an automobile manufacturing plant. Different locations in the manufacturing plant have strikingly different levels of ambient noise. Each employee is given a test for hearing acuity, and then the ambient noise level is measured at his or her workstation. Which of the following best describes this study design?
explanation: Correct: Exposure and outcome measured at a single point in time across a population = cross-sectional study【turn13file3†First Aid USMLE Step 1 2024 (1).pdf†L3-L6】. Incorrect: Case series lacks a comparison and describes cases only. Cohort follows exposed vs unexposed over time. Crossover randomizes subjects to sequences of interventions. RCT randomizes to treatment vs control.
educational_objective: Measuring exposure and outcome simultaneously in a population is a cross-sectional study.

question: A 27-year-old woman with a 15-year history of recurrent urinary tract infections develops hypertension, proteinuria, and renal failure. Her serum creatinine concentration is 2.6 mg/dL. X-rays show irregular scarring of the kidneys and blunting of the renal calyces, most prominent in the upper and lower poles. Which of the following is the most likely cause of the renal abnormalities?
explanation: Correct: Chronic pyelonephritis results from recurrent/inadequately treated acute pyelonephritis, often due to vesicoureteral reflux; findings include coarse, asymmetric corticomedullary scarring with blunted calyces, classically at the poles【turn12file0†First Aid USMLE Step 1 2024 (1).pdf†L53-L59】. Incorrect: Acute GN causes nephritic syndrome without polar scarring pattern. Amyloidosis/diabetes cause different glomerular changes (eg, Kimmelstiel–Wilson nodules) rather than polar scarring and calyceal blunting【turn10file5†First Aid USMLE Step 1 2024 (1).pdf†L92-L100】【turn10file5†First Aid USMLE Step 1 2024 (1).pdf†L112-L120】.
educational_objective: Recurrent acute pyelonephritis (often from VUR) leads to chronic pyelonephritis with polar scarring and blunted calyces.

question: A 30-year-old primigravid woman develops severe uterine bleeding in the hospital after vaginal delivery of a 3827-g (8-lb 7-oz) male newborn at term. Pregnancy was uncomplicated. Delivery lasted 7 hours and was assisted with the use of forceps; delivery of the placenta followed. External uterine massage does not result in decrease of the postpartum hemorrhage. A medication is administered by continuous intravenous infusion to improve uterine contraction. This patient's bleeding is most likely to be decreased via which of the following mechanisms of action?
explanation: Correct: Oxytocin given by IV infusion binds Gq-coupled oxytocin receptors on myometrium, increasing IP₃-mediated Ca²⁺ release and uterine contraction, which compresses spiral arteries and reduces postpartum hemorrhage. Incorrect mechanisms include β-agonism (would relax uterus), α₁-agonism (primarily vascular smooth muscle), or prostacyclin signaling (vasodilation/relaxation).
educational_objective: Oxytocin reduces postpartum hemorrhage by increasing uterine smooth muscle Ca²⁺ (via IP₃) to enhance contraction and tamponade bleeding.

question: A screening program was instituted for detection of depressive symptoms among college students. At the first examination, evidence of depression was found in 250 of 1250 subjects. During the following year, an additional 100 students developed depressive symptoms. Which of the following is the annual incidence of depression in this population of students?
explanation: Correct: Incidence = new cases / population at risk over time. At risk at baseline = 1250 − 250 = 1000; new cases = 100; incidence = 100/1000 = 0.10 = 10%. Incorrect: Using the full 1250 (8%) or including prevalent cases (inflates denominator) miscalculates incidence.
educational_objective: Incidence counts new cases among those initially disease-free over a specified period.

question: A 23-year-old woman comes to the physician for prenatal care. On examination, she appears euthyroid and the thyroid gland is not palpable. Uterine size is consistent with dates, and fetal pulse is normal. Changes in which of the following hormones during pregnancy is primarily responsible for the thyroid test results?
explanation: Correct: Estrogen increases hepatic production of TBG, raising total T₄/T₃ while free T₄ and TSH remain normal (clinically euthyroid). Incorrect: hCG can mildly stimulate the thyroid early but TBG rise from estrogen is the main driver of pregnancy thyroid test changes; prolactin, cortisol, or progesterone do not explain the typical thyroid panel.
educational_objective: In pregnancy, ↑estrogen → ↑TBG → ↑total thyroid hormone with normal free hormone and euthyroidism.

question: A 60-year-old man comes to the physician for an examination prior to employment. Physical examination shows no abnormalities. Flow cytometry analysis of peripheral lymphocytes shows a surface kappa to surface lambda ratio of 47% to 3%. Which of the following is most predictive of a clonal lymphoid proliferation in this patient?
explanation: Correct: A highly skewed κ:λ ratio (~94%:6%) indicates light-chain restriction, consistent with a monoclonal B-cell population. Incorrect: Polyclonal/reactive processes maintain a near-normal κ:λ (~2:1); surface marker heterogeneity and mixed immunoglobulin expression argue against clonality.
educational_objective: A markedly abnormal κ:λ ratio suggests a monoclonal B-cell proliferation.

question: A 70-year-old man comes to the emergency department 2 hours after the sudden onset of severe left- sided low back pain that radiates to his abdomen. He has a 25-year history of hypertension and type 2 diabetes mellitus. He is in severe distress. His pulse is 110/min, and blood pressure is 80/60 mm Hg. Physical examination shows diaphoresis and a soft, nontender abdomen; there is no tenderness of the back or spine. Neurologic examination shows no abnormalities. Urinalysis shows no blood. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation: Correct: Sudden severe back/flank pain with hypotension and risk factors (HTN, age) suggests ruptured AAA; absence of hematuria and spinal tenderness argues against renal colic or vertebral causes. Incorrect: Renal colic causes colicky pain with hematuria; aortic dissection typically causes chest/tearing pain radiating to the back; musculoskeletal strain is hemodynamically stable.
educational_objective: Sudden back pain and hypotension in an older hypertensive patient is classic for ruptured AAA.

question: A 35-year-old woman comes to the physician because of severe nonradiating low back pain for 2 weeks. She recently began a vigorous exercise program. Her back pain has been partially relieved by bed rest and aspirin. She has ulcerative colitis that has been treated with corticosteroid therapy for 5 years and is currently in remission. Physical examination shows mild localized tenderness over several lumbar vertebrae. Which of the following best explains these radiographic findings?
explanation: Correct: Chronic glucocorticoid therapy causes decreased bone formation and increased resorption → osteoporosis and vertebral compression (wedge) fractures presenting with localized vertebral tenderness. Incorrect: Spondyloarthropathy (e.g., ankylosing spondylitis) shows sacroiliitis; disc herniation produces radicular pain; osteomyelitis causes fever and elevated inflammatory markers.
educational_objective: Long-term steroids predispose to osteoporosis and vertebral compression fractures.

question: A 53-year-old man comes to the physician to learn the results of a series of tests to evaluate his severe abdominal pain. The testing occurred over a 3-week period and the recent results indicate pancreatic cancer. When the physician reviews the results with the patient and discusses the diagnosis, the patient becomes angry and asks, "Why did it take you so long to figure this out?" Which of the following is the most appropriate response by the physician?

options.A: "I think all of the tests were done within a reasonable time frame."
options.B: "It must be very difficult to hear this news."
options.C: "The most important thing now is to find you a good oncologist."

explanation: Correct: Acknowledge emotion, validate, and invite discussion—empathetic, non-defensive communication. Incorrect: Arguing, deflecting blame, minimizing concerns, or providing premature reassurance undermines the therapeutic alliance.
educational_objective: Use empathy and open dialogue when patients express anger about delays or care concerns.

question: An 18-year-old man has had temperatures to 38.3°C (101°F), a sore throat, and cervical lymph node enlargement for 8 days. A latex agglutination test result for Epstein-Barr virus antibody is positive. Atypical cells with abundant lacey cytoplasm in the peripheral blood smear are most likely derived from which of the following types of cells?
explanation: Correct: "Atypical lymphocytes" in mononucleosis are activated CD8⁺ T cells reacting to EBV-infected B cells. Incorrect: B cells are infected but not the source of the atypical morphology; neutrophils/monocytes are not the characteristic atypical cells in EBV infection.
educational_objective: EBV mononucleosis features reactive CD8⁺ T cells with abundant cytoplasm ("atypical lymphocytes").

question: A previously healthy 55-year-old man comes to the physician because of a 2-day history of pain with urination, urinary frequency, low back pain, and nausea. His temperature is 38.5°C (101.3°F), pulse is 88/min, respirations are 20/min, and blood pressure is 144/88 mm Hg. Physical examination shows acute low back tenderness. Urinalysis shows 3+ protein; numerous WBCs, epithelial cells, and bacteria; and a few RBCs. Treatment with a quinolone antibiotic is initiated, but his symptoms do not resolve. Urine culture grows Escherichia coli resistant to ciprofloxacin. The most likely cause of this resistance is a mutation in which of the following elements?
explanation: Correct: Fluoroquinolones inhibit bacterial DNA gyrase and topoisomerase IV; resistance commonly arises via mutations in gyrA/parC (target modification) or efflux pumps. Incorrect: β-lactamases target penicillins/cephalosporins; altered PBPs confer β-lactam resistance; ribosomal mutations affect protein synthesis inhibitors, not fluoroquinolones.
educational_objective: Fluoroquinolone resistance often results from mutations in DNA gyrase/topoisomerase IV.

question: A 60-year-old man comes to the physician for a routine health maintenance examination. Physical examination shows no abnormalities. Urinalysis shows blood 3+ and atypical cells on microscopic examination. A CT scan of the abdomen discloses a lesion of the right kidney. Which of the following compounds is the most significant predisposing risk factor for this patient's condition?
explanation: Correct: Smoking is the most important risk factor for renal cell carcinoma; carcinogens in tobacco smoke (e.g., polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbons) drive oncogenesis. Incorrect: Aromatic amines (β-naphthylamine) are classically linked to bladder cancer; aflatoxin to HCC; vinyl chloride to angiosarcoma of the liver.
educational_objective: Cigarette smoking is the leading risk factor for renal cell carcinoma.

question: Restriction of valine in the diet is most likely to be effective in treatment of patients with which of the following?
explanation: Correct: MSUD results from impaired catabolism of branched-chain amino acids (leucine, isoleucine, valine); dietary restriction of these (including valine) is therapeutic. Incorrect: Phenylketonuria (phenylalanine restriction), homocystinuria (methionine restriction), or urea cycle defects require different dietary strategies.
educational_objective: In MSUD, restrict branched-chain amino acids (valine, leucine, isoleucine) to reduce toxic metabolite buildup.

question: A 37-year-old woman is found to have a 1-cm thyroid nodule on routine physical examination. There is no adenopathy. Fine-needle aspiration of the nodule confirms papillary thyroid carcinoma. She undergoes thyroidectomy and postoperative radioiodine (131I) ablation. When the radioiodine is administered, there is a large concentration of homogenous iodine uptake in the superior mediastinum. Which of the following best explains this finding?

options.C: Uptake of the 131I by the thymus

explanation: Correct: Thyroid tissue can be ectopic along its embryologic descent path; substernal/mediastinal thyroid tissue concentrates iodine and appears as homogeneous uptake after radioiodine. Incorrect: Thymus and lymph nodes do not concentrate iodine; diffuse metastatic uptake is typically heterogeneous.
educational_objective: Ectopic thyroid along the descent pathway (including mediastinum) concentrates radioiodine after thyroidectomy.

question: A 35-year-old woman, gravida 1, para 1, comes to the physician because of a 2-month history of generalized weakness and fatigability that are significantly exacerbated by exercise. The symptoms began during her pregnancy. Physical examination shows diplopia. There is reduction in arm muscle strength with repetitive movement, but preservation of deep tendon reflexes. A therapeutic trial of oral pyridostigmine provides symptomatic relief. Serum studies will most likely show antibodies to which of the following proteins?
explanation: Correct: Myasthenia gravis is due to antibodies against postsynaptic nicotinic ACh receptors, causing fatigable weakness and ocular symptoms; improves with acetylcholinesterase inhibitors. Incorrect: Lambert-Eaton targets presynaptic Ca²⁺ channels; antibodies to MuSK are less common; GABA or voltage-gated Na⁺ channels are unrelated.
educational_objective: Myasthenia gravis features antibodies to postsynaptic nicotinic ACh receptors causing fatigable weakness.

question: A previously healthy 71-year-old man comes to the emergency department because of a 12-hour history of fever and cough. Current medications include ramelteon nightly. His temperature is 39.6°C (103.2°F), pulse is 100/min, respirations are 20/min, and blood pressure is 100/60 mm Hg. Crackles are heard over the right lower lung with dullness to percussion. Laboratory studies show a leukocyte count of 52,000/mm³. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation: Correct: Marked neutrophilic leukocytosis in the setting of acute lobar pneumonia represents a leukemoid reaction (reactive process), not leukemia. Incorrect: CML shows basophilia, low LAP score, and chronic course; medication effect (ramelteon) is irrelevant.
educational_objective: Severe infection can cause a leukemoid reaction with very high WBC counts.

question: A 35-year-old man comes to a new physician because of a 3-day history of abdominal pain and daily loose stools. He has a 2-year history of recurrent epigastric pain and a 4-month history of peptic ulcer disease treated with acid suppression medications. He takes no other medications. He was told on three separate occasions that he had ulcers in his duodenum and jejunum but no infection. His blood pressure is 120/78 mm Hg. The abdomen is soft. There is tenderness to palpation of the epigastric area but no rebound tenderness. Which of the following is the most likely cause of this patient's condition?

options.A: Eosinophilic infiltration into the gastric wall

explanation: Correct: Multiple/refractory ulcers extending beyond the duodenal bulb with diarrhea suggest gastrinoma with hypergastrinemia and acid hypersecretion. Incorrect: NSAID use, H. pylori, or stress ulcers would not explain jejunal ulcers and persistent diarrhea in this pattern.
educational_objective: Zollinger–Ellison syndrome causes hypergastrinemia, refractory peptic ulcers (often distal), and secretory diarrhea.

question: A 52-year-old man with acute myelogenous leukemia comes to the physician because of a 3-day history of fever and a 2-week history of nonproductive cough. He received ablative chemotherapy and received a bone marrow transplant 2 months ago. He has had neutropenia since the transplant. His temperature is 38.8°C (101.8°F), pulse is 96/min, respirations are 20/min, and blood pressure is 100/65 mm Hg. Crackles are heard over the right lung base. His serum 1,3-β-D-glucan concentrations are increased. A chest x-ray shows a cavitary lesion in the right lower lobe. This patient's serum study result most likely indicates the presence of which of the following?
explanation: Correct: The 1,3-β-D-glucan assay detects a fungal cell wall component; neutropenia and cavitary lung lesions strongly suggest invasive aspergillosis. Incorrect: Bacterial, mycobacterial, or viral infections do not elevate 1,3-β-D-glucan.
educational_objective: Elevated serum 1,3-β-D-glucan points to invasive fungal infection such as aspergillosis.

question: A 65-year-old man receives a liver transplant for primary biliary cirrhosis. To prevent organ rejection, immunosuppressive therapy that inhibits T-lymphocyte activation with cyclosporine is planned. The activity of which of the following molecules involved in T-lymphocyte activation is most likely to be inhibited by this treatment?
explanation: Correct: Cyclosporine binds cyclophilin and inhibits calcineurin, preventing NFAT activation and IL-2 transcription, thereby blocking T-cell activation. Incorrect: mTOR inhibition (sirolimus), JAK/STAT blockade, or CTLA-4-Ig costimulation blockade are different immunosuppressive mechanisms.
educational_objective: Cyclosporine suppresses T-cells by inhibiting calcineurin and IL-2 transcription.

question: A 72-year-old man with chronic obstructive pulmonary disease comes to the physician for a follow-up examination. Current medications include albuterol and ipratropium. He smokes 1 pack of cigarettes daily. He does not drink alcohol. His respirations are 24/min. Pulse oximetry on room air shows an oxygen saturation of 87%. Breath sounds are decreased bilaterally. His baseline FEV₁ is 0.88 (38% of predicted). Which of the following hematologic abnormalities is most likely in this patient?
explanation: Correct: Chronic hypoxemia in COPD stimulates EPO production, causing secondary polycythemia. Incorrect: Anemia of chronic disease, leukemoid reaction, or thrombocytopenia are not expected consequences of chronic hypoxemia.
educational_objective: Chronic hypoxemia (e.g., COPD) leads to ↑EPO and secondary polycythemia.

question: A 53-year-old man is brought to the emergency department because of progressive fever, cough, fatigue, and shortness of breath during the past 3 days. His temperature is 39.2°C (102.6°F), and respirations are 21/min. Physical examination shows diaphoresis. There is increased tactile fremitus, dullness to percussion, and bronchovesicular breath sounds over the left lower hemithorax posteriorly. Arterial blood gas analysis on oxygen via nasal cannula (2 L/min) shows hypoxemia. Which of the following is the primary cause of the hypoxemia in this patient?

options.A: Inadequate concentration of oxygen through nasal cannula
options.B: Pulmonary arterial blood shunting directly into pulmonary veins

explanation: Correct: Lobar pneumonia fills alveoli with exudate, creating shunt units that do not respond well to supplemental O₂, causing hypoxemia. Incorrect: Pure hypoventilation produces normal A-a gradient; diffusion limitation is uncommon at rest; low FiO₂ is not relevant on supplemental oxygen.
educational_objective: Consolidated lung segments create right-to-left shunt physiology, causing refractory hypoxemia.

question: A 25-year-old woman comes to the physician because of palpitations and insomnia for 5 months; she also has had a 5-kg (11-lb) weight loss during this period. Her pulse is 125/min. Physical examination shows exophthalmos, thyromegaly, and hand tremors. Serum studies show a thyroid-stimulating hormone concentration of less than 0.1 μU/mL, thyroxine (T₄) concentration of 18 μg/dL, and triiodothyronine (T₃) concentration of 250 ng/dL. The signs and symptoms in this patient are most likely caused by hormones acting on which of the following receptors?
explanation: Correct: T₃/T₄ bind nuclear receptors that act as transcription factors; clinical hyperthyroidism results from increased transcriptional activity (and β-adrenergic upregulation). Incorrect: G-protein or tyrosine kinase membrane receptors mediate other hormones (e.g., catecholamines, insulin), not thyroid hormone.
educational_objective: Thyroid hormone acts via nuclear receptors to alter gene transcription.

question: A 79-year-old woman comes to the physician because of swollen, painful joints in her hands and knees for 6 months. Her hematocrit is 39%. Serum protein electrophoresis shows a monoclonal IgG spike of 1.3 g serum IgA and IgM concentrations are within the reference range. Her urine does not contain Bence Jones protein. A bone marrow biopsy specimen shows no abnormalities. Which of the following is the most likely explanation for the increased serum IgG concentration in this patient?
explanation: Correct: An isolated small monoclonal IgG spike with normal marrow, no end-organ damage, and no light chains in urine is typical of MGUS. Incorrect: Multiple myeloma requires CRAB features and ≥10% clonal plasma cells; chronic infection/inflammation causes polyclonal, not monoclonal, increases.
educational_objective: A small monoclonal spike without myeloma features is consistent with MGUS.

question: A 35-year-old woman is brought to the emergency department because of a 3-hour history of sharp cramping pain in the right flank. Urinalysis shows blood. A noncontrast CT scan is obtained, and a renal calculus is found to be lodged in the ureter just above the sacroiliac joint. At this point, the ureter narrows as it passes over which of the following structures?
explanation: Correct: The ureter narrows at three sites: ureteropelvic junction, crossing the iliac vessels at the pelvic brim (near SI joint), and ureterovesical junction. Incorrect: Psoas, gonadal vessels, or femoral vessels are not the classic constriction point at this level.
educational_objective: The ureter constricts where it crosses the iliac vessels at the pelvic brim, a common site for stones to lodge.

question: A 20-year-old man with intellectual disability is brought to the physician for a routine examination. Physical examination shows a long face, prominent ears, and large testes. His younger brother and a maternal uncle have similar features. Analysis of the patient's DNA shows 300 CGG repeated sequences (N<60) in the 5' untranslated region of the FMR1 gene. This region of expanded CGG trinucleotide repeats is heavily methylated. Which of the following is the most likely effect of these expanded nucleotide repeats on transcription of FMR1 mRNA?
explanation: Correct: Fragile X involves CGG expansion in the FMR1 5′ UTR causing hypermethylation and heterochromatin formation → decreased transcription. Incorrect: Repeat expansion does not enhance transcription; splicing/translation effects are secondary to transcriptional silencing here.
educational_objective: CGG expansion in FMR1 leads to methylation-mediated transcriptional silencing (Fragile X).

question: A 65-year-old man comes to the physician because of difficulty swallowing solids for 2 months. He has a history of dilated cardiomyopathy. X-rays of the esophagus with barium contrast show indentation and posterior displacement of the esophagus. Enlargement of which of the following structures is the most likely cause of the dysphagia?
explanation: Correct: The esophagus lies posterior to the left atrium; LA enlargement (e.g., due to cardiomyopathy/mitral disease) compresses and displaces the esophagus posteriorly, causing dysphagia. Incorrect: Aortic arch or right atrium typically cause different displacement patterns; vertebral enlargement is not applicable.
educational_objective: Left atrial enlargement can compress the esophagus and cause dysphagia.

question: A 21-year-old man comes to the physician because of intermittent episodes of light brown urine during the past year associated with upper respiratory tract infections. His blood pressure is 145/85 mm Hg. Physical examination shows no other abnormalities. Urinalysis shows microscopic blood, 3+ protein, and several RBC casts. Immunohistochemical staining of a renal biopsy specimen is most likely to show granular deposits in the glomerular mesangium predominantly consisting of which of the following immunoglobulins?
explanation: Recurrent gross/microscopic hematuria following mucosal infections with mesangial immune complex deposition is classic for IgA nephropathy (Berger disease). Mesangial granular deposits are predominantly IgA.
educational_objective: IgA nephropathy presents with hematuria after URIs and mesangial IgA deposition.

question: For aerobic catabolism of compounds with equivalent numbers of carbon atoms, the greatest amount of energy in the form of ATP is obtained from compounds with the largest number of which of the following?
explanation: Energy yield depends on the degree of reduction. More C–H bonds (e.g., in fatty acids) provide more reducing equivalents (NADH/FADH₂) for oxidative phosphorylation than more oxidized substrates.
educational_objective: The more reduced a molecule (more C–H bonds), the greater the ATP yield during aerobic catabolism.

question: A 25-year-old man comes to the emergency department 5 hours after developing shortness of breath and chest pain during exercise; he has had no cough or bloody mucus. He has asthma and major depressive disorder. Current medications include fluticasone inhaler and albuterol. His temperature is 37.1°C (98.3°F); pulse is 110/min, respirations are 30/min, and blood pressure is 90/60 mm Hg. Pulse oximetry on room air shows an oxygen saturation of 93%. Cardiac examination shows a normal S₁ and S₂ with no murmurs and no increase in jugular venous pressure. Laboratory studies show: Hemoglobin 13 g/dL, Hematocrit 39%. Arterial blood gas analysis on room air: pH 7.46, PCO₂ 26 mm Hg, PO₂ 60 mm Hg. A chest x-ray is shown. Which of the following pulmonary findings are most likely in this patient?

options.A: Crackles on the right lung base
options.B: Decreased breath sounds on the left

explanation: Acute pleuritic chest pain, tachycardia, hypoxemia with respiratory alkalosis and a (often normal) CXR suggests PE. Occluded perfusion creates high V/Q areas and increased physiologic dead space, causing a widened A–a gradient.
educational_objective: Pulmonary embolism causes ventilation–perfusion mismatch with increased physiologic dead space and hypoxemia.

question: A 42-year-old woman with type 2 diabetes mellitus comes to the physician because of a 1-day history of increasingly severe right knee pain. She now has difficulty walking because of the pain. She recalls no trauma to the knee and has never had similar symptoms. She is 152 cm (5 ft) tall and weighs 100 kg (220 lb); BMI is 43 kg/m². Her temperature is 39.3°C (102.7°F); pulse is 110/min, respirations are 12/min, and blood pressure is 160/90 mm Hg. Physical examination shows a 10-cm area of erythema surrounding the right knee, which is warm to the touch and exquisitely tender with movement. There is a moderate effusion. Arthrocentesis yields cloudy yellow synovial fluid. Analysis of the synovial fluid shows a leukocyte count of 90,000/mm³ (95% neutrophils) and no crystals. A Gram stain of the fluid shows numerous segmented neutrophils but no organisms. Which of the following is the most likely cause of the findings in this patient?
explanation: Very high synovial WBCs with neutrophil predominance and fever indicate septic arthritis; S. aureus is the most common cause. Gram stain can be negative initially. Diabetes and obesity increase risk.
educational_objective: Septic arthritis (often S. aureus) presents with hot, swollen joint and neutrophilic effusion; treat urgently.

question: A 6-year-old girl of Mediterranean ancestry has severe anemia. Analysis shows normal production of α- globin gene mRNA. Production of β-globin gene mRNA is decreased 75% because of a splice-site mutation within both of the patient's β-globin genes. Which of the following is the most likely explanation for the anemia?

options.A: Decreased production of β₄ tetramers compared with normal individuals
options.B: Imbalance in the synthesis of the α- and β-globin gene products

explanation: Splice-site mutations reduce β-globin mRNA, leading to markedly decreased β-chain production. Unpaired α chains precipitate, causing intramedullary destruction and hemolysis → severe microcytic anemia.
educational_objective: β-thalassemia reduces β-globin synthesis; excess unpaired α chains damage RBCs and marrow precursors.

question: A 50-year-old man with schizophrenia is admitted to the hospital because of chest pain. He develops acute fever, lethargy, and muscular rigidity 5 days later. He has been receiving haloperidol treatment since admission. His temperature is 41°C (105.8°F), pulse is 120/min, and blood pressure is 140/80 mm Hg. He is disoriented and agitated and has diffusely increased muscle tone. Serum creatine kinase activity is 1500 U/L. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation: NMS presents with hyperthermia, "lead-pipe" rigidity, autonomic instability, altered mental status, and elevated CK after dopamine-blocking antipsychotics (e.g., haloperidol).
educational_objective: Fever, rigidity, autonomic instability, and high CK after antipsychotic use indicate neuroleptic malignant syndrome.

question: A 1-month-old boy with X-linked severe combined immunodeficiency is enrolled in a gene therapy trial. Bone marrow stem cells are extracted from the patient and are treated ex vivo with a retrovirus expressing the wild-type gene. Although the patient initially responds well, 30 months after treatment he develops a form of T-lymphocyte leukemia. Molecular studies show that the T lymphocytes are monoclonal. Which of the following viral processes is the most likely cause of the leukemia in this patient?
explanation: Retroviral vectors integrate into host DNA; integration near/within a proto-oncogene (via LTR enhancers) can drive clonal T-cell proliferation and leukemia.
educational_objective: Retroviral gene therapy can cause leukemia by proviral integration that activates oncogenes (insertional mutagenesis).

question: A 72-year-old man with severe congestive heart failure is brought to the emergency department because of a 5-day history of malaise and vomiting. He takes no medications. His pulse is 104/min, respirations are 35/min, and blood pressure is 90/64 mm Hg. Physical examination shows dusky-colored skin, peripheral cyanosis, and 10-cm jugular venous distention. Crackles are heard over the lung bases bilaterally. Cardiac examination shows an S₃. There is 2+ pitting edema to the knees bilaterally. Laboratory studies show: Serum Na⁺ 127 mEq/L, K⁺ 5.2 mEq/L, Cl⁻ 79 mEq/L, HCO₃⁻ 17 mEq/L, Urea nitrogen 100 mg/dL, Glucose 171 mg/dL, Creatinine 8.4 mg/dL. Urine Glucose 1+, Ketones absent. Arterial blood gas analysis on 28% oxygen: pH 7.35, PCO₂ 32 mm Hg, PO₂ 154 mm Hg, HCO₃⁻ 17 mEq/L. Which of the following is the most likely cause of the anion gap in this patient?
explanation: Anion gap = 127 − (79+17) ≈ 31. The markedly elevated BUN/Cr indicate renal failure with retained sulfates, phosphates, and organic acids causing high–anion gap metabolic acidosis.
educational_objective: Advanced renal failure causes high–anion gap metabolic acidosis due to retention of unmeasured acids.

question: Diisopropyl fluorophosphate, a potent inhibitor of acetylcholinesterase, reacts with which of the following specific amino acids at the active site of the enzyme?
explanation: Organophosphates phosphorylate the active-site serine hydroxyl of acetylcholinesterase, inactivating the enzyme (aging stabilizes the bond).
educational_objective: Organophosphates inhibit AChE by phosphorylating the active-site serine.

question: A male newborn develops vomiting and convulsions 4 hours after delivery. There is slight bulging of the fontanelles. Which of the following organisms is most likely responsible for these findings?
explanation: Early-onset neonatal meningitis within hours of birth is most commonly due to GBS acquired during delivery; seizures and bulging fontanelle are typical.
educational_objective: Early neonatal meningitis is classically caused by group B Streptococcus.

question: A 23-year-old woman comes to the physician because of a 2-week history of increasingly severe itching and yellow-tinged skin. Three months ago, she started taking a combination oral contraceptive. She does not smoke. She consumes two to three alcoholic beverages only on the weekends. Physical examination shows mild jaundice and scleral icterus. The liver span is 11 cm with no tenderness. Serum studies show: Bilirubin, total 7.3 mg/dL, Direct 5.8 mg/dL, Alkaline phosphatase 440 U/L, AST 30 U/L, ALT 70 U/L, γ- Glutamyltransferase (GGT) 234 U/L (N=0-30). Serologic studies for acute viral hepatitis are negative. Which of the following is the most likely cause of these findings?
explanation: Markedly elevated conjugated bilirubin, ALP, and GGT with pruritus and minimal transaminase elevation indicate cholestasis. Estrogens (OCPs) impair bile flow, causing intrahepatic cholestasis.
educational_objective: Estrogens can cause intrahepatic cholestasis with pruritus and conjugated hyperbilirubinemia.

question: A 17-year-old boy is brought to the emergency department because of a 2-day history of fever and shortness of breath. He underwent bone marrow transplantation for acute myelogenous leukemia 2 months ago. His temperature is 39°C (102.2°F), and respirations are 32/min. Diffuse crackles are heard over the lung fields on auscultation. A chest x-ray shows interstitial pneumonia. A photomicrograph of a biopsy specimen of the lung tissue is shown. Decreased function of which of the following most likely predisposed this patient to infection?
explanation: Post–bone marrow transplant patients with impaired T-cell function are prone to CMV interstitial pneumonia (classically in transplant recipients).
educational_objective: Impaired cell-mediated immunity predisposes to CMV interstitial pneumonia after transplantation.

question: A 63-year-old man from southern China has had a bloody nasal discharge for the past 5 months. Physical examination shows an enlarged, fixed lymph node in the upper posterior cervical triangle of the left neck. Examination of tissue obtained on needle biopsy of the lymph node shows neoplastic cells that are positive for keratin and Epstein-Barr nuclear antigen. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation: EBV-associated, keratin-positive epithelial tumor endemic in southern China commonly presents with cervical node metastases and epistaxis.
educational_objective: EBV is strongly linked to nasopharyngeal carcinoma, especially in southern Chinese populations.

question: A 55-year-old man comes to the physician because of pain and stiffness of his right hand and wrist for 3 months. The pain is exacerbated by hand movement and is relieved by rest. He was a professional boxer for 15 years. Physical examination shows moderate swelling over the dorsum of the right wrist. Examination of fluid aspirated from the wrist shows: Appearance Clear, yellowish, Leukocyte count 250/mm³ (N<200), Neutrophils 5% (N<25%), Glucose 101 mg/dL (N=80-100). Which of the following is the most likely cause of this patient's condition?
explanation: Noninflammatory synovial fluid with low leukocytes and pain worsened by use, improved by rest is OA. Prior repetitive trauma (boxing) is a risk factor.
educational_objective: Osteoarthritis presents with activity-related pain and noninflammatory synovial fluid.

question: A 34-year-old woman has a 3-year history of recurring episodes of tenesmus, mucoid bloody diarrhea, and cramping abdominal pain. A section of bowel removed following a severe episode is shown. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation: UC causes continuous mucosal inflammation starting in the rectum with friable mucosa and pseudopolyps; clinical features include tenesmus and bloody, mucoid diarrhea.
educational_objective: Ulcerative colitis presents with continuous colitis, rectal involvement, and bloody diarrhea with tenesmus.

question: A 22-year-old woman is admitted to the hospital because of a 10-day history of polydipsia and polyuria. She says that the urge to urinate often awakens her at night. She has been taking lithium carbonate for 2 years for bipolar disorder; her dosage was increased 6 months ago because of recurrent severe manic episodes. Her vital signs are within normal limits. Physical examination shows no abnormalities. Over the next 24 hours, urine excretion totals 6.5 L. Laboratory studies at this time show a serum sodium concentration of 148 mEq/L, serum osmolality of 315 mOsmol/kg, and urine osmolality of 75 mOsmol/kg. After administration of desmopressin, urine output and osmolality do not change. Which of the following findings in the nephron best describes the tubular osmolality, compared with serum, in this patient? Hypertonic Hypotonic Hypotonic Hypertonic Hypotonic Hypotonic Hypertonic Hypotonic

options.A: Proximal Tubule: Hypertonic, Juxtaglomerular Apparatus: Hypertonic, Medullary Collecting Duct:
options.B: Proximal Tubule: Hypertonic, Juxtaglomerular Apparatus: Hypotonic, Medullary Collecting Duct:
options.C: Proximal Tubule: Isotonic, Juxtaglomerular Apparatus: Isotonic, Medullary Collecting Duct:
options.D: Proximal Tubule: Isotonic, Juxtaglomerular Apparatus: Hypertonic, Medullary Collecting Duct:

explanation: Lithium causes nephrogenic DI (no response to desmopressin). Without ADH action, the collecting ducts are water-impermeable, so tubular fluid that becomes hypotonic in the TAL/DCT stays hypotonic through the collecting duct (no final concentration).
educational_objective: In nephrogenic DI, collecting ducts are ADH-resistant, so distal tubular fluid remains hypotonic (cannot concentrate urine).

question: A 58-year-old woman with type 2 diabetes mellitus is brought to the emergency department because of an 18-hour history of fever, confusion, and pain of her left leg. Her temperature is 39.6°C (103.3°F); pulse is 124/min, respirations are 22/min, and blood pressure is 94/60 mm Hg. Physical examination shows a diffuse, erythematous rash and conjunctival injection. Erythema and edema extend from the dorsum of the left foot to the knee. She is oriented to person but not to place or time. Neurologic examination shows no other abnormalities. Serum studies show: Urea nitrogen 36 mg/dL, Creatinine 2.8 mg/dL, Total bilirubin 2.2 mg/dL, AST 470 U/L, ALT 385 U/L. One day later, blood cultures grow gram-positive cocci in chains. These bacteria most likely produced a toxin that caused this patient's condition via which of the following mechanisms? apoptosis

options.A: Blockade of protein synthesis by depurination of ribosomal RNA
options.B: Catalyzing of the formation of cAMP from ATP
options.C: Disruption of cytoskeleton architecture by glycosylating Rho

explanation: Streptococcus pyogenes (gram-positive cocci in chains) can cause toxic shock–like syndrome via pyrogenic exotoxins acting as superantigens, leading to fever, rash, hypotension, and multiorgan dysfunction.
educational_objective: Streptococcal superantigen toxins cause toxic shock by nonspecifically activating many T cells (MHC II–TCR bridging).

question: A 25-year-old man comes to the physician because of a 2-month history of recurrent episodes of chest pain and shortness of breath. He has a 2-year history of nodules on his hands and feet. Physical examination shows numerous 1- to 2-cm yellow nodules that are palpable on both Achilles tendons and on the extensor tendons of the hands. Ophthalmologic examination shows corneal arcus. Serum studies show: Creatine kinase 35 U/L, Cholesterol, total 350 mg/dL, HDL-cholesterol 50 mg/dL, LDL-cholesterol 300 mg/dL, Triglycerides 100 mg/dL, Troponin I 0.1 ng/mL (N<0.4). An ECG shows no abnormalities. This patient most likely has an impairment in function involving which of the following structures?
explanation: Tendon xanthomas, corneal arcus, and very high LDL with normal TG suggest familial hypercholesterolemia due to defective LDL receptor (or ApoB-100), impairing hepatic LDL clearance.
educational_objective: Familial hypercholesterolemia is due to impaired LDL receptor–mediated uptake → ↑LDL and tendon xanthomas.

question: Patients who have recurrent infections involving Neisseria species are most likely to have a genetic deficiency in which of the following serum factors?
explanation: Recurrent Neisseria meningitidis/gonorrhoeae infections are classically associated with deficiencies of the membrane attack complex (C5–C9).
educational_objective: Deficiency of C5–C9 (MAC) predisposes to recurrent Neisseria infections.

question: A 17-year-old boy comes to the physician because of a 3-month history of worsening acne. Treatment over the past year with tetracycline had been effective. His symptoms began when he started taking the medication in the morning with a glass of milk. Which of the following best explains the ineffectiveness of tetracycline in this patient?
explanation: Tetracyclines form nonabsorbed chelates with divalent cations (Ca²⁺ in milk), reducing bioavailability and efficacy.
educational_objective: Avoid coadministration of tetracyclines with dairy/antacids/iron due to chelation and reduced absorption.

question: A 50-year-old woman has azotemia. Renal ultrasonography shows bilateral hydroureters and hydronephrosis. The most likely cause of these findings is primary carcinoma of which of the following?
explanation: In women, bilateral hydronephrosis/hydroureter is commonly due to ureteral obstruction from cervical carcinoma.
educational_objective: Cervical cancer can compress/obstruct ureters, causing bilateral hydronephrosis and azotemia.

question: A 45-year-old woman is brought to the emergency department because of the sudden onset of severe abdominal pain. Examination shows an irregularly irregular pulse, a grade 3/6, apical diastolic murmur, and an opening snap. An x-ray of the abdomen shows distention of the small intestine, the ascending colon, and a portion of the transverse colon. Which of the following is the most likely underlying cause of these findings?
explanation: Irregularly irregular pulse with an opening snap/diastolic murmur indicates MS with AF. Mesenteric ischemia from an embolus (LA thrombus) causes severe abdominal pain and bowel distention.
educational_objective: Atrial fibrillation (often from mitral stenosis) predisposes to arterial emboli causing mesenteric ischemia.

question: A 67-year-old man comes to the physician because of a 2-month history of pain in his feet. The discomfort is more severe in bed at night and is relieved by taking a hot bath. He has type 2 diabetes mellitus treated with glipizide. His pulse is 60/min, respirations are 12/min, and blood pressure is 130/88 mm Hg. Strength is normal and symmetric in the distal and proximal upper and lower extremities. The Achilles deep tendon reflexes are decreased and quadriceps deep tendon reflexes are normal. Sensation to pinprick and vibration is decreased from just above the ankles distally. This patient is most likely to describe his pain as which of the following?
explanation: Findings are consistent with distal symmetric diabetic polyneuropathy causing neuropathic pain (burning, shooting, dysesthesias), often worse at night and relieved by warmth.
educational_objective: Diabetic peripheral neuropathy causes distal burning/tingling neuropathic pain with sensory loss.
