question: In a sample of 100 individuals, the mean leukocyte count is 7500/mm3, with a standard deviation of 1000/mm3. If the leukocyte counts in this population follow a normal (gaussian) distribution, approximately 50% of individuals will have which of the following total leukocyte counts?

options.A: Compression of the trigeminal nerve by an acoustic neuroma (vestibular schwannoma)
options.C: Inflammation of the trigeminal nerve by a multiple sclerosis plaque
options.D: Recurrent transient ischemia in the vertebrobasilar system

explanation: In a normal distribution, ~68% of values lie within ±1 SD (6500–8500); this is the closest band among the options to "about half" (50%). The other choices correspond to ~32% (outside ±1 SD), ~95% (±2 SD), or ~2.5% (> +2 SD).
educational_objective: For normal data, ~68% lie within ±1 SD, ~95% within ±2 SD, and ~99.7% within ±3 SD of the mean.

question: A 55-year-old woman comes to the clinic because of a 2-month history of increasingly severe vaginal pain and itching during sexual intercourse. She avoids intercourse with her husband because of the symptoms. She has been in a monogamous relationship with her husband for the past 25 years. She has type 2 diabetes mellitus. Her vital signs are within normal limits. Pelvic examination shows edematous and erythematous vaginal mucosa with white discharge. A photomicrograph of a vaginal smear is shown. Which of the following is the most likely causal infectious agent?

options.A: Alloimmune hemolytic disease of the newborn

explanation: Pruritic, erythematous, edematous mucosa with thick white discharge in a diabetic patient is classic for vulvovaginal candidiasis (pseudohyphae, budding yeasts on smear). Chlamydia and HSV typically cause cervicitis/ulcers; Trichomonas causes a frothy green discharge and "strawberry cervix."
educational_objective: Vulvovaginal candidiasis presents with pruritus and thick white discharge, especially in patients with diabetes, recent antibiotics, or pregnancy.

question: A 39-year-old man comes to the physician because of a 6-month history of progressive shortness of breath. He has had a cough productive of white sputum for 2 years. He smoked 1 pack of cigarettes daily for 16 years but quit 10 years ago. He is in mild respiratory distress with pursed lips and a barrel chest; he is using the accessory muscles of respiration. Breath sounds are distant and crackles are present in the lower lung fields bilaterally. Pulmonary function tests show a decreased FEV1:FVC ratio, increased residual volume, and decreased diffusion capacity. An x-ray of the chest shows hyperinflation and hypertranslucency of the lower lobes of both lungs. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation: Obstructive pattern with increased RV and reduced DLCO plus hyperinflated, hyperlucent lungs and "pursed-lip" breathing are typical of emphysema. Asthma usually has normal/increased DLCO; bronchiectasis has copious purulent sputum; fibrosis causes a restrictive pattern.
educational_objective: Emphysema causes airflow obstruction with hyperinflation and decreased DLCO due to alveolar wall destruction.

question: A previously healthy 33-year-old woman is brought to the emergency department by the Secret Service for stalking the president of the USA for 2 months. She claims to be married to the president's twin brother and states that the president just had his twin kidnapped to avoid competition. She speaks rapidly and is difficult to interrupt. Her associations are often loose. She says, "I haven't slept for days, but I won't even try to sleep until my husband is rescued. God has been instructing me to take over the White House. I can't wait to be reunited with my husband. I hear his voice telling me what to do." When asked about drug use, she says she uses only natural substances. She refuses to permit blood or urine tests, saying, "I don't have time to wait for the results." Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation: Elevated/irritable mood with decreased need for sleep, grandiosity, pressured speech, and psychotic symptoms is a manic episode with psychotic features. Schizophrenia requires chronic psychosis and functional decline; delusional disorder lacks mania and overt disorganization; brief psychotic disorder is acute and not driven by mania.
educational_objective: A manic episode can include psychotic features (hallucinations/delusions); diagnosis is bipolar disorder with psychotic features.

question: During an experiment, a mouse is vaccinated with live attenuated bacteria at two different times. The results following immunization are shown in the graph. The subject's serum total antibody concentration (Y-axis) was measured at various time points (X-axis). The response to the first immunization is indicated by Peak A, while that of the second immunization with the same bacterial antigen is indicated by Peak B. The phase of the immune response represented by the asterisk is most likely the direct result of which of the following?
explanation: After the peak, the contraction phase of the immune response reflects apoptosis of most short-lived effector lymphocytes; memory cells persist. Antigen recognition/T-cell or B-cell expansion occur earlier in the response.
educational_objective: The post-peak decline in antibody levels is due to contraction of the immune response via apoptosis of effector lymphocytes.

question: A 53-year-old man comes to the physician because of a dry scaly rash on his body for the past year. He has had a 15- kg (33-lb) weight loss during the past year. He is 178 cm (5 ft 10 in) tall and now weighs 54 kg (120 lb); BMI is 17 kg/m2. His stools have a large volume and float. Which of the following nutrient deficiencies is most likely?

options.B: Fracture of the distal radius and ulna
options.C: Salter-Harris type I fracture of the humerus

explanation: Steatorrhea from fat malabsorption leads to fat-soluble vitamin deficiency. Vitamin A deficiency causes xerosis and a dry scaly rash (and night blindness). B12 deficiency causes anemia/neuropathy; zinc deficiency causes periorificial dermatitis/alopecia; magnesium deficiency causes neuromuscular irritability.
educational_objective: Chronic fat malabsorption causes deficiencies of fat-soluble vitamins (A, D, E, K); vitamin A deficiency can present with xerosis and scaly rash.

question: In screening for prostate cancer, the current serum prostate-specific antigen concentration at which biopsy is recommended is 4.1 ng/mL. If the threshold for recommending a biopsy procedure were lowered to 2.0 ng/mL, which of the following changes would occur to the positive and negative predictive values of the test? Positive Predictive Value Negative Predictive Value
explanation: Lowering the threshold increases sensitivity and decreases specificity: PPV decreases (more false positives), while NPV increases (fewer false negatives among negatives).
educational_objective: Lowering a test threshold increases sensitivity and NPV while decreasing specificity and PPV.

question: In informing a couple that their newborn has Down syndrome, there is a specific, relatively limited amount of information that the consulting physician should give immediately. The rest can be discussed at a later time. Which of the following best explains the purpose of using this approach to disclosure?
explanation: In practice, initial disclosure should be concise and compassionate to avoid overwhelming families; more details are provided as they're ready. (The aim is to pace information to the family's coping capacity—i.e., to avoid excessive immediate distress—rather than to transfer responsibility or steer decisions.)
educational_objective: When delivering life-changing diagnoses, provide essential information first and pace further details to avoid overwhelming distress.

question: A 62-year-old man comes to the physician because of a 6-month history of urinary hesitancy and dribbling after urination. He has to urinate two to three times nightly. Physical examination shows a diffusely enlarged, firm, and nontender prostate. Which of the following is most likely to have contributed to the development of this patient's condition?
explanation: Benign prostatic hyperplasia is driven by DHT (from testosterone via 5-α-reductase) acting on prostatic stromal/epithelial tissue. α1 receptor activation mediates dynamic tone but not hyperplasia; estradiol and PSA do not drive growth.
educational_objective: DHT promotes prostatic growth in BPH; 5-α-reductase inhibitors reduce DHT and prostate size.

question: An 18-year-old woman with sickle cell disease is brought to the emergency department by her parents because of a 2- hour history of severe abdominal pain and nausea. Her parents say that she had a cheeseburger, milk shake, and chocolate bar for lunch. Her temperature is 37°C (98.6°F). Physical examination shows tenderness over the right upper quadrant of the abdomen, radiating to the right shoulder. Ultrasonography of the right upper quadrant of the abdomen shows gallstones. Which of the following is the most likely underlying cause of this patient's current condition?
explanation: Chronic hemolysis increases unconjugated bilirubin, forming black pigment stones. Cholesterol stones result from a high cholesterol:bile acid ratio or impaired bile salt recycling; lecithin decreases predispose to cholesterol stones.
educational_objective: Chronic hemolysis causes black pigment gallstones due to excess unconjugated bilirubin in bile.

question: A 45-year-old man is brought to the emergency department 30 minutes after the sudden onset of crushing chest pain. His father, maternal aunt, and paternal uncle all died of myocardial infarctions under the age of 50 years. Physical examination shows tendinous xanthomas on the hands and thickened Achilles tendons. Serum lipid studies show a total cholesterol concentration of 410 mg/dL, HDL-cholesterol concentration of 30 mg/dL, and triglyceride concentration of 140 mg/dL. The diagnosis of myocardial infarction is made. This patient most likely has a deficiency of which of the following?

options.A: The case fatality rate is higher among women
options.B: The duration of the disease is shorter in men
options.C: The number of new cases in women is increasing
options.D: Women use medical care facilities more often than men

explanation: The intended pathophysiology is familial hypercholesterolemia due to defective LDL receptors or ApoB-100 (not ApoB-48) leading to very high LDL and tendon xanthomas. Among the provided options, none perfectly matches; ApoB-48 (intestinal, chylomicrons) is not causative, but it is the closest "ApoB" option listed.
educational_objective: Familial hypercholesterolemia presents with very high LDL and tendon xanthomas due to defective LDL receptor or ApoB-100; recognize the phenotype even if options are imperfect.

question: An experimental animal is created in which the germinal centers of the reactive lymph nodes show shrinkage of cells, cytoplasmic budding, no adjacent inflammation, and intact plasma membranes. These cellular findings are most likely caused by which of the following mechanisms?
explanation: These are hallmark features of apoptosis (cell shrinkage, membrane blebbing, intact membranes, minimal inflammation), which is mediated by caspase activation (often via mitochondrial cytochrome c release). Lysosomal enzymes/inflammation suggest necrosis.
educational_objective: Apoptosis features include caspase-mediated cell death with membrane blebbing and minimal inflammation.

question: Investigators conduct a study that evaluates the effect of finasteride on the incidence of prostate cancer in 500 patients. The investigators recruit an additional 1000 patients for the study. Which of the following effects will this have on the research study?
explanation: Increasing sample size increases power (reduces Type II error) if α is unchanged; the Type I error rate (α) does not inherently change. None of the provided specific error options precisely matches; the key predictable effect is increased power.
educational_objective: Larger sample sizes reduce standard error and generally increase power (lower Type II error) if α is held constant.

question: A 76-year-old man dies of a massive cerebral infarction shortly after admission to the hospital. During the past 10 years, he has had several smaller cerebral infarctions and two transient ischemic attacks. Examination of a cerebral cortex specimen obtained at autopsy shows extensive gliosis. This finding is most likely caused by the growth and proliferation of which of the following?
explanation: CNS injury/healing leads to astrocyte proliferation and hypertrophy (gliosis). Fibroblasts are limited in the CNS; oligodendrocytes remyelinate; ependymal cells line ventricles and do not drive gliosis.
educational_objective: Reactive gliosis after CNS injury is due to astrocyte proliferation/hypertrophy.

question: A 65-year-old woman is brought to the emergency department because of a 10-minute history of chest tightness and severe pain of her left arm. Physical examination shows jugular venous distention. Crackles are heard over the lung fields. An ECG shows ST-segment elevation greater than 1 mm in leads V4 through V6 and new Q waves. Serum studies show an increased troponin I concentration. Which of the following labeled points in the graph best represents the changes in cardiac function that occurred during the first 10 seconds after the onset of pain in this patient?
explanation: Acute transmural MI causes an immediate drop in contractility (within seconds), shifting the pressure–volume loop to lower systolic pressure and higher end-systolic volume (reduced slope of ESPVR). This corresponds to a transition from normal to a reduced contractility loop.
educational_objective: Early MI rapidly decreases contractility, reducing stroke volume and shifting the PV loop down/right.

question: A previously healthy 52-year-old woman comes to the physician because of a 2-month history of fatigue, constipation, and frequent urination. Her temperature is 37.1°C (98.8°F), pulse is 80/min, respirations are 14/min, and blood pressure is 140/90 mm Hg. Diffuse crackles are heard bilaterally. Her serum calcium concentration is 11.1 mg/dL, and serum parathyroid hormone concentration is decreased. A chest x-ray shows bilateral hilar lymphadenopathy and interstitial infiltrates. Which of the following is the most likely cause of this patient's hypercalcemia?
explanation: Granulomatous diseases (eg, sarcoidosis) produce 1α-hydroxylase in macrophages, increasing 1,25-(OH)2 vitamin D and intestinal calcium absorption, causing PTH-independent hypercalcemia.
educational_objective: Macrophage 1α-hydroxylase in granulomatous disease increases calcitriol, causing PTH-independent hypercalcemia.

question: A 66-year-old man who was recently diagnosed with Parkinson disease comes to the physician for a follow-up examination. Carbidopa-levodopa therapy was initiated at the time of diagnosis. The patient tells the physician that he still has episodes during which he "freezes." He has a clumsy gait, and there is rigidity of his upper extremities and hands. An adjunct therapy designed to inhibit which of the following enzymes is most likely indicated in this patient?
explanation: MAO-B inhibitors (eg, selegiline, rasagiline) reduce central dopamine breakdown and can help motor fluctuations. AADC and tyrosine hydroxylase are already addressed by levodopa/carbidopa pathway; DBH converts dopamine to NE, not the target here.
educational_objective: MAO-B inhibitors reduce CNS dopamine metabolism and are useful adjuncts in Parkinson disease motor fluctuations.

question: A study is conducted to assess the effects of epinephrine on total peripheral resistance. An anesthetized experimental animal is injected with a bolus of the drug in both the presence and absence of doxazosin. The results are shown in the graph. Which of the following best represents the signal transduction pathways used by epinephrine to produce these results? Epinephrine Without Doxazosin Epinephrine With Doxazosin
explanation: Epinephrine activates α1 (Gq → phosphoinositide/IP3-DAG → vasoconstriction) and β2 (Gs → ↑ cAMP → vasodilation). With α1 blocked by doxazosin, β2-mediated cAMP predominates → vasodilation and ↓TPR.
educational_objective: Epinephrine's vascular effects reflect α1-Gq-IP3/DAG (vasoconstriction) and β2-Gs-cAMP (vasodilation); α1 blockade unmasks β2 vasodilation.

question: A 46-year-old woman comes to the physician because of a 3-day history of intermittent pain with urination and increased urinary frequency. She says that she had one similar episode during the past 6 months. She also has had irregular menses, and her last menstrual period occurred 2 months ago. She has not had fever, nausea, vomiting, or blood in her urine. She is sexually active with one male partner. Physical examination shows no abnormalities. Urinalysis shows: RBC 3–5/hpf WBC 10–20/hpf Nitrites positive Leukocyte esterase positive Bacteria positive Which of the following is the strongest predisposing risk factor for the development of this patient's condition?
explanation: Decreased estrogen in perimenopause/postmenopause leads to urogenital atrophy and altered vaginal flora, increasing UTI risk. Pregnancy is a risk but not present; fibroids (leiomyomata) are unrelated.
educational_objective: Estrogen deficiency in peri/postmenopause predisposes to UTIs by altering vaginal/urethral mucosa and flora.

question: A 28-year-old man comes to the physician because of a 2-month history of a rash on his wrists and hands. He is a first-year mortuary science student. He also works on his grandfather's farm each weekend. His hobbies include raising homing pigeons and repairing vintage motorcycles. He recently changed to a different type of laundry detergent to save money. Physical examination shows a diffuse erythematous rash involving both hands up to the wrist creases. The rash does not extend over any other parts of the body. Which of the following is the most likely cause of this patient's rash?
explanation: Hand-limited erythematous dermatitis confined by glove borders is classic for allergic contact dermatitis (type IV) to latex. Detergent rash would affect other skin; pigeons cause hypersensitivity pneumonitis; solvents can irritate but typically affect exposed forearms too.
educational_objective: Allergic contact dermatitis from latex presents as hand-limited erythema/eczema confined to glove areas.

question: A 10-year-old boy is brought to the emergency department in the middle of summer because of fever, headache, and photophobia. Several of his camp mates have had a similar illness. Physical examination shows mild nuchal rigidity. A lumbar puncture is performed. Laboratory studies show: Serum glucose 90 mg/dL Cerebrospinal fluid Pressure, opening 50 mm H2O Glucose 65 mg/dL Total protein 70 mg/dL Leukocyte count 43/mm3 (95% lymphocytes) Which of the following infectious agents is the most likely cause of these findings?
explanation: Viral meningitis (especially summer/fall outbreaks) is most commonly due to enteroviruses (echovirus/coxsackie). Normal CSF glucose with lymphocytic predominance supports viral etiology.
educational_objective: Enteroviruses are the most common cause of aseptic meningitis in children, often in summer outbreaks.

question: A healthy 30-year-old woman participates in a study of the relationship between cardiovascular function and posture. Placed in a room with a comfortable temperature (72°F) and humidity (40%), she moves from a standing to a supine position. Which of the following sets of changes is most likely in the reflex control of this woman's cardiovascular system? Carotid Sinus Vagal Efferent Baroreceptor Atrial Stretch Activity Activity Receptor Activity to the Heart
explanation: Supine position increases venous return and arterial pressure → ↑ carotid sinus firing → ↑ vagal efferent outflow to the heart (↓ HR). Increased venous return also ↑ atrial stretch receptor activity.
educational_objective: Moving supine increases venous return and baroreceptor firing, augmenting vagal tone and atrial stretch receptor activity.

question: A 31-year-old woman with a 5-year history of fatigue comes to the physician for an initial visit. She has seen four other physicians for the same condition within the past 6 months, but no abnormalities were found. She gives the physician a large folder that contains her medical records. She says, "I can barely get out of bed most mornings, but nobody can figure out why because all of my tests turn out normal. I really think I have chronic fatigue syndrome. What do you know about this condition?" The physician has not treated any patient with chronic fatigue syndrome before. Which of the following initial statements by the physician is most appropriate to establish rapport with this patient?
explanation: Honest disclosure of limits plus commitment to partner in care builds trust. The other options minimize, stigmatize, or prematurely psychologize the symptoms.
educational_objective: Combine honesty with a collaborative stance to build rapport when you have limited experience with a condition.

question: A 3-week-old girl delivered at term with no complications is brought to the physician by her mother because of a 1- week history of yellow eyes and skin, tan-colored stools, and dark brown urine. The newborn has been breast-feeding without difficulty. She is alert and appears to be in no distress. She is at the 50th percentile for length and weight. Physical examination shows scleral icterus and jaundice. There is mild hepatomegaly; the spleen is not palpable. Laboratory studies show: Hemoglobin 14.4 g/dL Hematocrit 43% Leukocyte count 8000/mm3 Serum Albumin 3.5 g/dL Bilirubin, total 14 mg/dL Direct 12.5 mg/dL AST 50 U/L ALT 45 U/L Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation: Conjugated hyperbilirubinemia with pale stools, dark urine, and hepatomegaly in a neonate suggests biliary atresia (extrahepatic obstruction). Physiologic jaundice is unconjugated; Gilbert/Crigler-Najjar are unconjugated disorders.
educational_objective: Neonatal conjugated hyperbilirubinemia with pale stools/dark urine strongly suggests biliary atresia.

question: A 65-year-old woman comes to the physician for a follow-up examination after blood pressure measurements were 175/105 mm Hg and 185/110 mm Hg 1 and 3 weeks ago, respectively. She has well-controlled type 2 diabetes mellitus. Her blood pressure now is 175/110 mm Hg. Physical examination shows no other abnormalities. Antihypertensive therapy is started, but her blood pressure remains elevated at her next visit 3 weeks later. Laboratory studies show increased plasma renin activity; the erythrocyte sedimentation rate and serum electrolytes are within the reference ranges. Angiography shows a high-grade stenosis of the proximal right renal artery; the left renal artery appears normal. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation: Correct: Atherosclerotic renal artery stenosis classically affects the proximal segment in older patients and causes renovascular hypertension with elevated renin. First Aid lists renal artery stenosis (atherosclerosis vs fibromuscular dysplasia) among secondary causes of hypertension【turn1file7†First Aid USMLE Step 1 2024 (1).pdf†L57-L63】. Incorrect: Congenital hypoplasia is not the typical cause in late-onset, resistant HTN; fibromuscular dysplasia is classically distal and in younger women; temporal arteritis involves large vessels of the head/neck, not typically the renal artery.
educational_objective: Atherosclerotic narrowing of the proximal renal artery is a common cause of secondary hypertension in older patients.

question: Results of a study that examined the impact of risk factors on cardiovascular health are being evaluated. In the study, serum LDL-cholesterol (LDL) concentration is found to have a correlation of 0.6 with serum high-sensitivity C- reactive protein (hs-CRP) concentration. Which of the following statements best describes the relationship between LDL concentration and hs-CRP concentration based on this finding?
explanation: Correct: A positive correlation coefficient (r=+0.6) indicates that higher values of one variable are associated with higher values of the other; it does not establish causation【turn11file0†First Aid USMLE Step 1 2024 (1).pdf†L95-L102】. Incorrect: A negative association (lower hs-CRP with higher LDL) would have r<0; correlation ≠ causation, so "causes" is wrong.
educational_objective: A positive correlation (r>0) means the variables increase together, but correlation does not imply causation.

question: A pharmaceutical company is developing a new bronchodilator agent. The graph shows concentration-response curves for three investigational drugs (Drugs X, Y, and Z), describing their effect on bronchial smooth muscle relaxation. Based on these data, which of the following best describes the relationship among these three agents?

options.C: More than three bowel movements daily

explanation: xplanation: Efficacy refers to the maximal biological response a drug can produce, reflected by the plateau of the concentration–response curve. Drug Z achieves a higher maximal relaxation of bronchial smooth muscle compared to Drugs X and Y, making it more efficacious. Potency, in contrast, refers to the concentration required to achieve a given effect (leftward shift of the curve). Although Drug X may be more potent if its curve is left-shifted, potency does not change the maximal achievable effect. Thus, the main difference in this case is efficacy. Incorrect options: • Drug X is more potent than Drugs Y or Z — potency is about curve position, not maximum effect; this ignores the efficacy difference. • Drug X has greater efficacy than Drugs Y or Z — incorrect because X does not reach as high a maximum effect as Z. • Drug Y is more potent than Drugs X or Z — not supported by the data. • Drug Z is more potent than Drugs X or Y — Z may or may not be more potent, but the defining feature in the graph is its higher efficacy.
educational_objective: Potency is determined by the drug concentration needed to achieve an effect (left-right shift), whereas efficacy is determined by the maximal effect (plateau height) on the dose–response curve.

question: A 72-year-old man comes to the physician for a health maintenance examination. He has no personal or family history of major medical illnesses. He has never smoked cigarettes. Pulse oximetry on room air shows an oxygen saturation of 98%. Physical examination shows plethoric skin and splenomegaly. Laboratory studies show: Hemoglobin 21.1 g/dL Hematocrit 61% Leukocyte count 15,000/mm3 Segmented neutrophils 68% Basophils 4% Lymphocytes 28% Platelet count 501,000/mm3 Leukocyte alkaline phosphatase increased A peripheral blood smear shows occasional giant platelets. The primary hematologic defect in this patient most likely occurred in which of the following cells?

options.C: Increased removal of cellular debris by glial cells

explanation: Correct: Polycythemia vera is a myeloproliferative neoplasm driven by JAK2 mutation at the hematopoietic stem cell (multipotent) level, causing panmyelosis (↑RBCs, WBCs, platelets) and splenomegaly; LAP can be increased in inflammatory states and is not specific for CML【turn19file7†First Aid USMLE Step 1 2024 (1).pdf†L120-L146】. Incorrect: Erythroid or lymphatic progenitor defects would not explain trilineage proliferation; a pluripotent embryonic stem cell is not the cell of origin in PV.
educational_objective: Myeloproliferative neoplasms arise from mutated hematopoietic stem cells, producing trilineage overgrowth.

question: A 45-year-old man comes to the physician because of a 10-year history of heartburn that occurs after he eats late at night or consumes spicy food. He has had no weight loss or difficulty swallowing. He takes over-the-counter antacids as needed, but they relieve his discomfort only temporarily. Physical examination shows no abnormalities. An endoscopy is done. The distal esophagus is shown in the photograph. Which of the following is the most likely cause of this patient's symptoms?
explanation: Correct: GERD symptoms are driven by excessive transient lower esophageal sphincter relaxations with reflux of acidic gastric contents【turn1file1†First Aid USMLE Step 1 2024 (1).pdf†L84-L88】. Incorrect: Secretin defects are duodenal; hypergastrinemia suggests Zollinger-Ellison; failure of saliva production causes dysphagia and caries rather than classic nocturnal GERD.
educational_objective: GERD commonly results from transient LES relaxations leading to acid reflux and heartburn.

question: A 21-year-old man comes to the emergency department in the winter because of headache, nausea, and dizziness for 4 hours. He has not had fever, chills, or shortness of breath. He has no history of major medical illness. He lives in a basement apartment of a three-story house. He smokes 1½ packs of cigarettes daily. Physical examination shows no abnormalities. It is most appropriate for the physician to ask the patient for more information about which of the following historical factors?

options.D: Inhibition of hepatic protein kinase A

explanation: Correct: Carbon monoxide exposure is a key wintertime environmental risk; additional questioning about exposure sources (often occupational/environmental) is appropriate. First Aid notes CO toxicity in the breath-odor/toxin tables and hypoxia section, emphasizing exogenous toxins causing hypoxia【turn18file3†First Aid USMLE Step 1 2024 (1).pdf†L99-L104】【turn20file2†First Aid USMLE Step 1 2024 (1).pdf†L78-L86】. Incorrect: Travel or OTC meds are not relevant to acute winter headache/dizziness patterns; "substance use" is already disclosed (tobacco) and less informative than pinpointing CO sources.
educational_objective: In suspected CO exposure, focus the history on environmental/occupational sources of combustion (eg, heaters, engines).

question: A 56-year-old woman comes to the physician because of a 2-year history of recurrent urinary tract infections accompanied by left flank pain. Physical examination shows no abnormalities. Renal ultrasonography shows left- sided hydronephrosis. A T2-weighted coronal MRI of the abdomen is shown; the arrow indicates the hydronephrosis. The left renal collecting system is most likely obstructed at which of the following anatomic locations in this patient?
explanation: Correct: The ureterovesical junction (UVJ) is a common point of obstruction and can lead to unilateral hydronephrosis; distal obstruction predisposes to recurrent infections. (FA highlights the typical ureteral narrowing sites with stones—UPJ, crossing over iliac vessels [mid-ureter], and UVJ.) Incorrect: Bladder neck obstruction causes bilateral effects; mid-ureter and renal calyx are less consistent with chronic UVJ-type obstruction on one side.
educational_objective: The UVJ is a common physiologic narrowing where obstruction can cause hydronephrosis.

question: A 25-year-old woman comes to the physician because of a long history of pain with menses. The pain occurs on the first day of her 5-day menstrual period and lasts all day. She rates the pain as 10 on a 10-point scale. The most appropriate initial pharmacotherapy to relieve this patient's pain has which of the following mechanisms of action?
explanation: Correct: Primary dysmenorrhea is mediated by endometrial prostaglandins causing uterine contractions and ischemic pain; NSAIDs relieve pain by inhibiting prostaglandin synthesis【turn19file1†First Aid USMLE Step 1 2024 (1).pdf†L9-L12】. Incorrect: Estrogen synthesis inhibition and LH stimulation are not first-line for primary dysmenorrhea; 11β-hydroxylase inhibition is unrelated.
educational_objective: NSAIDs treat primary dysmenorrhea by blocking prostaglandin synthesis, reducing uterine contractions.

question: A 35-year-old man is brought to the emergency department 30 minutes after he sustained a cut on his hand while loading cargo at his job. He lives alone and takes most of his meals at a local restaurant. He eats mostly snack foods at the bar and fast food. He drinks four to six 12-oz beers daily and double that amount on weekends. He takes no medications. Physical examination shows a 3-cm laceration on the right hand that is bleeding steadily. Laboratory studies show a hemoglobin concentration of 11 g/dL, leukocyte count of 4000/mm3, and platelet count of 150,000/mm3. A photomicrograph of a peripheral blood smear is shown. A deficiency of which of the following is the most likely cause of this patient's anemia?
explanation: Correct: Chronic alcohol use can cause sideroblastic anemia due to vitamin B6 (pyridoxine) deficiency; FA lists alcohol-associated sideroblastic anemia【turn19file8†First Aid USMLE Step 1 2024 (1).pdf†L112-L114】. Incorrect: Iron deficiency fits microcytosis with low ferritin; folate deficiency causes macrocytosis; G6PD deficiency causes hemolysis with oxidative stress, not chronic sideroblastic changes.
educational_objective: Alcohol can cause vitamin B6 deficiency leading to sideroblastic anemia.

question: A 3800-g (8-lb 6-oz) newborn is delivered vaginally at 39 weeks' gestation after an uncomplicated pregnancy. Apgar scores are 9 and 9 at 1 and 5 minutes, respectively. The newborn is crying, has pink skin, and appears vigorous. Physical examination shows a vagina and also a structure that appears to be a penis, with the urethra located at the base near the opening of the vagina. Chromosomal analysis is ordered. Which of the following is the most likely cause of the intersex findings in this newborn if the karyotype is found to be 46,XX?
explanation: Correct: Virilization of a 46,XX infant suggests excess androgens; maternal androgen exposure during pregnancy can masculinize female external genitalia. FA's discussion of androgen excess (eg, aromatase deficiency) highlights fetal and maternal virilization from androgen excess【turn19file2†First Aid USMLE Step 1 2024 (1).pdf†L9-L15】. Incorrect: 5α-reductase deficiency and ↑MIS affect 46,XY or internal ducts; "17α-hydroxyprogesterone deficiency" is not a standard cause of virilization in 46,XX (21-hydroxylase deficiency is typical but not listed).
educational_objective: In 46,XX infants, maternal androgen excess can cause virilized external genitalia.

question: A 65-year-old man is admitted to the hospital because of a 12-hour history of chest pain. Physical examination shows no abnormalities. Serum studies show an increased troponin I concentration. The diagnosis of myocardial infarction is made. It is suspected that this patient's condition deteriorated as a result of ischemia-reperfusion injury. The increased serum troponin I concentration in this patient most likely occurred as a result of which of the following processes?
explanation: Correct: Irreversible cell injury causes breakdown of the plasma membrane with leakage of cytosolic enzymes (eg, troponin) into the blood【turn20file4†First Aid USMLE Step 1 2024 (1).pdf†L11-L17】; MI evolution also notes cell content release into blood【turn20file8†First Aid USMLE Step 1 2024 (1).pdf†L57-L65】. Incorrect: Increased synthesis/secretion is not the mechanism; karyolysis is nuclear dissolution; mitochondrial swelling is a reversible/structural change, not the direct cause of enzyme leakage.
educational_objective: Troponin rises after myocyte membrane breakdown causes enzyme leakage into blood during necrosis.

question: A randomized clinical trial is conducted to compare wound healing and cosmetic differences between two surgical procedures for closing skin wounds following cesarean delivery. A total of 1000 women undergoing cesarean delivery during a 6-month period are enrolled in the study, which was 85% of the total number of patients undergoing the procedure. The results show a wound infection rate of 12 cases per 1000 women for Procedure A and 18 cases per 1000 women for Procedure B. Which of the following is the best estimate of the absolute risk reduction for wound infection following Procedure A compared with Procedure B?
explanation: Correct: ARR = risk in control − risk in treatment = 18/1000 − 12/1000【turn11file0†First Aid USMLE Step 1 2024 (1).pdf†L102-L111】. Incorrect: Multiplying by 0.85 (enrollment fraction) is irrelevant to ARR; the ratio expression provided is relative risk reduction, not ARR.
educational_objective: Absolute risk reduction is control risk minus treatment risk.

question: A 22-year-old man is brought to the emergency department 15 minutes after diving off a pier into shallow water, striking his forehead on the bottom of the pond. He says that he felt immediate pain in his neck and then lost all ability to move or feel his legs. Physical examination shows that all muscle function above the level of the injury is preserved. A lateral x-ray of the cervical spine is shown. Which of the following functions is most likely spared in this patient?
explanation: C5 innervates biceps (elbow flexion), which is preserved since the fracture is at the C5 level. Elbow extension (C7), wrist flexion (C7), and finger abduction (T1) would be lost below the lesion.
educational_objective: A spinal cord lesion at C5 preserves C5-mediated elbow flexion but causes paralysis of functions mediated by lower cervical nerves.

question: A 4-year-old girl with type 1 diabetes mellitus is brought to the emergency department by her father because of a 4- hour episode of restlessness, sweating, and confusion that occurred during the night. Yesterday, he allowed her to eat cupcakes and cotton candy at a county fair. At her bedtime that evening, he increased her dose of subcutaneous intermediate-acting and long-acting insulin. Her symptoms began 6 hours later, then resolved spontaneously. After being informed this morning of this nighttime episode, the mother insisted the father bring the patient to the hospital. On arrival, the patient is alert. Her vital signs are within normal limits. Examination shows no abnormalities. Her fingerstick blood glucose concentration is 72 mg/dL. Urinalysis is negative for glucose and ketones. Which of the following is the most likely explanation for this patient's nighttime symptoms?
explanation: Correct: The temporal relationship to increased evening insulin, nocturnal symptoms (sweating, confusion), and spontaneous resolution are classic for nocturnal hypoglycemia from excessive insulin dosing. FA emphasizes that insulin excess produces hypoglycemia; counterregulatory hormones (glucagon/epinephrine) respond but are not the cause of the episode【turn20file8†First Aid USMLE Step 1 2024 (1).pdf†L152-L156】. Incorrect: Hyperglycemia explanations and parasomnias do not fit the timing and adrenergic neuroglycopenic symptoms.
educational_objective: Excess insulin dosing can cause nocturnal hypoglycemia with adrenergic and neuroglycopenic symptoms.

question: A previously healthy 65-year-old woman comes to the physician because of several episodes of fainting during the past 2 months. Each episode lasted several minutes. Her pulse is 82/min, respirations are 20/min, and blood pressure is 135/87 mm Hg. Cardiac examination shows S3 and S4. Echocardiography shows a pedunculated intracardiac mass. The lesion is resected. A photomicrograph of the resected lesion is shown. This lesion was most likely obtained from which of the following locations?
explanation: Correct: Cardiac myxomas are pedunculated masses most commonly arising in the left atrium【turn1file8†First Aid USMLE Step 1 2024 (1).pdf†L58-L60】. Incorrect: Ventricular or septal locations are less common for myxomas.
educational_objective: Atrial myxomas typically originate in the left atrium and can cause episodic obstruction/syncope.

question: A male newborn is delivered at term to a 28-year-old primigravid woman. Physical examination shows a broad, flat nose; low-set ears; a receding chin; prominent infraorbital folds; and bilateral abdominal masses. The newborn develops cyanosis, difficulty breathing, and polyuria and dies 24 hours after birth. At autopsy, examination shows pulmonary hypoplasia and enlarged, polycystic kidneys. Genetic testing shows two copies of a gene having a pathogenic mutation with a disease incidence rate in the general population of 1 in 10,000. Which of the following best describes the mutation occurrence rate for this newborn's disease?
explanation: Correct: For an autosomal recessive disease, incidence ≈ q²; if incidence is 1/10,000, then q ≈ 1/100. (Hardy-Weinberg relationships summarized in FA.) Incorrect: 1/400, 1/1000, 1/10,000 do not match √(1/10,000).
educational_objective: For AR disorders, the mutant allele frequency q ≈ √incidence (q²).

question: A 75-year-old woman comes to the physician because of a 3-year history of pain in her wrists and hands. She says that the pain has become more severe during the past 3 months. She has difficulty buttoning her coat because of the pain. Physical examination shows the findings in the photograph. Which of the following additional hand findings is most likely in this patient?

options.A: Activated CD8+ cytotoxic T lymphocyte effectors in the circulation
options.B: Activated CD8+ cytotoxic T lymphocyte effectors in the gut
options.D: Neutralizing secretory IgA antibodies in the gut

explanation: Correct: Osteoarthritis shows degenerative cartilage changes with osteophytes/Heberden and Bouchard nodes【turn19file12†First Aid USMLE Step 1 2024 (1).pdf†L99-L107】【turn19file12†First Aid USMLE Step 1 2024 (1).pdf†L145-L155】. Incorrect: RA has pannus (synovial thickening) and tendon inflammation; cortical thinning is osteoporosis, not OA.
educational_objective: OA is a degenerative cartilage disease with osteophytes and DIP/PIP nodal changes.

question: A previously healthy 64-year-old man is brought to the emergency department 3 hours after the sudden onset of severe flank pain. He has no history of similar pain or serious illness. He takes no medications. He appears to be in distress. His pulse is 100/min, and blood pressure is 168/92 mm Hg. Physical examination shows a soft abdomen with left- sided tenderness. Urinalysis shows microscopic hematuria. A CT scan of the abdomen shows a small ureteric calculus. Analgesic therapy is initiated and the pain resolves 1 hour later. The urine is then strained and a uric acid calculus is found. Which of the following processes is most likely impaired in this patient?

options.C: Lacunar infarcts of the basal ganglia

explanation: Correct: Calcium carbonate decreases levothyroxine absorption when co-administered, leading to hypothyroid symptoms and elevated TSH (drug interaction noted in FA pharmacology/endocrine discussions). Incorrect: Distribution/metabolism/elimination changes are not the main issue; the temporal association with starting calcium fits reduced absorption.
educational_objective: Calcium carbonate impairs levothyroxine absorption; separate dosing to avoid hypothyroidism.

question: A 32-year-old woman with hypothyroidism comes to the physician because of a 6-week history of cold intolerance, constipation, and severe fatigue. She also has had a 4.5-kg (10-lb) weight gain during this period. Her current medication is daily levothyroxine. She also started taking calcium carbonate supplements 2 months ago for osteopenia of the lumbar spine. At that time, serum concentrations of thyroid-stimulating hormone (TSH) and free thyroxine (FT4) were within the reference ranges. Today, physical examination shows coarse, dry skin. Serum studies show a TSH concentration of 16.6 μU/mL and FT4 concentration of 0.3 ng/dL. Which of the following pharmacokinetic changes of levothyroxine is the most likely cause of this patient's current condition?
explanation: Correct: Reactivation of varicella-zoster virus (shingles) is associated with impaired cellular (T-cell) immunity; T cells control viral infections【turn10file5†First Aid USMLE Step 1 2024 (1).pdf†L81-L89】. Incorrect: Complement and humoral deficiency predispose to encapsulated bacteria; TLR deficiency affects innate sensing rather than VZV control.
educational_objective: T-cell–mediated immunity is crucial for controlling VZV; decline predisposes to shingles.

question: A 71-year-old woman comes to the physician because of a 5-day history of a painful rash. The rash began as a burning sensation over the right lower side of her chest. Three days ago, small, flat, painful macules appeared that rapidly progressed to vesicular lesions. During this period, the pain has continually increased in severity. Her temperature is 37.8°C (100°F), pulse is 72/min, respirations are 22/min, and blood pressure is 129/78 mm Hg. Physical examination shows the findings in the photograph. The rash does not cross the midline. The most likely cause of this patient's illness is a deficiency in which of the following components of the immune system?
explanation: Correct: Accessory spleens arise from splenic tissue developing in the dorsal mesogastrium【turn6file1†First Aid USMLE Step 1 2024 (1).pdf†L82-L83】. Incorrect: Ventral pancreas/lesser curvature/celiac origin are not the splenic primordium sites.
educational_objective: The spleen develops from mesenchyme within the dorsal mesogastrium; accessory spleens are common.

question: A 48-year-old man comes to the physician requesting treatment for alcohol withdrawal. He reports a 30-year history of consuming 6 to 10 beers daily. He has had two citations for driving while intoxicated. He has previously experienced alcohol-associated seizures and withdrawal symptoms. His vital signs are within normal limits. Physical examination shows palmar erythema. The most appropriate pharmacotherapy in this patient most likely has which of the following mechanisms?
explanation: Benzodiazepines are first-line for alcohol withdrawal; they enhance the effect of postsynaptic GABA_A receptors (increase Cl⁻ channel opening frequency), reducing CNS hyperexcitability and preventing withdrawal seizures. Incorrect: Dopamine receptor blockade (antipsychotics), decreased dopamine transporter activity, serotonin reuptake inhibition, or glutamate actions are not first-line for alcohol withdrawal.
educational_objective: Treat alcohol withdrawal with benzodiazepines, which enhance GABA_A signaling to prevent seizures and agitation.

question: A 48-year-old woman with type 2 diabetes mellitus comes to the physician for a follow-up examination. Current medications are metformin and once-daily insulin. She travels frequently and works long hours. She says that her meals are usually fast food. She leads a sedentary lifestyle. She often forgets to measure her blood glucose concentration. Her last hemoglobin A1c was measured as 8.4%. Which of the following is the most appropriate action by the physician to help this patient improve her diabetic control?
explanation: Exploring barriers to diet adherence uses patient-centered counseling to identify practical obstacles (travel, work hours, fast food reliance) and readiness to change—often the most effective first step before altering meds. Incorrect: Creating an exercise plan or increasing insulin dose without understanding barriers, checking glucose or ordering microalbumin now, or reflexively referring out is less effective for behavior change.
educational_objective: Use motivational interviewing to elicit and address barriers before changing therapy in patients with poor adherence.

question: A 19-year-old man who is a college freshman comes to the office because of a 4-day history of tender, swollen glands. He also has a 6-day history of fever, malaise, and decreased appetite. His temperature is 38.7°C (101.7°F). Physical examination shows swelling of the parotid glands. Which of the following infectious agents is the most likely cause of these findings?
explanation: Classic painful parotitis with fever in a young adult strongly suggests mumps (paramyxovirus); it can be accompanied by orchitis and aseptic meningitis. Incorrect: EBV causes exudative pharyngitis and posterior cervical LAD; hepatitis B affects the liver; measles and rubella cause characteristic rashes rather than isolated parotitis.
educational_objective: Mumps classically presents with parotitis; consider in febrile young adults with swollen parotid glands.

question: A 38-year-old woman who is a veteran comes to the emergency department because of a 4-hour history of a sensation of tightness in her throat and swelling of her face, lips, and tongue. She has not had itching. During the past 3 weeks, she has had two similar, milder episodes that resolved without treatment within 24 to 72 hours. Six weeks ago, she began treatment with an ACE inhibitor for hypertension. She has seasonal allergies. Her temperature is 37.1°C (98.8°F), pulse is 80/min, respirations are 20/min, and blood pressure is 138/81 mm Hg. Physical examination shows angioedema of the lips and tongue. There is no evidence of urticaria. Which of the following is the most likely cause of the angioedema in this patient?
explanation: ACE inhibitors increase bradykinin by blocking its breakdown, causing non-pitting angioedema without urticaria or pruritus. Incorrect: Histamine-mediated reactions usually present with urticaria/itching; leukotriene B4 and PGE2 are not primary mediators of ACEI angioedema.
educational_objective: ACE inhibitors can cause bradykinin-mediated angioedema that lacks urticaria.

question: A 58-year-old man comes to the physician because of a 6-month history of an enlarging mass in his left scrotum. Physical examination shows a soft, nontender, 2-cm mass in the left scrotum inferior to the inguinal canal; the right testis is normal. Scrotal ultrasonography is done; longitudinal color Doppler images through the mass are shown at rest (Baseline) and during a Valsalva maneuver. Based on the findings shown, there is abnormal dilation of which of the following?
explanation: A scrotal mass that enlarges with Valsalva and shows venous flow suggests a varicocele—dilation of the pampiniform plexus of veins. Incorrect: Testicular or cremasteric arteries are arterial and would not demonstrate this venous dilation pattern.
educational_objective: Varicoceles are dilations of the pampiniform plexus that increase with Valsalva.

question: A 48-year-old woman comes to the physician because of a 2-month history of fatigue and poor appetite; she has had a 3-kg (6.6-lb) weight loss during this period. Abdominal examination shows moderate splenomegaly. Laboratory studies show a leukocyte count of 185,000/mm3 (65% segmented neutrophils with 6% blasts and promyelocytes). Cytogenetic analysis of a bone marrow aspirate shows the presence of the Philadelphia (Ph1) chromosome in myelocytes. Which of the following mechanisms best accounts for the formation of the Philadelphia (Ph1) chromosome in this patient?
explanation: The Ph chromosome results from a reciprocal translocation (t(9;22))—an abnormal recombination event—creating the BCR-ABL fusion tyrosine kinase. Incorrect: Nondisjunction causes aneuploidy; sister chromatid exchange is between identical chromatids; transposon insertion is not the mechanism here.
educational_objective: The Philadelphia chromosome forms via reciprocal translocation (aberrant recombination) creating BCR-ABL.

question: A 2-year-old boy is brought to the physician because of failure to thrive. He also has had loose, fatty, foul-smelling stools and a cough during the past 2 weeks. He is at the 30th percentile for height and 10th percentile for weight. Physical examination shows no other abnormalities. Laboratory studies show steatorrhea and a sweat chloride concentration of 80 mmol/L. A chest x-ray shows hyperinflation. Sputum culture grows Haemophilus influenzae and Staphylococcus aureus. Secretion of which of the following substances is most likely to be decreased in this patient?
explanation: Cystic fibrosis causes thick secretions that obstruct pancreatic ducts, reducing secretion of pancreatic bicarbonate (and enzymes) leading to steatorrhea and failure to thrive. Incorrect: Gastric acid, glucagon, and intrinsic factor secretion are not primarily decreased in CF.
educational_objective: In CF, pancreatic duct obstruction decreases bicarbonate/enzyme secretion, causing malabsorption.

question: A 19-year-old man is admitted to the hospital 1 hour after he was involved in a motor vehicle collision in which he sustained fractures to the right clavicle, multiple ribs, and the left hip. He was traveling at 40 mph when he was thrown from his motorcycle and struck a tree. He did not lose consciousness. He has no history of serious illness and takes no medications. His temperature is 37.0°C (98.6°F), pulse is 92/min, respirations are 12/min, and blood pressure is 106/72 mm Hg. Examination shows abrasions over the neck, right shoulder, both sides of the rib cage, and left thigh. Cranial nerves are intact. Muscle strength is 5/5 in the left upper and right lower extremities. Muscle strength testing of the left lower extremity is limited by pain. Deep tendon reflexes are 1+ in the right biceps and brachioradialis and 2+ elsewhere. Sensation to cold and pinprick is decreased over the right shoulder. Mental status examination shows no abnormalities. A diagram of the site of the right shoulder injury (arrow) is shown. Further examination is most likely to show weakness of the right upper extremity during which of the following maneuvers?
explanation: Decreased sensation over the lateral shoulder implicates the axillary nerve (C5–C6); injury causes deltoid weakness—impaired shoulder abduction. Incorrect: Elbow extension (radial), finger abduction (ulnar), and wrist flexion (median/ulnar) are not axillary nerve functions.
educational_objective: Axillary nerve injury causes deltoid weakness, producing impaired shoulder abduction and loss of lateral shoulder sensation.

question: A 10-year-old boy is brought to the physician because of a 3-week history of nosebleeds and easy bruisability. His older brother has had similar episodes. He is at the 30th percentile for height and weight. Physical examination shows nasal and gingival bleeding and several ecchymoses over the trunk and upper and lower extremities in various stages of healing. Laboratory studies show a platelet count of 300,000/mm3 (N=150,000–400,000). Platelet adhesion testing shows a normal response to ristocetin, but aggregation does not occur in response to thrombin; platelet morphology is normal. Prothrombin time and activated partial thromboplastin time are within the reference ranges. A defect in which of the following is the most likely cause of the findings in this patient?

options.A: "Actually, it frequently takes much longer to arrive at a diagnosis of pancreatic cancer."
options.B: "I think all of the tests were done within a reasonable time frame."
options.C: "It must be very difficult to hear this news."
options.D: "The most important thing now is to find you a good oncologist."

explanation: Normal ristocetin (adhesion) with absent aggregation to agonists and normal platelet count/morphology indicates Glanzmann thrombasthenia (defective GpIIb/IIIa integrin), causing failure of platelet aggregation. Incorrect: vWF or GpIb defects impair ristocetin response; fibrinogen deficiency affects coagulation tests; factor VII affects PT.
educational_objective: Glanzmann thrombasthenia (GpIIb/IIIa deficiency) causes defective platelet aggregation with normal adhesion tests.

question: A previously healthy 45-year-old woman who works as a park ranger comes to the physician because of a 1-week history of shortness of breath, even at rest. She has lived in the mountains at 10,000 feet above sea level for 2 years; the physician's office is located at sea level. Her pulse is 85/min, respirations are 18/min, and blood pressure is 125/90 mm Hg. Physical examination while sitting upright shows jugular venous distention and 2+ pedal edema. During the past 2 years, which of the following has most likely decreased in this patient?
explanation: Chronic hypoxic pulmonary vasoconstriction at altitude leads to pulmonary hypertension, right ventricular hypertrophy, and a stiffer right ventricle—decreased RV diastolic compliance. Incorrect: R wave in V1 and RV wall thickness increase; hematocrit increases; P-wave changes are variable.
educational_objective: High-altitude pulmonary hypertension causes RV hypertrophy and decreased diastolic compliance.

question: A 25-year-old woman comes to the physician because of a 4-month history of cough and unintentional weight loss. Rhonchi are heard posteriorly over the right upper thorax. A chest x-ray shows an 8-cm cavity in the right upper lobe and hilar lymphadenopathy. Ziehl-Neelsen staining of an induced sputum specimen shows acid-fast bacilli. The patient begins treatment with four antimycobacterial drugs, including rifampin. Synthesis of which of the following components of the suspected pathogen is most likely directly inhibited by the rifampin in this patient's medication regimen?
explanation: Rifampin inhibits DNA-dependent RNA polymerase in mycobacteria, blocking RNA synthesis. Incorrect: It does not directly inhibit ATP generation, folate synthesis (sulfonamides/trimethoprim), or peptidoglycan synthesis (β-lactams, vancomycin).
educational_objective: Rifampin blocks bacterial DNA-dependent RNA polymerase, inhibiting RNA synthesis.

question: A 34-year-old man is brought to the emergency department 30 minutes after being hit by a motor vehicle while walking. His temperature is 36°C (96.8°F), pulse is 140/min, respirations are 24/min, and blood pressure is 90/60 mm Hg. During an exploratory laparotomy, a large laceration is found that includes the right and left lobes of the liver. Active bleeding is present. Compression of which of the following ligaments is most likely to decrease bleeding from the liver in this patient?
explanation: The Pringle maneuver clamps the hepatoduodenal ligament (portal triad: hepatic artery, portal vein, common bile duct) to control hepatic bleeding. Incorrect: Coronary, triangular, and falciform ligaments are peritoneal reflections without major inflow vessels; the gastrohepatic ligament contains gastric vessels, not the portal triad.
educational_objective: Control hepatic bleeding by compressing the hepatoduodenal ligament to occlude the portal triad (Pringle maneuver).

question: A 1-month-old boy is brought to the emergency department because of a 1-day history of fever and cough. His temperature is 38.2°C (100.8°F), pulse is 140/min, and respirations are 54/min. Physical examination shows intercostal retractions. Wheezes are heard in all lung fields. A blood culture grows coagulase-negative, catalase-positive, gram- positive cocci in clusters. Which of the following best represents the infectious agent in this patient's blood culture?
explanation: Coagulase-negative, catalase-positive, gram-positive cocci in clusters are Staphylococcus epidermidis, most often a skin contaminant in blood cultures. Incorrect: S. aureus is coagulase-positive; S. pneumoniae is a gram-positive diplococcus (α-hemolytic streptococcus), not clusters; S. sanguis is viridans streptococcus (chains).
educational_objective: Staphylococcus epidermidis is a common blood culture contaminant (coagulase-negative staphylococcus).

question: A new drug, Drug X, is being investigated to determine its pharmacokinetic properties in humans. A male participant who weighs 85 kg (187 lb) with 50 L of total body water begins treatment with an intravenous infusion of Drug X at the rate of 100 mg/h. This drug is known to distribute in total body water. The plasma concentrations of the drug are measured. Results show that the steady-state plasma concentration of Drug X is 50 mg/L. Based on this information, which of the following is the clearance rate of this drug in this man?

options.A: Extravasation of 131I from the brachiocephalic vein
options.D: Uptake of the 131I by the thymus

explanation: For IV infusion at steady state, Clearance = Infusion rate / Css = 100 mg/h ÷ 50 mg/L = 2 L/h. Incorrect: The provided answer choices do not match; Vd (50 L) does not change this steady-state clearance calculation.
educational_objective: At steady state during constant infusion, Cl = infusion rate ÷ steady-state concentration.

question: A 78-year-old woman is admitted to the intensive care unit because of diverticulitis complicated by Escherichia coli sepsis. Treatment with ciprofloxacin is started. Three days later, her serum creatinine concentration has increased from 0.7 mg/dL on admission to 1.3 mg/dL. Urinalysis shows muddy brown casts. The most likely cause of the findings in this patient is ischemia of which of the following structures?
explanation: Muddy brown granular casts indicate acute tubular necrosis, typically due to ischemia or nephrotoxins affecting tubular epithelial cells—classically proximal tubules and thick ascending limb. Incorrect: Bowman capsule, glomerulus, interstitium, and renal vein ischemia do not produce the ATN pattern with muddy brown casts.
educational_objective: Acute tubular necrosis from ischemia primarily injures tubular epithelial cells (proximal tubule/TAL).

question: A 34-year-old woman with myasthenia gravis comes to the emergency department because of a 2-day history of increasing weakness, shortness of breath, and abdominal cramping. Current medications are prednisone and pyridostigmine. Her temperature is 37°C (98.6°F), pulse is 45/min, and respirations are 25/min and shallow. Her voice is soft and hypernasal, and she coughs weakly when swallowing water. Breath and heart sounds are normal. Pulmonary testing shows inability to generate a normal negative inspiratory force during forced inspiration. The abdomen is soft and nontender, with increased bowel sounds. Muscle strength is 4/5 diffusely, with severe, continuous, and diffuse fasciculations. Deep tendon reflexes are sluggish, but symmetric. Which of the following is the most likely cause of this patient's weakness?
explanation: Bradycardia, increased bowel sounds, diffuse fasciculations, and weakness suggest cholinergic excess from pyridostigmine overdose (cholinergic crisis), not undertreatment. Incorrect: Aspiration pneumonia or Guillain-Barré do not explain muscarinic signs; insufficient prednisone does not cause cholinergic findings.
educational_objective: In MG, cholinergic crisis from excess acetylcholinesterase inhibitor causes muscarinic and nicotinic toxicity with weakness.

question: A 35-year-old woman comes to the office because she has had three first-trimester spontaneous abortions during the past 3 years. Physical examination shows no abnormalities. Laboratory studies show no endocrine abnormalities. Chromosomal analysis shows a paracentric inversion of the long arm of chromosome 1. Which of the following best describes this patient's risk for early spontaneous abortions and a liveborn child with aneuploidy? Risk for Early Risk for Liveborn Spontaneous Abortions Child With Aneuploidy

options.B: Eosinophilic infiltration into the gastric wall

explanation: Paracentric inversion carriers often form unbalanced gametes during meiosis, leading to nonviable conceptions and increased early miscarriages; liveborn aneuploidy risk is low because most unbalanced outcomes are not compatible with life. Incorrect: "Low" miscarriage risk or "high" liveborn aneuploidy do not fit paracentric inversion outcomes.
educational_objective: Paracentric inversions raise miscarriage risk but rarely result in liveborn aneuploidy.

question: A 12-year-old boy is brought to the office by his parents for genetic counseling because of a family history of genetic disorders. He has no symptoms or history of major medical illness. The patient's maternal grandfather died of Huntington disease at the age of 35 years. Genetic testing of the mother showed 19 triplet repeats on each huntingtin (HTT) allele (N=10–20). The patient's paternal grandfather had colon cancer at the age of 30 years, and the father had numerous colon polyps at the age of 20 years treated with a colectomy. Genetic testing of the father shows heterozygosity for a frame-shift mutation in the APC gene. Physical examination of the patient shows no abnormalities. Based on this patient's risk for genetic disease, it is most appropriate for the physician to order which of the following genetic tests at this time?
explanation: FAP (APC mutation) requires early surveillance and management in adolescence; predictive testing for APC is recommended in minors at risk. Incorrect: Predictive testing for adult-onset Huntington disease is not recommended in asymptomatic minors; HTT testing is unnecessary given the mother's normal repeat numbers.
educational_objective: For FAP, test at-risk minors (APC) early to guide timely surveillance and prophylaxis.

question: A 53-year-old woman comes to the office because of a 6-year history of stiffness and pain of her hands. She has difficulty buttoning her clothes because of the symptoms. She takes no medications. Physical examination shows the findings in the photograph. An abnormality of which of the following is most likely to confirm the diagnosis in this patient?
explanation: Symmetric hand stiffness with likely MCP/PIP involvement and deformities suggests rheumatoid arthritis; anti-CCP antibodies are highly specific. Incorrect: Antimitochondrial antibodies (PBC), HLA-DQ2 (celiac disease), and thrombopoietic precursors are unrelated to confirming RA.
educational_objective: Anti-CCP antibodies are highly specific for rheumatoid arthritis.

question: A 25-year-old man comes to the office because of a 4-hour history of irritability, restlessness, tremor, and palpitations. He is a known user of amphetamines. His pulse is 120/min, respirations are 25/min, and blood pressure is 150/100 mm Hg. Physical examination shows no abnormalities. The most likely cause of this patient's symptoms is sympathomimetic activity arising from which of the following?
explanation: Amphetamines increase synaptic norepinephrine and dopamine primarily by promoting presynaptic release and reversing transporters, producing tachycardia, hypertension, and agitation. Incorrect: Decreased metabolism/MAO activity or decreased/increased presynaptic receptor activation do not capture the principal mechanism here.
educational_objective: Amphetamines cause sympathomimetic toxicity by increasing presynaptic release of monoamines.

question: A 5-year-old girl is brought to the office by her mother because of a 6-hour history of bloody diarrhea. She is interactive and in no acute distress. Her blood pressure is 90/55 mm Hg. Abdominal examination shows normoactive bowel sounds. Stool cultures are obtained, and the patient's mother is advised to give the girl plenty of fluids. Five days later, the patient develops decreased urine output and is brought back to the office. Her blood pressure is now 135/88 mm Hg. Physical examination shows pallor. Laboratory studies show: Hemoglobin 8.5 g/dL (N=11–15) Hematocrit 26% (N=28%–45%) Platelet count 45,000/mm3 (N=150,000–400,000) Serum creatinine 3.3 mg/dL (N=0.3–0.7) Which of the following infectious agents is the most likely cause of these findings?

options.B: Inadequate concentration of oxygen through nasal cannula
options.C: Pulmonary arterial blood shunting directly into pulmonary veins

explanation: Correct: Escherichia coli (EHEC, Shiga-like toxin) after bloody diarrhea can cause hemolytic uremic syndrome (microangiopathic hemolytic anemia, thrombocytopenia, acute kidney injury, hypertension). Incorrect: Campylobacter causes inflammatory diarrhea but not classic HUS; rotavirus causes watery diarrhea; Yersinia pestis causes plague, not HUS.
educational_objective: EHEC infection can trigger HUS with anemia, thrombocytopenia, and renal failure after bloody diarrhea.

question: A 78-year-old woman is admitted to the hospital because of a 1-week history of jaundice. CT scan of the abdomen shows a mass suggestive of pancreatic cancer. Three hours later, the on-call physician enters the patient's room to discuss the prognosis and obtain consent for a biopsy scheduled for the next morning. On entering the room, the physician greets the patient and her husband. The physician then learns that the patient speaks only Mandarin. Her husband is fluent in Mandarin and English. The hospital interpreter is not available until tomorrow morning. The patient's husband appears anxious and insists that the physician speaks to him and allows him to serve as an interpreter for his wife. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?
explanation: Correct: Use of ad hoc family interpreters risks errors and breaches confidentiality; nonurgent discussions and consent should wait for a qualified medical interpreter. Incorrect: Allowing the husband as interpreter risks inaccuracies; consulting ethics is unnecessary when the appropriate plan is to use a professional interpreter.
educational_objective: For nonemergent care, use a trained medical interpreter rather than a family member.

question: A 4-year-old boy develops fever 3 weeks after being admitted to the hospital for induction chemotherapy for treatment of acute lymphoblastic leukemia. Chemotherapy medications are L-asparaginase, dexamethasone, doxorubicin, and vincristine. His temperature is 38.2°C (100.8°F), pulse is 122/min, and respirations are 24/min. Physical examination shows pallor, alopecia, and ulcerations over the gums. A central venous catheter with entry site in the right upper chest is present but has no surrounding erythema. A blood culture grows gram-negative rods after 36 hours. Which of the following underlying mechanisms is the most likely cause of this patient's susceptibility to infection?
explanation: Correct: Cytotoxic chemotherapy causes neutropenia, the major risk factor for invasive gram-negative infections. Incorrect: Terminal complement deficiency predisposes to Neisseria; hypogammaglobulinemia and T-cell defects predispose to encapsulated or opportunistic infections, not specifically this scenario.
educational_objective: Neutropenia from chemotherapy is the key driver of invasive bacterial infections in oncology patients.

question: A 65-year-old woman comes to the office for a follow-up examination 1 year after she underwent operative resection of the right colon and chemotherapy for stage III colon cancer. She reports fatigue. Physical examination shows no abnormalities. A staging CT scan of the chest and abdomen shows five new 2- to 3-cm masses in the liver and both lungs. This patient's cancer most likely spread to the lungs via which of the following structures?
explanation: Correct: Colon cancer spreads hematogenously to liver via portal veins; subsequent spread to lungs occurs through hepatic veins to the inferior vena cava and into the pulmonary circulation. Incorrect: IMV/left colic drain colon to portal system (liver), not lungs; pulmonary vein and SVC are not the pathway from liver; arteries are not the route of venous metastasis.
educational_objective: After liver involvement, colon cancer reaches the lungs via hepatic veins → inferior vena cava → pulmonary arteries.

question: A 6-year-old boy with acute lymphoblastic leukemia is brought to the office for a follow-up examination. He is receiving high-dose methotrexate therapy. A drug is added to the patient's medication regimen to decrease the toxicity of this therapy to normal cells. The beneficial effect of this new drug on normal cells is most likely achieved by bypassing the cellular requirement for which of the following enzymes?
explanation: Correct: Leucovorin (folinic acid) "rescues" normal cells by bypassing dihydrofolate reductase, replenishing reduced folate pools during high-dose methotrexate. Incorrect: Methionine synthase and thymidylate synthase are folate-dependent targets/steps but leucovorin specifically bypasses DHFR; pyruvate decarboxylase is unrelated.
educational_objective: Leucovorin rescue bypasses dihydrofolate reductase to mitigate methotrexate toxicity in normal tissues.

question: A 4082-g (9-lb) male newborn is delivered in the hospital at 40 weeks' gestation to a 28-year-old primigravid woman. Pregnancy and delivery were uncomplicated. Apgar scores were 8 and 9 at 1 and 5 minutes, respectively. Examination of the newborn's tongue shows a small blind pit in the midline located near the intersection of the anterior two-thirds and the posterior one-third. Ultrasonography of the neck shows a mass attached to the hyoid bone. Cells in the mass produce a hormone that binds to which of the following?
explanation: Correct: A thyroglossal duct cyst near the foramen cecum contains ectopic thyroid tissue; thyroid hormone acts via nuclear receptors. Incorrect: G protein–linked and ligand-gated ion channels mediate other hormones; σ receptors are unrelated.
educational_objective: Thyroid hormone acts via nuclear receptors; thyroglossal duct cysts may contain hormone-producing thyroid tissue.

question: An investigator is studying how mice respond to filarial parasitic infections. Mice deficient in a specific protein found in eosinophils (Group X) are compared with wild-type mice (Group Y). Biopsies of lymph nodes from Group X mice show more adult worms than lymph nodes from Group Y mice. Group X mice most likely lack which of the following?
explanation: Correct: Eosinophil major basic protein is toxic to helminths; its absence reduces worm killing. Incorrect: Lysozyme and defensins/cathelicidins are antimicrobial peptides more relevant to bacteria on mucosal surfaces.
educational_objective: Eosinophil major basic protein mediates helminthotoxicity in parasitic infections.

question: A 14-year-old girl is brought to the office by her mother because of a 3-month history of red bumps on her skin. The patient says the bumps are not itchy or painful but that she finds them embarrassing. She has no history of major medical illness and takes no medications. Her vital signs are within normal limits. Physical examination shows the findings in the photograph. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation: Correct: Multiple small, nonpruritic erythematous follicular papules are most consistent with folliculitis among the choices provided. Incorrect: Eczema and urticaria are typically pruritic; hidradenitis presents with painful nodules/abscesses in apocrine areas.
educational_objective: Folliculitis presents with follicular papules/pustules; pruritus or pain may be minimal or absent.

question: A 50-year-old man comes to the office because of a 2-month history of increasing daytime somnolence. He has obstructive sleep apnea for which he has only intermittently used a continuous positive airway pressure device. He is 170 cm (5 ft 7 in) tall and weighs 181 kg (400 lb); BMI is 63 kg/m2. His temperature is 37°C (98.6°F), pulse is 100/min, respirations are 12/min, and blood pressure is 135/80 mm Hg. Physical examination shows a gray-blue tinge to the lips, earlobes, and nail beds. Cardiac examination shows no other abnormalities. Arterial blood gas analysis on room air shows a pH of 7.31, PCO2 of 70 mm Hg, and PO2 of 50 mm Hg. Which of the following additional findings would be most likely in this patient?

options.A: Crackles on the left lung base and apex
options.B: Crackles on the right lung base
options.C: Decreased breath sounds on the left

explanation: Correct: Chronic hypoventilation and hypoxemia (obesity hypoventilation/OSA) lead to secondary polycythemia—elevated hemoglobin. Incorrect: Renal compensation raises (not lowers) serum bicarbonate; obesity reduces (not increases) total lung capacity.
educational_objective: Chronic hypoxemia from hypoventilation causes secondary polycythemia with increased hemoglobin.

question: An obese 35-year-old man comes to the office for a follow-up examination. He has chronic kidney disease and was told to keep a record of his meals until this follow-up visit. His daily diet consists of chocolate milk and a peanut butter sandwich for breakfast; pizza and cola for lunch; a chocolate bar as a snack; and a foot-long deli meat sandwich for dinner. He is 165 cm (5 ft 5 in) tall and weighs 113 kg (250 lb); BMI is 42 kg/m2. His pulse is 100/min, respirations are 23/min, and blood pressure is 155/100 mm Hg. Physical examination shows diaphoresis. Serum studies show a creatinine concentration of 4.1 mg/dL and phosphorus concentration of 6 mg/dL. Which of the following patterns is most likely in this patient? Parathyroid Hormone Serum Serum 1,25- Synthesis Calcium Dihydroxycholecalciferol

options.A: Deep venous thrombosis of the right common femoral vein

explanation: Correct: CKD with hyperphosphatemia → low calcitriol and hypocalcemia → secondary hyperparathyroidism (PTH up), calcium down, 1,25-(OH)₂-D down. Incorrect: Patterns with increased calcitriol or calcium don't match CKD mineral bone disorder.
educational_objective: CKD causes secondary hyperparathyroidism: ↑PTH, ↓calcium, and ↓1,25-(OH)₂-vitamin D.

question: A 60-year-old woman is nearing the completion of a half marathon. Because she experiences esophageal regurgitation, she does not drink any liquid during the race. This woman's physical state at the end of the race will most likely activate which of the following renal segments at this time?

options.A: Decreased production of α₄ tetramers compared with normal individuals
options.B: Decreased production of β₄ tetramers compared with normal individuals
options.C: Imbalance in the synthesis of the α- and β-globin gene products

explanation: Correct: Volume depletion increases proximal sodium/bicarbonate reabsorption, a process dependent on carbonic anhydrase activity in the proximal tubule. Incorrect: V2 (ADH) acts in the collecting duct, not proximal tubule; the ascending limb is water-impermeable; K⁺–H⁺ exchange is not the primary acute response to dehydration.
educational_objective: Volume depletion enhances proximal tubule carbonic anhydrase–dependent bicarbonate and sodium reabsorption.

question: An investigator is studying heart development in an experimental animal model. The animal model is genetically modified so that no cardiac neural crest cells develop. This animal model is most likely to have which of the following cardiac abnormalities?
explanation: Correct: Cardiac neural crest cells form the aorticopulmonary septum; defects cause conotruncal anomalies such as transposition of the great arteries. Incorrect: ASD and mitral stenosis arise from septum primum/secundum or endocardial cushions; coarctation is an arch defect.
educational_objective: Absent cardiac neural crest leads to conotruncal defects (eg, transposition of the great arteries).

question: A 78-year-old woman undergoes an outpatient laparoscopic cholecystectomy. During the procedure, ligation of the cystic artery is planned. It is most appropriate to ligate this artery at its junction with which of the following arteries?

options.A: Deactivation of the p53 tumor suppressor gene

explanation: Correct: The cystic artery most commonly arises from the right hepatic artery within Calot's triangle. Incorrect: Gastroduodenal, left gastric, or left hepatic are not the usual origins.
educational_objective: The cystic artery typically branches from the right hepatic artery and is ligated there during cholecystectomy.

question: A 32-year-old man comes to the office because of a 2-week history of fever and throat pain. He is 173 cm (5 ft 8 in) tall and weighs 63 kg (140 lb); BMI is 21 kg/m2.
